What this is about Almost all servers on the internet, many devices from Wi Fi routers to TVs and most tools for data analysis, machine learning and IT security run on Linux. If you want to work with them, you need a Linux to practice on. But most students' computers run Windows, and this Windows, with all the files on it, should stay intact. This chapter pursues one question How do you get a Linux of your own to practice on without putting Windows or its data at risk? There are three ways to do it. You can run Linux alongside Windows, you can operate it in a simulated computer, or you can start it from a USB stick. The chapter shows all three, explains what happens inside the computer along the way and says exactly where the risks lie and how to protect yourself against them. At the end, you have a running Linux and know why it works. How to work with this chapter. The sections build on each other, and every new term has its own subsection with an example. Expandable boxes contain background why something is the way it is and where it comes from and derivations; you do not need them to read on. Boxes marked “Caution” state rules that always apply to practical exercises. Try the exercises ★ to ★★★ yourself first; the solution expands right below each exercise.

Before you set up a Linux, you need to know what it actually is that you are setting up. This section clarifies what an operating system does, which part of it really controls the hardware, how ordinary programs get access to that part's services and what exactly the word “Linux” refers to. The operating system A laptop runs a browser, an editor, a music program and perhaps a program that is saving photos from a phone, all at the same time. All of them need the processor, the main memory, the SSD, the network and the screen. Someone has to share out this hardware and make sure that the browser does not accidentally overwrite the photos. And none of these programs should have to know exactly which SSD is installed. Figure 1 abb 1 shows where this task is handled in a layer of its own between the hardware and the programs you work with. The operating system lies as a layer between the hardware and the programs. The programs request services from it; only the operating system controls the hardware. The operating system is the software that manages a computer's hardware, makes it available to the other programs through uniform services and keeps the programs apart from one another. A program that runs under an operating system and performs a task for the user is called an application program , or program for short. Well known operating systems are Windows, macOS, Android and the Linux systems that this series is about. In the editor, you press Ctrl+S. The editor does not know whether the file ends up on an SSD, a USB stick or a network drive, and it does not need to know. It asks the operating system “Write these 2 000 characters to the file notiz.txt .” The operating system looks for free space on the storage device, writes the data, remembers where it is and reports to the editor whether it worked. If a second program saves another file at the same time, the operating system makes sure that the two write operations do not get in each other's way. ⁠ In short The operating system manages the hardware, offers services to the programs and keeps them apart from one another. The tasks of an operating system can be traced back to three ideas. ⁠ Abstraction. An SSD knows only numbered blocks of 512 or 4 096 bytes each. The operating system turns them into files with names and folders. Every program works with files, and only the operating system needs to know the blocks. ⁠ Sharing. A processor core can run only one program at any one time. The operating system switches back and forth between the programs many times per second, and each one gets a region of main memory of its own. This way, each program seems to have a computer of its own. ⁠ Protection. Because all accesses to the hardware go through the operating system, it can check whether a program is allowed to do something. A program that crashes then does not take the others down with it. The second idea is remarkable from a single set of hardware, the operating system creates the illusion of many machines. Two operating modes of the processor Protection works only if a program cannot simply get around it. After all, a malicious or faulty program could try to address the SSD itself instead of asking the operating system. Only the hardware can prevent this, namely the processor itself. Two levels of permission. You can picture the processor as a machine with a key switch. In one position, it may do everything; in the other, only what is harmless. You can switch over only in the “everything” position. A processor has at least two operating modes. In kernel mode , the running program may execute any instruction of the processor. In user mode , certain instructions are blocked, such as direct access to devices and setting which program may use which part of main memory. Such a blocked instruction is called a privileged instruction . If a program in user mode attempts a privileged instruction, the processor does not execute it it interrupts the program and hands control to the operating system. A program in user mode contains an instruction that is supposed to send data directly to the SSD. The processor recognizes the blocked instruction and does not execute it, but jumps into the operating system instead. The operating system determines that the program has tried something forbidden and terminates it. The SSD has noticed nothing of the attempt. ⁠ In short The processor itself ensures that ordinary programs cannot touch the hardware directly. The kernel If everything is allowed only in kernel mode, there must be a part of the operating system that runs in this mode. This part is so important that it has a name of its own. The kernel the core of the system is the part of the operating system that runs in kernel mode. It controls the hardware directly, divides the processor and main memory among the programs, manages the files and checks for every access whether it is allowed. All other programs run in user mode. The drivers also belong to the kernel pieces of software that can control a particular device, such as a particular network card or a particular SSD. Other parts of an operating system, by contrast, for example the window in which you type commands or the programs for copying files, run in user mode like any application program. A video program reads a file, converts the stored data into images and displays them. The kernel reads the file, using the SSD's driver. In this example, the video program converts the data into images itself, in user mode, because this requires no devices, only arithmetic instructions. The finished image is again brought to the screen by the kernel, using the graphics driver. ⁠ In short The kernel is the only part of the system that is allowed to control the hardware directly. The system call A program in user mode is not allowed to touch the SSD, but it still has to read and write files. So it needs a way to ask the kernel for a service without entering kernel mode itself. A counter with fixed forms. As at the counter of a government office, you cannot go behind the counter; you fill in one of the forms provided and hand it through. The office checks the application and either handles it or rejects it a picture, not a mechanism . Figure 2 abb 2 shows the mechanism. A program gets to the hardware only through a system call it states the number of the desired service and the details for it, a special processor instruction switches to kernel mode, and the kernel checks and carries out the request. The processor blocks any direct access from user mode. A system call is a request from a program to the kernel to perform a particular service, for example to open a file, read data or provide memory. The program puts the number of the service and the necessary details in place and executes a special processor instruction. This instruction switches to kernel mode and jumps to a location in the kernel that the kernel itself set when the computer started. The kernel checks the request, handles it, switches back to user mode and gives the program the result. Linux has a tool called strace that records every system call of a program. Here it is attached to the program gnucat , the classic version of a program that displays the contents of a file; the file shown is the one that contains the computer's name. You can see the calls for opening, reading, writing and closing The first line asks the kernel to open the file /etc/hostname for reading; it replies with the number 3, under which the program then refers to the file. The second line reads up to 262 144 bytes; the kernel delivers 6 bytes, the word labor and a line end. The third line writes these 6 bytes to the output with the number 1, which is the window in which the program runs. The second read attempt delivers 0 bytes the file has come to an end. Finally, the program closes the file. In total, this tiny program makes 114 system calls; the others mainly serve to load parts of the program at startup. ⁠ In short Programs get hardware services only by asking the kernel for them through a system call. A system call raises the processor's privileges. If the program could freely choose the address in the kernel, it could jump into the middle of a kernel function, right behind the point where the kernel checks the permission, and would thus have all privileges. That is why, at startup, when the processor is running in kernel mode anyway, the kernel sets a fixed entry point in the processor every system call jumps exactly there. A program can only name the number of a service. At the entry point, the kernel itself looks up in its table of services which kernel function belongs to this number, and it checks the details before carrying it out. Setting the entry point is itself a privileged instruction, and the table lies in a memory region that programs in user mode are not allowed to write to. The only way into kernel mode thus leads through a gate that the kernel itself has built and guards. Linux People use the word “Linux” for two different things sometimes a whole system with windows and programs, sometimes only one very specific part of it. For this chapter, the difference matters. Linux is a kernel. Linus Torvalds began it in 1991 as a student in Helsinki; today it is maintained by thousands of developers, at companies, at universities and in their spare time. Its source code is freely available under the GNU General Public License GPL , version 2. In the strict sense, “Linux” refers only to this kernel; in everyday language, people often mean the whole system built on it. The same Linux kernel, slightly adapted in each case, is found in very different devices in most servers on the internet, in Android smartphones, in many Wi Fi routers and TVs and in the Linux systems for PCs. So an Android phone and an Ubuntu laptop both use Linux as their kernel, but they have almost no other programs in common. ⁠ In short Strictly speaking, Linux is only the kernel of an operating system. The GPL allows anyone to use, modify and pass on the source code of the kernel, even for money. In return, it requires that anyone who passes on a modified version also makes its source code available under the same license. That is why any company and any group can build a system of its own around the kernel, and improvements flow back into the common kernel. The programs that a Linux system needs around the kernel come to a large extent from the GNU project, which Richard Stallman had started in 1983 to create a free operating system; at the beginning of the 1990s, the only thing it still lacked was a kernel. That is why some people speak of “GNU/Linux”. The distribution A kernel on its own cannot talk to you. It has no window into which you could type something, no programs for copying files and no browser. For a usable system to come about, someone has to assemble thousands of programs to match the kernel, coordinate them with one another and supply them with bug fixes for years. A distribution is a complete operating system that a vendor or a community assembles from the Linux kernel, tools, application programs and default settings and maintains as a whole. Every distribution comes with a package manager a program with which you install, update and remove software from the distribution's sources. Chapter 9 explains how it works. Table 1 tab 1 lists four distributions that appear in this series. Table 1 Four distributions. All of them use the Linux kernel, but they differ in their selection of programs, in their package manager and in how long a release is supported. | Distribution | Maintained by | Characteristics | | | | | | Debian | a worldwide community of volunteers | very stable, basis of many other distributions | | Ubuntu | the company Canonical together with a community | builds on Debian, widely used, well documented; this series uses Ubuntu 26.04 LTS | | Fedora | a community, supported by the company Red Hat | brings new software early, basis for Red Hat Enterprise Linux | | Kali Linux | the company OffSec | builds on Debian, contains hundreds of tools for security testing; its publishers explicitly advise Linux newcomers against it | ⁠ In short Linux is the kernel; a distribution turns it into a complete system. For a practice system, three things count that it runs on almost any computer, that you can find help when there are problems and that it is maintained for a long time. Ubuntu is one of the most widely used distributions for desktops and servers, its documentation is freely available, and Windows comes with its own way to a Linux, which sets up Ubuntu by default. Because Ubuntu builds on Debian, almost everything you learn here also applies to Debian and Kali Linux. Releases and long term support A distribution keeps appearing in new releases. If you set up a practice system, you have to choose one, and with Ubuntu, the version number already tells you almost everything you need to know. An Ubuntu release is named after the year and month in which it appeared 26.04 appeared in April 2026. In addition, each release has a code name; 26.04 is called “Resolute Raccoon”. Every two years in April, an LTS release Long Term Support appears, for which Canonical supplies security fixes and bug fixes for five years. In between, interim releases appear, which are supported for only nine months. A number like 26.04.1 denotes a point release the same system with the fixes collected up to that point and new installation media. Ubuntu 26.04 LTS appeared on 23 April 2026 and is supported until April 2031; its first point release, 26.04.1, appeared on 27 August 2026. Ubuntu 26.10 appeared in October 2026 and is an interim release; it is supported until July 2027. Ubuntu 24.04 LTS, the previous long term release, is still supported until April 2029. This series uses 26.04 LTS. ⁠ In short For a practice system, you choose the current LTS release, because it receives fixes for five years. New releases bring new programs, but also new bugs and changes in how things are operated. Anyone who runs a server, a lab or a course wants a system that behaves the same way for years and still gets every newly discovered security vulnerability closed. An LTS release separates the two for five years, it receives fixes, but no new features that could change anything. For even longer support, Canonical offers an add on called Ubuntu Pro. Exercises for Section 1 stufe 1 Classify each activity Does it run in user mode or in kernel mode? Is a system call involved? A spreadsheet program calculates the average of 1 000 numbers that are already in main memory. The spreadsheet program saves the spreadsheet. The SSD's driver writes the blocks of the spreadsheet to the SSD. A browser asks for 200 MB of additional main memory. a User mode, no system call. The numbers are already in the program's main memory, and adding and dividing are ordinary arithmetic instructions that every program may execute. The kernel is not involved. b The spreadsheet program itself runs in user mode, but saving means getting data onto a storage device, and the program is not allowed to do that itself. It makes system calls, for example to open the file, to write and to close it. The actual work is then done by the kernel in kernel mode. c Kernel mode. The driver is part of the kernel and addresses the device directly. It does not make a system call itself; instead, it carries out the request that came in with a system call in b . d System call. Which program may use which part of main memory is set only by the kernel; this is a privileged operation. So the browser asks the kernel via a system call, the kernel sets up the memory in kernel mode and tells the browser where it is. Is the statement true? Justify each answer in one sentence. “Android is a Linux.” “Ubuntu and Kali Linux use the same kernel, so they are the same system.” “If you install Linux, you install a distribution.” “The package manager is part of the kernel.” a In the strict sense, it is true Android uses the Linux kernel. But Android is not a Linux distribution like Ubuntu, because around the kernel there are almost exclusively other programs. If you mean “Linux” in the everyday sense, that is, a system with a terminal and the usual tools, then Android is something different. b False. Both use the Linux kernel, but each builds it itself in its own version, and everything around the kernel, the selection of programs, the default settings and the maintenance, differs. The same kernel alone does not make the same system. c True. A kernel alone is not usable; what you download and install is always a distribution with a kernel, tools and a package manager. d False. The package manager is an ordinary program of the distribution and runs in user mode. When it installs files, it makes system calls for this like any other program. A program in user mode tries three things, one after another 1 to send data directly to the network card, 2 to change the entry point for system calls or the table of services so that a system call jumps into its own code, 3 to make a system call with a number that does not exist at all. What happens in each case, and why can the program not gain control of the computer by any of the three routes? 1 Direct access to the network card is a privileged instruction. In user mode, the processor does not execute it; instead, it interrupts the program and hands over to the kernel, and the kernel terminates the program. 2 Setting the entry point is a privileged instruction; such an attempt ends the same way as 1 . The table of services is in a memory region of the kernel that programs in user mode are not allowed to write to; this attempt, too, is interrupted by the processor. The kernel set up both at startup in kernel mode, and nobody can change them from user mode. 3 The system call itself is allowed. In the process, the processor jumps to the fixed entry point of the kernel, not to a location that the program chooses. There, the kernel looks up the number in its table, finds no service for it and returns an error code to the program. The program keeps running but has achieved nothing. The reason for all three There are exactly two ways to get into kernel mode, namely an interruption, for example when the processor traps a blocked instruction, or a system call, and both end up at locations that the kernel itself has set. Everything with which you could change these locations or reach the hardware directly is blocked in user mode. A point release is not a release of its own If you install 26.04 and update it, you afterward have the same state as with 26.04.1.

There are three proven ways to get a Linux to practice on under Windows. This section sets them side by side, helps you choose with a decision tree and explains what is at the end of each way a window into which you type commands. The three ways at a glance A Linux to practice on should do two things it should be a real Linux on which everything the series shows works, and it should not put Windows and your files at risk. Figure 3 abb 3 shows the three ways that do both, each in its own way. Three ways to a Linux on a Windows computer. WSL 2 runs Linux invisibly alongside Windows, a virtual machine simulates a whole computer, and from the live USB stick, the computer itself starts a Linux while Windows rests untouched on the disk. ⁠ WSL 2. In the background, Windows starts a small, invisible computer within the computer, in which a Linux runs. You open a window and work in Linux while the familiar Windows programs keep running alongside it. This is the fastest way, and it is enough for programming, data analysis and all exercises on the command line. ⁠ Virtual machine. A program like VirtualBox simulates a complete computer, in which you install Linux as on a real PC. This computer is separate from the real one; you can save its state and bring it back at any time. This is the way for labs in which you are allowed to break things. ⁠ Live USB stick. You write a Linux onto a USB stick and start the computer from it. Then Linux runs directly on the real hardware, and Windows rests untouched on the internal disk. After you switch off, everything is as before. This is the first real Linux practice on your own device; however, it requires the most care, because you write to a storage device and start the computer in an unfamiliar way. Table 2 tab 2 compares the three ways. Table 2 The three ways compared. | | WSL 2 | virtual machine | live USB stick | | | | | | | runs | alongside Windows | in a window under Windows | instead of Windows | | good for | command line, programming, data analysis | labs, trying things out with a way back | experiencing Linux on real hardware | | needs | Windows 10 version 2004 or later, or Windows 11 | enough memory and disk space | a USB stick of 8 GB or more | | limits | its own small network, no direct access to USB devices | slower than the real computer | without an add on, everything is gone after switching off | | risk for Windows | very low | very low | low if you heed the warnings | ⁠ In short WSL 2 is the fastest way, the virtual machine is the lab and the live USB stick is real Linux on real hardware. The decision tree Which way is right depends on what you plan to do with Linux. The decision tree in Figure 4 abb 4 asks two questions. Which way fits? If you need Linux for programming, for data analysis or for practicing on the command line, you end up with WSL 2. Next to each way, you can see which sections of this chapter it needs; Sections 1 and 2 apply to all of them. The ways do not exclude one another. Many people work with WSL 2 day to day and keep a virtual machine ready for experiments in which something is allowed to go wrong. If you want to see a Linux on real hardware for the first time, start it once from the stick, even if you otherwise use WSL 2. Lea wants to program in Python and analyze data; her laptop has Windows 11. WSL 2 is right for her she does not have to restart anything, and her files can be reached from Windows and from Linux. Jonas wants to examine network traffic between two computers without disturbing his home network, and in doing so, he also wants to try out settings that can damage the system. He needs a virtual machine. Mira wants to know whether her laptop gets along with Linux at all, whether Wi Fi, graphics and sound work. She starts Linux from the USB stick, because only then does it run on her real hardware. ⁠ In short For programming and the command line, you choose WSL 2, for labs a virtual machine and for real Linux on real hardware the live USB stick. The three ways lie on a scale between two goals that contradict each other. The closer to the real hardware a Linux runs, the more real the experience on the live stick, Linux controls the network card, the graphics and the USB ports itself. The more software lies between Linux and the hardware, the better it is isolated and the easier it is to undo mistakes. WSL 2 sacrifices some isolation for convenience, because it shares files with Windows. Each of the three ways is a different compromise between the two goals. The terminal All three ways end at the same place at a window into which you type commands. Most of the work in this series happens there, because a typed command is exact, repeatable and can be written down. A terminal is a program with a window into which you type commands as text and in which the computer's responses appear as text. When it is ready, it shows a prompt at the beginning of the line. In a Linux terminal, the prompt looks something like this student@labor ~ for Linux and PS for Windows. Type the few commands in this chapter exactly as they appear and then press Enter. Chapter 2 explains what exactly a command is and how it is structured. The command cat /etc/os release displays the contents of a file in which every distribution enters its name and its version. This is how Ubuntu 26.04.1 replies The line VERSION contains the point release and the code name from subsection 1.7 betriebssystem kernel und distribution.html stufe 1 7 , and ID LIKE=debian says which distribution Ubuntu builds on. This output is the same with each of the three ways, because the file belongs to the distribution. ⁠ In short The terminal is the window in which you talk to the system in text form; at the end of each way, you open one. Exercises for Section 2 stufe 2 Use the decision tree to choose a way, and justify it in two sentences. Tom has a Windows 11 laptop and wants to learn Python next semester. In an IT security course, Sara wants to try out settings that can damage a system, and afterward start cleanly again each time. Ali is considering switching his old laptop entirely to Linux and wants to see beforehand whether Wi Fi and graphics work. And you? Which way do you choose, and why? a WSL 2. Tom needs a Linux for the command line and for programming, not for the hardware and not for a lab. With Windows 11, WSL 2 is set up in a few minutes, and he can use Windows and Linux at the same time. b A virtual machine. Sara wants to try out things that can damage a system and afterward start cleanly again; that is exactly what a snapshot provides. In the process, the VM is separated from the host. c The live USB stick. Only with it does Linux run directly on Ali's real hardware and have to control Wi Fi and graphics itself. In a VM or in WSL 2, Linux would see only virtual devices and would reveal nothing about the real hardware. d There is no wrong answer here, as long as the justification matches the question in the decision tree. If you read this series for programming or data analysis, take WSL 2; if you follow the Cybersecurity series, also set up a VM and start once from the stick. PS C \Users\anna\Documents is PowerShell on Windows; it is currently working in the folder C \Users\anna\Documents . If the chapter shows and the space after it are already part of the prompt.

Two of the three ways rest on the same idea a program simulates a whole computer in which a second operating system runs. This section explains how this works, why the guest does not notice, how you capture such a computer in a particular state and how it gets onto the internet without being reachable from there. The virtual machine A second PC for trying things out would be ideal you could install anything on it, change any setting and, in the worst case, start over without your own computer taking any harm. Such a second PC can also be built in software. Figure 5 abb 5 shows the idea. The real computer runs Windows as usual. Within it, a program provides a second, simulated computer with its own processor, main memory, hard disk and network card. Linux runs in this simulated computer as if it were sitting on real hardware. A virtual machine. The hypervisor, a program on the host, gives the guest simulated hardware. The guest kernel controls this virtual hardware as if it were real; its hard disk is actually a file on the host's SSD. A virtual machine VM is a computer simulated by software, with its own processor, main memory, storage devices and network card. It runs a complete operating system with its own kernel, which behaves as if it were running on real hardware. A laptop has 8 processor cores, 16 GB of memory and a 512 GB SSD. A VM for Ubuntu gets 2 cores, 6 GB of memory and a 25 GB hard disk of this. For the Ubuntu in the VM, there are only these 2 cores, these 6 GB and these 25 GB; it does not see the rest of the laptop. On the laptop, the VM's 25 GB hard disk is a single file that is initially only as large as the data actually stored in it. ⁠ In short A virtual machine is a computer made of software in which a whole operating system runs. Host and guest As soon as two operating systems run on one computer, you need names to tell them apart. The host is the real computer with the operating system under which the virtual machine runs. The guest is the operating system that runs in the virtual machine. A laptop with Windows 11 runs two virtual machines, one with Ubuntu 26.04 and one with Debian. Windows 11 is the host; Ubuntu and Debian are two guests. If the Debian guest crashes, Windows and the Ubuntu guest keep running, because each guest has its own kernel in its own virtual machine. ⁠ In short The host is the real computer, the guest is the system in the VM. The hypervisor Some program has to provide the virtual hardware, allot the guest a share of the real hardware and make sure that it does not get more. A hypervisor is the software that creates and runs virtual machines. It allots them processor time, main memory and storage devices, simulates their devices and separates them from one another and from the host. For Windows computers, these are the main hypervisors to consider VirtualBox from Oracle, open source and free of charge; VMware Workstation Pro , free of charge for everyone since November 2024; Hyper V from Microsoft, which is included in the Pro, Enterprise and Education editions of Windows 10 and 11, but not in Windows Home; and QEMU , an open source hypervisor that is used mainly under Linux. This chapter sets up a VM with VirtualBox. ⁠ In short The hypervisor builds the virtual machines and watches over them. A hypervisor like VirtualBox is an ordinary program that runs under Windows and uses its kernel to access the hardware. It is called a type 2 hypervisor . A type 1 hypervisor , by contrast, starts directly on the hardware, before any operating system, and all operating systems run on top of it. Hyper V is such a type 1 hypervisor. When it is switched on, even Windows itself no longer runs directly on the hardware, but in a special area above the hypervisor, which Microsoft calls the root partition; there, however, it is the only system with direct access to the devices. This is not an exotic case. The hypervisor itself, on which Hyper V is built, is also included in Windows Home; only the programs with which you create VMs of your own are missing there. Many Windows computers switch on this Microsoft hypervisor for security features and for WSL 2 without the user noticing. If it is running, VirtualBox uses it as its foundation instead of accessing the hardware directly itself. Hardware virtualization The guest kernel is an ordinary Linux kernel. It wants to run in kernel mode and execute privileged instructions, for example to set where a system call jumps or to address a device. But if it really ran in the kernel mode of the real processor, it could control the whole real machine, and the hypervisor would no longer have any say. How the guest runs fast and is still locked in. The way out is the same as with the system call in subsection 1.4 betriebssystem kernel und distribution.html stufe 1 4 , only one level lower. The guest kernel runs directly on the processor, instruction by instruction, and therefore almost as fast as on real hardware. However, the processor runs it in a separate operating mode for guests. Settings that the guest kernel makes in this mode apply only to its VM. As soon as it wants to do something that would affect the real machine, such as addressing a device, the processor stops it and hands control to the hypervisor. The hypervisor looks at what the guest wanted, carries it out on the virtual hardware and lets the guest continue. The guest notices nothing of this. Hardware virtualization is an extension of the processor with which a hypervisor lets guest systems run directly on the processor and itself gets control as soon as a guest wants to do something that would affect the real machine. At Intel it is called VT x Virtualization Technology , at AMD it is called AMD V. All of today's PC processors have it; on some computers, however, it is switched off at the factory and must be switched on in the computer's basic settings. On Windows, open Task Manager Ctrl+Shift+Esc , select “Performance” on the left and then “CPU”. At the bottom right, it says “Virtualization Enabled” or “Disabled”. If it says “Enabled”, both ways with a VM are possible. The command systeminfo in PowerShell gives a second indication. If a Microsoft hypervisor is already running on the computer, for example because WSL 2 is set up, its long output contains the line “Hyper V Requirements A hypervisor has been detected.” In that case, hardware virtualization is switched on anyway, because without it, no hypervisor would run. ⁠ In short With hardware virtualization, a guest kernel runs directly on the processor, but everything that would affect the real machine ends up with the hypervisor. Without a separate operating mode for guests, a hypervisor has only one option it lets the guest kernel run in user mode and traps its privileged instructions. This method, “execute directly, trap privileged instructions”, works only if every instruction that can change the state of the machine or depends on it is actually trapped in user mode. Gerald Popek and Robert Goldberg formulated this condition precisely in 1974. The x86 processors of PCs did not meet it for a long time about seventeen instructions simply behaved differently in user mode instead of triggering a trap. One example is the instruction POPF , which among other things determines whether interrupts from devices are allowed; in user mode, it silently ignores this part. A guest kernel that uses it would thus get a wrong result, and the hypervisor would learn nothing about it. Early hypervisors therefore had to rewrite the guest's code before running it. Since 2005 and 2006, Intel and AMD have provided a separate operating mode for guests, in which the processor passes exactly the necessary instructions on to the hypervisor. The snapshot The greatest advantage of a VM for a lab is that you can undo mistakes. You capture the state before you try something out and return to it afterward, no matter what you have done in the meantime. Figure 6 abb 6 shows how this works for the VM's hard disk without the hypervisor having to copy the whole disk. How a snapshot captures the hard disk of a VM. The previous image file is frozen; all later write accesses go to a new file, the differencing image. When reading, the hypervisor looks there first and otherwise in the base image. Returning to the snapshot throws the differencing image away. A snapshot is a saved state of a virtual machine to which you can return at any time. It comprises the settings of the VM and the contents of all its virtual hard disks; if you take it while the VM is running, it also contains the contents of its main memory. After installing Ubuntu in the VM, you create a snapshot named “sauber” German for “clean” . Then you try out settings, accidentally delete important system files, and the VM no longer starts. You return to the snapshot “sauber” the VM is exactly as it was directly after the installation. A file that you created after the snapshot has disappeared too, because it was stored in the discarded differencing image. ⁠ In short A snapshot freezes the state of a VM, and restoring it discards everything that came afterward. A snapshot copies nothing. The hypervisor merely declares the previous image file unchangeable and creates an empty new file, in which from now on it records every block that is written; the method is called copy on write . The differencing image therefore grows only as much as the guest actually changes. Several snapshots in a row result in a chain of such files. If you delete a snapshot without returning to it, the hypervisor has to merge its changes into the neighboring file; with large changes, this can take a while and temporarily need a lot of space. The virtual network NAT A VM should be able to get onto the internet, for example to download updates. On the other hand, nobody from outside should be able to get at the practice system, on which you may be trying out something insecure at that very moment. Like a router at home. Every device in a network has a number under which others reach it, its address . At home, your laptop and phone have addresses in a small private network that are not valid on the internet. The router sends their requests to the internet under its own address, remembers which device asked and passes the reply on to that device. A request that comes from outside without any device inside having started it cannot be assigned to anyone by the router. Figure 7 abb 7 shows that a hypervisor can play exactly this role for its VM. NAT mode. The VM has an address in a small network that exists only between it and the hypervisor. The hypervisor sends its connections out under the host's address and passes the replies back. A connection that starts from outside does not reach the VM. In NAT mode Network Address Translation , the hypervisor works like a router for the VM. The VM has an address of its own in a private network that exists only between it and the hypervisor. The hypervisor forwards the VM's connections under the host's address and passes the replies back to the VM. Connections that start from outside do not reach the VM as long as you do not set up forwarding. An Ubuntu VM in VirtualBox runs in NAT mode; this is the default, and the VM usually gets the address 10.0.2.15. From inside the VM, you can open web pages and download updates, because the VM starts these connections itself. A phone on the same Wi Fi network, on the other hand, cannot reach a web server in the VM it does not know the address 10.0.2.15, and even a request to the laptop could not be assigned to anyone by the hypervisor. ⁠ In short In NAT mode, the VM gets out onto the network, but nobody gets in from outside. The protection is a side effect of the translation. So that the hypervisor can deliver a reply to the right VM, it keeps a table Which VM started which connection to which destination? When a packet comes from outside, it searches this table. If no VM started the connection, there is no entry, and the packet has no destination. Besides NAT, VirtualBox has other networking modes, in which a VM is connected differently to the host, to other VMs or to the home network; the Cybersecurity series covers which of them are suitable for an isolated practice lab. For a first Linux to practice on, NAT is the right choice. Exercises for Section 3 stufe 3 On Windows, collect four pieces of information about your computer. You do not change anything in the process. The edition and version of Windows Settings System About, section “Windows specifications”. The installed memory in the same place under “Device specifications”. The free space on drive C , in File Explorer under “This PC”. Whether hardware virtualization is switched on, as in the example in subsection 3.4 stufe 3 4 . In a VM, Ubuntu 26.04 needs at least 6 GB of memory and 25 GB of space. Is your computer sufficient for this if Windows is to keep at least 8 GB for itself alongside the VM? Is Hyper V available to you? The values depend on your computer. This is how you evaluate them ⁠ Memory. The VM needs 6 GB, and Windows is to keep 8 GB, so 14 GB together. With 16 GB, that is enough; with 8 GB, it is not, and then WSL 2 is the better way. ⁠ Space on C . The VM needs 25 GB, the image another 6.5 GB. With less than about 35 GB free, it gets tight. ⁠ Virtualization. If Task Manager says “Enabled”, everything is ready. If it says “Disabled”, the setting must be switched on in the firmware; Section 7 eine virtuelle maschine mit virtualbox.html stufe 7 shows how. ⁠ Hyper V. If “Windows specifications” lists a Pro, Enterprise or Education edition, you can use Hyper V; with Windows Home, you cannot. VirtualBox and WSL 2 run on all editions. For comparison, this chapter's test computer Windows 11 Home, 63.5 GB of memory. Memory and space are more than enough; Hyper V as a feature of its own does not exist on Home. Nevertheless, Microsoft's hypervisor runs on this computer systeminfo reports “A hypervisor has been detected”, because a security feature of Windows and WSL 2 use it. A guest kernel wants to a double a number in its VM's main memory, b set the location in its kernel to which a system call jumps, c write a block to its hard disk. Who does the work in each case, the processor directly or the hypervisor, and for whom does the result apply? Why would it be dangerous if the guest kernel were allowed to carry out b itself in the real kernel mode? a The processor directly. Doubling a number in the VM's main memory is an ordinary arithmetic instruction on memory that the hypervisor has assigned to the VM anyway. It runs without a detour, and that is why the VM is almost as fast as real hardware. b The setting applies only to the guest. In the operating mode for guests, the processor keeps a separate set of such settings for each guest; depending on the processor and the hypervisor, it makes the setting there directly, or it stops the guest and hands over to the hypervisor, which manages the setting for the guest. In both cases, system calls of the programs in the guest end up at the guest kernel, and the host's setting remains untouched. c The hypervisor. A write access to a device is privileged. The hypervisor traps it and writes the block into the image file of the virtual hard disk; as a type 2 hypervisor, it uses a system call of the host for this. If the guest kernel were allowed to carry out b in the real kernel mode, it would overwrite the entry point of the real processor. Then the system calls of all programs, including the programs of the host, would end up in its code, and it would have the whole machine in its hands. This is exactly what hardware virtualization prevents. A VM goes through the following steps in order install Ubuntu; snapshot “A”; create file x.txt ; snapshot “B”; create file y.txt ; delete x.txt ; back to “B”; create file z.txt ; back to “A”. Which of the three files exist at the end? How many differencing images did the hypervisor create along the way, and which ones did it discard? At the end, none of the three files exists. The way there, with the model from Figure 6 abb 6 A snapshot freezes the current image and creates a new differencing image; restoring discards the current differencing image and creates a new, empty one on top of the snapshot's state. Snapshot “A” The base image with the freshly installed Ubuntu is frozen, and differencing image 1 is created. x.txt is written to differencing image 1. Snapshot “B” Differencing image 1 is frozen and from now on belongs to “B”; differencing image 2 is created. Creating y.txt and deleting x.txt both in differencing image 2. Back to “B” Differencing image 2 is discarded, and differencing image 3 is created on top of the state of “B”. Now x.txt exists again, y.txt does not. z.txt is written to differencing image 3. Back to “A” Differencing image 3 is discarded, and differencing image 4 is created directly on top of the base image. The state is the one directly after the installation none of the three files. So four differencing images were created and two were discarded numbers 2 and 3 . Number 1 is kept, because snapshot “B” still exists; you could return to it at any time and would find x.txt there. A VM runs in VirtualBox in NAT mode. Does it work, and why or why not ? a The VM downloads updates from the internet. b A laptop on the same Wi Fi network calls up a web page offered by a program in the VM. c The VM opens a web page offered by a program on a phone on the same Wi Fi network. a Works. The VM starts the connection itself; the hypervisor sends it on under the host's address, remembers the connection and passes the replies back. b Does not work. The connection starts from outside. The other laptop does not know the address of the VM, and even a request to the host could not be assigned to any VM by the hypervisor, because none of them started it. Only a configured forwarding would change that. c Works. Here, too, the VM starts the connection; to the phone, it looks as if the laptop were asking. Whether the destination is on the internet or on your own Wi Fi network makes no difference.

The quickest way to a Linux under Windows is WSL 2. This section explains what WSL 2 is, namely a small virtual machine that Windows manages itself, how to set it up and check it, how Windows and Linux get at each other's files and where the limits of this way lie. The Windows Subsystem for Linux For work on the command line, you do not want a separate window with a whole second computer, but a Linux terminal that feels like any other program on Windows. That is exactly what WSL 2 offers, and under the surface, it is a virtual machine. Figure 8 abb 8 shows its structure. WSL 2. Via the Microsoft hypervisor, Windows starts a small virtual machine with a real Linux kernel, in which the distribution runs. Files cross the boundary of the VM in both directions Linux sees drive C under /mnt/c , and Windows sees the Linux files in File Explorer. The Windows Subsystem for Linux , version 2 WSL 2 , is a component of Windows that starts a real Linux kernel in a small virtual machine, which Windows itself creates, starts and stops. One or more distributions run in this VM, each kept apart from the others. Microsoft builds the Linux kernel from the official Linux source code and delivers it with updates; the distribution comes from its vendor, in the case of Ubuntu from Canonical. By default, the WSL 2 VM gets at most half of the computer's memory. On this chapter's test computer, Windows reports 63.5 GB of memory; the Ubuntu in WSL 2 reports 31 GB of it, just under half. A program that runs under Windows notices nothing of this VM; a program in Linux sees only the VM and not the rest of the computer. ⁠ In short WSL 2 is a real Linux in a small VM that Windows manages itself. The first version of WSL, now called WSL 1, had no Linux kernel. It translated every system call of a Linux program into suitable calls to the Windows kernel. This was elegant, but never complete some system calls had no counterpart under Windows, and programs that needed them did not run. WSL 2 takes the opposite approach. Because a real Linux kernel runs in it, it understands every system call, and every Linux program runs. The price is that Linux and Windows now live in two separate machines and have to exchange files across a boundary. If you set up WSL today, you get WSL 2. Setting up WSL 2 Setting it up consists of a single command, a few minutes of waiting and a restart. After that, you create a user in Ubuntu. Requirements. You need Windows 11 or Windows 10 version 2004 or later, administrator privileges on your computer and an internet connection. Windows Home is sufficient. Steps. This is how you set up WSL 2 with Ubuntu 26.04 Right click the Start button and select “Terminal Admin ”, on Windows 10 “Windows PowerShell Admin ”; confirm the User Account Control prompt. A PowerShell with administrator privileges opens. Type the following command and press Enter Windows switches on the necessary features, downloads the Linux kernel and the distribution and sets up both. Restart the computer when you are prompted to. After the restart, Ubuntu opens by itself; otherwise, you start it from the Start menu. On the first start, Ubuntu asks for a user name and a password. Choose a short name in lowercase letters without spaces, such as student . When you type the password, no characters appear; this is intentional. Remember the password well Linux asks for it later when you carry out system administration tasks. If WSL is already set up on the computer, for example with another distribution, wsl install only displays a help text. In that case, the command from step 2 still installs the distribution, and wsl list online shows which ones are available. The distribution comes as a single file that contains all the files of an Ubuntu system. For Ubuntu 26.04.1, Canonical provides it under the name ubuntu 26.04.1 wsl amd64.wsl , about 400 MB in size. During setup, WSL unpacks it into a virtual hard disk, which from then on contains the Linux system. ⁠ In short wsl install d Ubuntu 26.04 in an administrator PowerShell, restart, create a user. The user you create on the first start belongs only to this one distribution and has nothing to do with your Windows account. In Ubuntu, this user is an administrator of the system with their password, they may carry out tasks that require special privileges, such as installing software. Chapter 7 explains how this works. If you have forgotten the password, it can be reset from Windows, because Windows, as the host, has complete control over the VM. Listing the distributions After setting it up, you want to know whether everything worked. Three commands in an ordinary PowerShell, without administrator privileges, provide the information. The first command lists the distributions on this computer, the second the version numbers, the third all distributions that you could set up shortened here The first list contains a distribution named Ubuntu 26.04 ; the asterisk marks it as the default, that is, the one that WSL starts when nothing else is specified. STATE says whether it is currently running Running or stopped Stopped , and VERSION 2 confirms WSL 2. The second command gives the version of WSL itself and, in the line “Kernelversion” “Kernel version” on an English Windows , the version of Microsoft's Linux kernel; on your computer, the numbers may be newer. In the third list, Ubuntu without a number stands for whichever LTS release is the latest, Ubuntu 26.04 for exactly this one. ⁠ In short wsl l v shows which distributions are set up and whether they run under WSL 2. Opening and checking the terminal You open a Linux terminal in WSL in one of three ways from the Start menu, which lists the distribution by its name; in the Windows app “Terminal”, via the arrow next to the plus sign and the entry Ubuntu 26.04 ; or in a PowerShell with the command wsl . The prompt student@labor ~ \ instead of \\wsl.localhost\ ; both forms lead to the same place. From within a Linux terminal, the command explorer.exe . opens File Explorer in exactly the folder you are currently working in; the dot at the end is part of the command. In the home folder in Ubuntu, there is a folder linuxk1 and in it a folder pruefung with three small files. PowerShell displays them under the File Explorer address The order of the files here is not alphabetical, but the one in which the file server on the Linux side delivers them. The entire Linux system of WSL is contained in a single file named ext4.vhdx , which Windows stores deep in the AppData folder of your Windows user. Never open, move or delete this file with Windows programs, and do not edit anything in its folder this can damage the distribution so badly that it no longer starts. The safe way to Linux files always leads through the entry “Linux” in File Explorer, that is, via \\wsl.localhost . ⁠ In short Windows sees the Linux files in File Explorer under “Linux”; the address is \\wsl.localhost\Ubuntu 26.04 . Where should the practice files go? Because each side can get at the files of both, the question naturally arises where best to store your practice files. The answer is clear in the Linux part, for example in the home folder /home/student , and not under /mnt/c , if you mainly work with them in Linux. Microsoft recommends this too. For this chapter, a folder with 3 559 small files, 52 MB in total, was copied twice in WSL once into the home folder in Linux and once into a folder on C under /mnt/c . In the Linux part, this took between 0.13 and 0.69 seconds; under /mnt/c , about 37 seconds each time. That is roughly fifty to three hundred times as long, or about 10 milliseconds for each individual file. The script for this is included with the code files of this chapter. ⁠ In short Files that you work with in Linux belong in the Linux part, not in /mnt/c . Linux and Windows run in two separate machines, and neither can read the other's storage devices directly. When Linux accesses /mnt/c , every single step, that is, creating, opening, writing and closing a file and setting its properties, becomes a message to a program on the Windows side. This program, a file server, carries out the step with the Windows kernel and sends the reply back. The messages follow a fixed protocol called 9P. When many small files are copied, the work consists almost entirely of such individual steps, and each one costs a round trip across the boundary of the VM. In the Linux part, by contrast, the Linux kernel carries out the same steps directly on its own virtual hard disk. In the opposite direction, when Windows reads Linux files via \\wsl.localhost , a file server on the Linux side works in the same way. Limits of WSL 2 WSL 2 is sufficient for everything this series shows on the command line, in programming and in data analysis. In three places, however, you notice that Linux lives in a VM of its own. ⁠ Network. The WSL 2 VM is connected to Windows in the NAT mode from subsection 3.6 virtuelle maschinen der rechner im rechner.html stufe 3 6 and gets an address of its own, which can change at every restart. Linux gets onto the internet; without additional settings, it cannot be reached from other devices in the home network. Linux does not see the traffic of the computer's real network card. ⁠ Devices. Linux does not see USB devices, such as a USB Wi Fi stick or a card reader, on its own. You can pass them through to WSL with an add on program called usbipd win; as long as they are attached to WSL, Windows cannot use them. ⁠ Updates. Windows updates WSL and the Linux kernel, but not the programs of the distribution. You update those yourself in Linux, as Chapter 9 shows. If you want to build several computers in a network of your own or examine the network traffic of the real network card, use a VM with VirtualBox or the live USB stick. ⁠ In short WSL 2 is ideal for the command line and programming; for network labs and your own devices, it is too far removed from the hardware. Exercises for Section 4 stufe 4 Set up WSL 2 with Ubuntu 26.04 as described in subsection 4.2 stufe 4 2 . Then open an ordinary PowerShell and run wsl l v , then in the Ubuntu terminal cat /etc/os release and uname r . How can you tell from the three outputs that a Ubuntu 26.04 is set up, b it runs under WSL 2 and c the kernel comes from Microsoft? On this chapter's test computer, the outputs look like this a PRETTY NAME="Ubuntu 26.04.1 LTS" and VERSION ID="26.04" in /etc/os release show Ubuntu 26.04. b The column VERSION of wsl l v shows 2 . If the distribution is currently running, STATE shows Running . c The kernel name contains microsoft standard WSL2 it is the kernel of the WSL 2 VM, built by Microsoft. The numbers in front of it may be newer on your computer. On Windows, use Notepad to create a small text file hallo.txt in the “Documents” folder. What is its name in Linux? Display the contents of the folder with ls . Your Windows user name appears in File Explorer in the address of the folder. In the Ubuntu terminal, open File Explorer with explorer.exe . . Which address does it show? a If the file is at C \Users\<Name \Documents\hallo.txt on Windows, its name in Linux is /mnt/c/Users/<Name /Documents/hallo.txt ; <Name is your Windows user name. Note On a Windows in another language, File Explorer may show the folder under a translated name, a German Windows, for example, as “Dokumente”, but its real name on the disk is Documents . If you click in the address bar of File Explorer, the real path appears. The command is then, for example, ls /mnt/c/Users/<Name /Documents , and its output includes hallo.txt . If folder backup to OneDrive is switched on for you, however, “Documents” is in the OneDrive folder, and the path begins with /mnt/c/Users/<Name /OneDrive . b File Explorer opens the folder in which the terminal is currently working. Right after opening the terminal, that is your home folder. The address is then the following, where your Linux user name takes the place of the part in angle brackets \\wsl.localhost\Ubuntu 26.04\home\ . In your WSL terminal, collect three indications that Linux runs in a virtual machine. Use systemd detect virt , uname r and the command lsblk o NAME,SIZE,MODEL , which lists the system's storage devices with their size and model. What do you notice about the model of the storage devices? How does the size of the largest storage device compare with the free space on your real SSD? On this chapter's test computer, the three commands answer like this First indication systemd detect virt recognizes the environment and reports wsl ; on a real computer, it would report none . Second indication The kernel comes from Microsoft and not from Ubuntu. Third indication All storage devices are called Virtual Disk ; they are virtual hard disks that WSL provides to the VM as files, not real devices. The size of sdd , 1T , that is, 1 TiB, is neither the size of your SSD nor the free space on it, but the maximum size up to which the file ext4.vhdx may grow. In fact, it occupies only as much space on the SSD as Linux has written into it as data. A fellow student stores his Python project with 2 000 small files under C \Users\max\projekt and works in WSL in the folder /mnt/c/Users/max/projekt . He is surprised that every test run takes half a minute. Explain to him what is probably causing this, use the measured times from subsection 4.7 stufe 4 7 to estimate how much time it costs just to create all the files across the boundary once, and suggest a better place to store them. How does he then get at his files from Windows? The project is on the Windows side, and the tests run in Linux. Every file access of the tests therefore travels as a message across the boundary of the VM to the file server on the Windows side and back. With many small files, this takes many times as long. Estimate with the measurement from subsection 4.7 stufe 4 7 37 seconds for 3 559 files is about 10 ms per file. Just creating 2 000 files across the boundary once therefore takes roughly This is only an estimate, because reading, writing and checking cost different amounts depending on the kind of access; but it shows that half a minute per test run can easily arise from the boundary alone. Better Move the project into the Linux part, for example to /home/max/projekt , and work there. From Windows, Max then reaches it in File Explorer under “Linux” or at \\wsl.localhost\Ubuntu 26.04\home\max\projekt . Now the way across the boundary is taken only when he opens a file from Windows, not on every test run.

For a virtual machine and for the live USB stick, you download a whole operating system as a single file. This section explains what such a file contains and how to use a checksum to determine that it was not changed on the way. For this, you first need three basic concepts about storage devices. What you need for this the storage device Main memory forgets everything as soon as the power is gone. Whatever is to remain must be on a device that holds it permanently. A storage device is a device that stores data permanently without power, such as an SSD, a hard disk, a USB stick or a memory card. To the operating system, it is a long row of numbered blocks of equal size, usually 512 bytes each; these blocks are called sectors . A USB stick labeled “8 GB” has, for example, 15 633 408 sectors of 512 bytes, that is, 8 004 304 896 bytes. Manufacturers count in powers of ten bytes, so the stick has 8.00 GB. Windows and many Linux programs, on the other hand, calculate in powers of two, bytes. In this unit, the stick has Windows writes “7.45 GB” for this, although it means GiB. An SSD labeled “512 GB” usually has slightly more than bytes, namely 512 110 190 592 bytes, and therefore appears as 476.9 GB. Numbers like these let you reliably recognize a storage device in a list. ⁠ In short A storage device is a long row of numbered blocks that keep their contents even without power. What you need for this the partition An SSD often has to serve several purposes an area for the operating system, one for the boot files and one for recovery in an emergency. That is why it is divided into sections. A partition is a contiguous section of a storage device that the operating system treats like a storage device of its own. Where each partition begins and ends is recorded in the partition table at the beginning of the storage device. Today, a table following the GPT scheme is common; older storage devices and many USB sticks use the older MBR scheme. The SSD of a typical Windows computer holds four partitions at the front, a small EFI system partition of a few hundred MB that contains the boot files; a tiny partition that Windows reserves for its own purposes; the large partition that Windows shows as drive C ; and at the end, a recovery partition with tools for emergencies. Only drive C has a letter; the other three do not appear in File Explorer. ⁠ In short A partition is a section of a storage device; the partition table at the beginning says where each one lies. What you need for this the file system At first, a partition is merely a row of sectors. That it contains files with names and folders is an order that only the operating system brings into it. A file system is the order according to which an operating system stores files and folders in the sectors of a partition. It determines where the names are, in which sectors the contents of each file lie and where there is still free space; many file systems also record who may read a file. Windows uses the NTFS file system for drive C . USB sticks and memory cards are usually set up with FAT32 or exFAT, because almost every device can read them. Linux usually uses ext4 for its own partitions; the virtual hard disk of WSL 2 also contains an ext4. The boot files in the EFI system partition are in a FAT file system. Finally, CDs and DVDs use the ISO 9660 file system. When Windows “formats” a stick, it creates a new, empty file system on it; afterward, the old files can no longer be found. ⁠ In short The file system turns the sectors of a partition into files and folders. The image An operating system consists of thousands of files, plus a partition table and the boot files without which a computer cannot start it. To distribute it, all of this is packed into a single file, and in such a way that this file can be turned back into a bootable storage device. An image is a file that contains the contents of an entire storage device sector by sector, with partition table, file systems and boot files. An ISO image is an image in the format of a CD or DVD; it has the extension .iso . The ISO images of Ubuntu and many other distributions are built so that the same file works as a DVD and as a USB stick, on older and on newer computers. Ubuntu provides the system for desktop computers as ubuntu 26.04.1 desktop amd64.iso . The file is 6 482 409 472 bytes in size, that is, 6.48 GB or 6.04 GiB. It fits on an 8 GB stick, with a good 1.5 GB to spare; a 4 GB stick would be too small. The name also reveals which processors the image is built for amd64 stands for the 64 bit processors of PCs, from Intel as well as from AMD. The hard disk of a virtual machine from subsection 3.1 virtuelle maschinen der rechner im rechner.html stufe 3 1 and the WSL 2 file ext4.vhdx are also images in a broader sense files that represent an entire storage device for their guest. However, they do not contain it sector by sector, but in a format of their own that stores only the areas that have been written to. ⁠ In short An image is an entire storage device in a single file. If you simply copy the ISO file onto a USB stick, you then have a stick with a file on it, and no computer starts from it. For the stick itself to become the storage device from the image, a dedicated program must write the contents of the file onto the stick sector by sector. In the process, everything that was on the stick before is lost. A DVD and a USB stick are read in different ways at startup. For DVDs, there is a standard of its own that provides for a reference to the boot files at the beginning of the ISO 9660 file system. A USB stick, on the other hand, is read like a hard disk the computer's startup software looks for a partition table at the front and, in it, a partition with boot files. The Ubuntu images contain both at the same time. In the first sectors, which the DVD format leaves free, a partition table is additionally entered, and one of its partitions points to a small area with the boot files. Depending on whether the file is read as a DVD or as a disk, the computer finds one structure or the other. Such images are called hybrid . The checksum A 6.5 GB download can be damaged on the way, and a single wrong bit can make a boot program unusable. Worse would be an image into which someone has deliberately built malware. So you want to check whether the downloaded file is exactly the one that the publisher released, without having to compare the 6.5 GB byte by byte with the original. A fingerprint of the file. The idea from the contents of the file, a fixed method calculates a short number, a kind of fingerprint. The publisher publishes the fingerprint of its file, you calculate that of your copy, and if the two match, the copy is unchanged. Figure 9 abb 9 shows that even the smallest change results in a completely different fingerprint. The checksum as a fingerprint. Two files that differ in a single letter result in two completely different values with the SHA 256 method shortened here . Conversely, an equal value means equal contents. A checksum is a short value that a fixed method calculates from the contents of a file. The images of Linux distributions use the SHA 256 method, which is specified by the U.S. standard FIPS 180 4. From every file, no matter how large, it yields a value of 256 bits, written as 64 hexadecimal digits 0 – 9 and a – f . The same contents always result in the same value. SHA 256 is built so that every change, even that of a single bit, results in a completely different value and that, as far as is known today, nobody can deliberately produce a second file with the same value. The file gruss.txt contains the line Hallo Linux , the file gruss2.txt the line Hallo Linuy . On Linux, the command sha256sum calculates the checksum of a file Of the 64 positions, only 5 match by chance; for two completely unrelated values, on average would be equal. A single letter of difference has thus changed the value as thoroughly as if it came from a completely different file. ⁠ In short The checksum is the fingerprint of a file same contents, same value; any change, a different value. A simple checksum, such as the sum of all bytes, would often detect random transmission errors. But it has two weaknesses. If you swap two bytes, the sum stays the same. And anyone who changes something deliberately can adjust a byte elsewhere so that the sum is correct again. SHA 256 is one of the cryptographic hash functions , which are built to withstand both. Every bit of the result depends in an intricate way on every bit of the input, so that a small change flips half of all result bits on average. And no way is known to find a matching file for a given value that would be significantly faster than blind trial and error. With possible values, blind trial and error is hopeless. The Cybersecurity series covers how such functions are built. Checking first by eye, then with the tool The publisher publishes the checksums of its images in a small text file next to the images. For Ubuntu, it is called SHA256SUMS . For Ubuntu 26.04, it looks like this Each line contains a checksum, a space, an asterisk and the file name. The asterisk only says that the file is to be read as a sequence of bytes. The value for the image from subsection 5.4 stufe 5 4 is in the fourth line. By eye. The simplest way you calculate the checksum of your copy and compare it character by character with the line in SHA256SUMS . That is tedious with 64 characters, and it tempts you to compare only the beginning and the end. Against a random transmission error, that would be enough. Against a deliberate forgery, it is not if you compare only the first and last four characters, you check 8 hexadecimal digits, and an attacker finds a forgery that matches in exactly these 8 digits by trial and error after about billion attempts. Each attempt succeeds only with probability , which is why exactly that many attempts are needed on average. A computer that manages one billion attempts per second needs about 4 seconds on average for this. So either you compare all 64 characters, or you let the tool do the comparison. With the tool on Linux. The command sha256sum c reads a file like SHA256SUMS , calculates the checksum for each file listed in it and does the comparison itself. The following example shows this with the small file gruss.txt . The file PRUEFSUMMEN German for “checksums” contains a single line in the same format as SHA256SUMS . Then gruss.txt is changed to Hallo Linuy and checked again OK means same checksum, unchanged contents. FAILED means the file is no longer the one whose checksum is in the list. For the Ubuntu image, you put SHA256SUMS in the same folder as the ISO file and type sha256sum c SHA256SUMS ignore missing . The option ignore missing skips the files in the list that you have not downloaded. If ubuntu 26.04.1 desktop amd64.iso OK then appears, the image is unchanged. If the tool instead reports no file was verified , the ISO file is not in the same folder as the list. With the tool on Windows. In PowerShell, Get FileHash calculates the checksum, using SHA 256 by default. The addition | Format List writes the result as a list, one line below the other, so that the long value is not cut off. The file gruss.txt is now in the “Downloads” folder of the Windows user student The value is the same as on Linux, only in uppercase letters. The second line has PowerShell do the comparison between the quotation marks, you paste the value from SHA256SUMS . The comparison eq ignores the difference between uppercase and lowercase and answers True if the values are equal and False otherwise. ⁠ In short Compare checksums completely, preferably with sha256sum c or with Get FileHash and eq . What the checksum proves and what it does not If the checksum matches, the file is exactly the one whose value is in SHA256SUMS . This proves that nothing was damaged during the download. But it does not prove that the file comes from the publisher. Many people do not download large files directly from the publisher, but from a mirror server, for example at a university that provides copies. Suppose an attacker has taken over such a server and swapped the image there for one with built in malware. Then the attacker also swaps the file SHA256SUMS next to it and enters the checksum of the forged image. Anyone who downloads both from this server gets a reassuring OK when checking after all, the file matches the list. Except that the file and the list are both forged. So the checksum proves the integrity of the file with respect to the list, not its origin. That the list itself is genuine is only established by a digital signature from the publisher a kind of forgery proof seal that only the owner of a secret key can apply and that anyone can check with a matching public verification key. For Ubuntu, the signature of the list is in the file SHA256SUMS.gpg ; the Cybersecurity series explains how a signature works mathematically and how to verify it. For this chapter, it is enough to do the following download the image and SHA256SUMS from the publisher's official site, for Ubuntu from https //ubuntu.com/download/desktop https //ubuntu.com/download/desktop or https //releases.ubuntu.com https //releases.ubuntu.com , and always check the checksum. ⁠ In short A matching checksum proves that the file is unchanged, but not that it is genuine. Exercises for Section 5 stufe 5 On Windows, use Notepad to create a text file with a line of your choice. Calculate its checksum in PowerShell with Get FileHash . If you have set up WSL 2, also calculate it in Linux with sha256sum ; there, the path begins with /mnt/c . Do the values match? Then change a single character, save and calculate the checksum again. Both tools read the same bytes of the file and apply the same method, SHA 256, to them; the values therefore match, on Windows in uppercase letters, on Linux in lowercase letters. If the file is, for example, at C \Users\<Name \Documents\notiz.txt , the command in Linux is sha256sum /mnt/c/Users/<Name /Documents/notiz.txt . After changing a single character, the value is completely different, as in the example “One letter different”. If the values did not match before the change, the two tools did not read the same file, for example because Notepad had not yet saved the file or because two files with similar names exist. Checksums compare bytes, not the visible text An invisible difference, such as an additional space at the end of a line, results in a different value. In the two checksums from the example “One letter different”, count the positions at which both values have the same digit. How many equal positions do you expect on average for two random values, and why? Someone compares only the first six characters. Roughly how many attempts does an attacker need to find a forgery whose checksum begins with the same six characters? How many would it be if all 64 characters were compared? a The two values match at 5 of the 64 positions. If two values are unrelated, each position is independently one of the 16 hexadecimal digits, and the probability that they match at a given position is . On average, you therefore expect equal positions. A count of 5 is a perfectly ordinary random result; the two checksums behave like two unrelated values, although the files differ in only one letter. b Six hexadecimal digits can take different values. An attacker who keeps varying a forgery at an unimportant place therefore hits a checksum with the same six initial characters after about 17 million attempts, which for a computer is a matter of fractions of a second to seconds. For all 64 characters, the attacker would need about attempts; no conceivable computer can manage that. A partial comparison therefore protects against random errors, but not against intent. An image is 6 482 409 472 bytes in size. Windows displays the sizes 3.72 GB, 7.45 GB and 14.9 GB for three sticks. Which sticks does the image fit on? To find out, convert the size of the image into the same unit that Windows uses. In the unit that Windows uses, the image has So it does not fit on the stick with 3.72 a stick labeled 4 GB , but it does fit on the sticks with 7.45 8 GB and 14.9 16 GB . If you instead compare 6.48, the size the publisher states for the image, with 7.45 from the Windows display, you arrive at the same result here, but you are comparing two different units; in close cases, this leads you astray. In the example with the mirror server, the image and SHA256SUMS have the same flaw. Which of the following measures would have uncovered the forgery, and which would not? a sha256sum c instead of comparison by eye, b SHA256SUMS from https //releases.ubuntu.com https //releases.ubuntu.com , the image from the mirror server, c downloading the image and the list twice, d checking the signature SHA256SUMS.gpg . a Does not uncover the forgery. sha256sum c only compares more precisely than the eye; since the image and the list match each other, it reports OK . b Uncovers it. The genuine list from https //releases.ubuntu.com https //releases.ubuntu.com contains the checksum of the genuine image; the forged image has a different one, and the comparison reports FAILED or False . The prerequisite is that the official server itself has not been tampered with. c Does not uncover it. The mirror server delivers the same forged file and the same forged list both times. d Uncovers it. Only someone who has Ubuntu's secret key can produce a valid signature over SHA256SUMS ; the attacker does not have it. A forged list is therefore noticed when the signature is checked, provided that you check with Ubuntu's genuine verification key.

If you want to start Linux from a USB stick, or from an image in a virtual machine, you need to know what happens between pressing the power button and the running kernel. This section follows this chain link by link, as far as you need it to start safely from the stick What starts first, how do you choose the storage device, what loads the kernel, how does the computer check whether it can trust the boot program, and why does the encryption of Windows depend on this chain? The firmware After switching on, main memory is empty, and no operating system is running yet. Nevertheless, the computer finds Windows on the SSD after a few seconds. So some program must already be there beforehand and know where to look. The firmware is a program that is stored permanently in a memory chip on the main circuit board the motherboard and runs first when the computer is switched on. It checks and starts the hardware and then loads a boot program from a storage device. Today's PCs use firmware following the UEFI standard Unified Extensible Firmware Interface ; its predecessor was called BIOS, and many people still call the firmware “BIOS” today. A UEFI firmware reads its boot programs from a small, dedicated partition with a FAT file system, the EFI system partition ; it is the first of the four partitions from the example in subsection 5.2 datentrager abbild und prufsumme.html stufe 5 2 . In its own memory, the firmware keeps a list of boot entries, each with the storage device and the path of a boot file. For Windows, an entry named “Windows Boot Manager” points to the file \EFI\Microsoft\Boot\bootmgfw.efi in the EFI system partition of the SSD. PowerShell knows a value that Windows takes over from the firmware at startup On older computers, it says Legacy here; then the computer starts in the old BIOS mode. Computers with Windows 11 practically always start with UEFI. ⁠ In short The firmware runs first after switching on and loads a boot program from the EFI system partition. A USB stick that is plugged into a computer for the first time does not yet have a boot entry in that computer's firmware.
