So that every stick can nevertheless start on every computer, the UEFI standard specifies a fixed path for removable storage devices if the firmware finds an EFI system partition on such a storage device, it looks there for the file \EFI\BOOT\BOOTX64.EFI for 64 bit PCs and starts it. A bootable Linux stick contains exactly this file. That is why you do not need to set anything up in the firmware to start from the stick; you only need to select it. Boot order and boot menu If an SSD with Windows and a USB stick with Linux are both in the computer, the firmware has to decide what to start from. Normally, that should be Windows, and only as an exception the stick. In this context, starting a computer is usually called booting . The boot order is the list of boot entries in the order in which the firmware tries them at power on. The boot menu is a selection that the firmware displays when you press a key at power on; in it, you choose an entry once, without changing the boot order. Which key opens the boot menu depends on the manufacturer; Table 3 tab 3 lists the most common ones. You press it several times right after switching on, before the Windows logo appears. Table 3 Keys for the boot menu for common manufacturers. Individual models may differ; the device's manual is authoritative. | Manufacturer | Key for the boot menu | | | | | Dell | F12 | | HP | Esc, then F9 | | Lenovo | F12, on many IdeaPads Fn+F12, or the small Novo button | | ASUS laptop | hold down Esc while switching on | | MSI | F11 | | Acer | F12, must first be enabled in the firmware on some devices | If no key helps, there is a way via Windows Settings System Recovery Advanced startup “Restart now”. In the blue menu that appears afterward, many computers offer the item “Use a device”, with which you start directly from the stick. Otherwise, “Troubleshoot” “Advanced options” “UEFI Firmware Settings” leads to the settings of the firmware. ⁠ In short For a one time start from the stick, you use the boot menu and leave the boot order as it is. The boot loader The firmware knows its way around partitions and the FAT file system, but not around a Linux kernel and its settings. That is why another program stands between the firmware and the kernel. A boot loader is the boot program that the firmware loads and that in turn loads the kernel of the operating system into main memory and starts it. In doing so, it can display a menu in which you choose between several systems or startup variants. Linux distributions usually use the GRUB boot loader. Windows uses the Windows Boot Manager, the file from subsection 6.1 stufe 6 1 , and Ubuntu uses the GRUB boot loader. When you start an Ubuntu stick, GRUB displays a short menu after a few seconds; the first entry starts Ubuntu and is preselected. Once the kernel is loaded, it takes control, and the boot loader has done its job. ⁠ In short The firmware loads the boot loader, and the boot loader loads the kernel. Secure Boot The boot program runs before the operating system and any virus scanner are even there, and it determines which kernel is loaded. A secretly replaced boot loader would therefore have the whole computer in its hands. A check in the firmware protects against this. A seal on the boot program. The check is based on the digital signature from subsection 5.7 datentrager abbild und prufsumme.html stufe 5 7 , the forgery proof seal that only the owner of a secret key can apply and that anyone can check with the matching verification key. If a signed file is afterward changed by even a single bit, the seal no longer matches. Secure Boot is a function of the UEFI firmware that runs a boot program only if it carries a valid digital signature whose verification key is stored in the firmware as trusted and has not been revoked. Secure Boot is a check of authenticity, not encryption it hides nothing, it only prevents modified or unknown boot programs from starting. Figure 10 abb 10 shows how an Ubuntu stick starts with Secure Boot switched on. In almost all PCs, verification keys from Microsoft are stored at the factory. That is why Ubuntu comes with a small program called shim as its first boot program, which Microsoft has signed. shim contains Canonical's verification key, with which shim checks the GRUB boot loader, and GRUB checks the kernel in the same way. The boot chain of an Ubuntu stick with Secure Boot. Each link checks the seal of the next one before handing control over to it. The firmware trusts Microsoft, Microsoft has signed shim , and shim carries Canonical's key onward. An Ubuntu stick starts with Secure Boot switched on, because every link in its chain is suitably signed; you do not need to change anything in the firmware. Kali Linux, on the other hand, comes with a kernel without a signature; to start it from the stick, you would have to switch off Secure Boot in the firmware. For this chapter, Secure Boot always stays switched on. ⁠ In short Secure Boot starts only boot programs with a valid seal; it checks authenticity and encrypts nothing. The verification keys in the firmware are contained in certificates with an expiration date. The certificate with which Microsoft has signed the boot programs of other vendors, such as shim , since 2011 expired on 27 June 2026; its successor dates from 2023. The expiration alone does not prevent any start, because the firmware checks the seal against the stored certificate and not against the date. Problems arise in two places. A very new computer whose firmware knows only the 2023 certificate does not start a boot program that is signed only with the old one. Conversely, an older computer whose firmware was never updated does not start a boot program that is signed only with the new one. According to Canonical, the installation media of Ubuntu 26.04 need the 2011 certificate in the firmware. If a computer reports a security violation when starting from the stick, you first install all updates for the firmware, from Windows and from the manufacturer, and try again, instead of switching off Secure Boot. Windows device encryption On many Windows computers, the SSD is encrypted, often without the owners knowing it. In normal operation, you notice nothing of this. But if you change something in the boot chain, Windows may demand a long key at the next startup, and anyone who does not have it can no longer get to their data. BitLocker is the drive encryption of Windows; in Windows Home, it is called device encryption . It encrypts drive C , and Windows decrypts it by itself at startup if the boot chain is unchanged. If the boot chain has been changed, Windows demands the recovery key , a 48 digit number that was generated when the encryption was switched on. Windows 11 switches on device encryption by itself on suitable computers as soon as you sign in with a Microsoft account, and it stores the recovery key in this account. Since version 24H2, this applies to considerably more computers than before. You can see whether your drive is encrypted under Settings Privacy & security Device encryption; if this item is missing, the function is not available on your computer. In the Pro and Enterprise editions, you can also find the encryption in Control Panel under the name “BitLocker Drive Encryption”. Microsoft names, among others, these triggers for the recovery key prompt changes to the Windows Boot Manager, a firmware update, changes to settings that are included in the check of the boot chain, which includes Secure Boot, and, on older computers with a security chip of version 1.2, a changed boot order. A one time start from the stick via the boot menu, with Secure Boot switched on and without any change to the firmware, is not on this list; afterward, Windows normally starts as always. Even so, you back up the key beforehand, because not all computers behave the same way. Before you start from the stick or change any setting in the firmware, check whether your drive is encrypted. If it is, back up the recovery key so that you can read it without this computer On another device, such as your phone, sign in at https //aka.ms/myrecoverykey https //aka.ms/myrecoverykey with your Microsoft account and check that a key for your computer is listed there. Write it down on paper or print it out. If the computer is a device of your university or your employer, the key is held by its IT department. Do not start such a device from a stick without their permission. If you have to change a setting in the firmware, Microsoft advises temporarily suspending the encryption beforehand; after the next restart, it switches itself back on. In the Pro and Enterprise editions, you do this in Control Panel under “BitLocker Drive Encryption” with “Suspend protection”. Windows Home has no switch for this; there, the backed up key is the safeguard. ⁠ In short Before you do anything to the boot chain, you back up the 48 digit recovery key. The key with which Windows decrypts the drive is released only by a security chip on the motherboard, the TPM Trusted Platform Module . During startup, the firmware writes a kind of fingerprint of each loaded boot program and of important settings, such as whether Secure Boot is switched on, into this chip. The chip releases the key only if these fingerprints are exactly the same as when the encryption was switched on. That way, someone who starts the computer with a boot program of their own cannot grab the key; the flip side is that even a harmless change locks the key. The Cybersecurity series explains how the TPM measures the boot chain. Exercises for Section 6 stufe 6 Find out, without changing anything a Does your computer start with UEFI? Use \to \to$ Device encryption or BitLocker, you can see whether the drive is encrypted; at https //aka.ms/myrecoverykey https //aka.ms/myrecoverykey , there is a 48 digit key for every encrypted device that is linked to your Microsoft account. If you find none there although encryption is switched on, clear this up before you change anything at all in the boot process. d The key is given in the manual or on the manufacturer's support page, usually under “Boot Menu” or “Startup Menu”; Table 3 tab 3 lists the most common ones. A computer has Secure Boot switched on. At which link of the chain from Figure 10 abb 10 does booting stop, or does the system start? a Someone has changed a byte in GRUB on the stick. b The stick contains a kernel that nobody has signed. c An Ubuntu stick is plugged into a computer whose firmware does not contain Microsoft's verification key for third party boot programs. d An Ubuntu stick is started via the boot menu. Does d trigger a recovery key prompt on an encrypted Windows? a Booting stops at the transition from shim to GRUB. shim checks GRUB's seal with Canonical's verification key; after the change, the seal no longer matches. b Booting stops at the transition from GRUB to the kernel, because GRUB finds no valid seal on the kernel. This is exactly why you have to switch off Secure Boot for a kernel without a signature, such as that of Kali Linux. c The very first link fails The firmware does not know the verification key with which Microsoft signed shim , and does not start shim . Some computers come with their firmware set up like this. The remedy is a setting in the firmware that allows this key; this is a change to the boot chain, for which the recovery key must be backed up beforehand. d The system starts firmware, shim , GRUB and kernel are suitably signed. A recovery key prompt is normally not to be expected at the next start of Windows. The boot menu changes neither the Windows Boot Manager nor a setting of the firmware; at the next start, the boot chain of Windows is the same as before. Only on older computers with a security chip of version 1.2 can a changed boot order trigger the prompt. Nevertheless, you have backed up the key, in case a computer behaves differently.

This section sets up the second way a virtual machine with VirtualBox in which Ubuntu 26.04 is installed. It assumes the concepts from Section 3 virtuelle maschinen der rechner im rechner.html stufe 3 , the image from Section 5 datentrager abbild und prufsumme.html stufe 5 and the boot chain from Section 6 wie ein pc startet.html stufe 6 . At the end, you have a Linux to practice on with a snapshot that you can return to at any time. Setting up VirtualBox VirtualBox is the hypervisor this way works with. It is free of charge, runs on Windows, macOS and Linux and, at its core, is open source software under the GNU General Public License, version 3. Steps. This is how you set up VirtualBox On https //www.virtualbox.org https //www.virtualbox.org , download the “Windows hosts” package under “Downloads”. This series uses VirtualBox 7.2. Run the file and follow the installer with the suggested settings. It asks for administrator privileges and sets up a virtual network device; the network connection may drop briefly in the process. You do not need the Extension Pack , which is offered on the same page. It contains additional functions that play no role for a Linux to practice on, and it is under a license of its own that limits free use to personal and educational purposes. If WSL 2 is set up on the computer, or if a security function that uses the Microsoft hypervisor is active, VirtualBox cannot access hardware virtualization directly itself. It then uses the Microsoft hypervisor as its foundation, as described in the “Background” box in subsection 3.3 virtuelle maschinen der rechner im rechner.html stufe 3 3 . The VM still runs, but noticeably more slowly; VirtualBox indicates this with a small green turtle at the bottom right of the VM window. For a Linux to practice on, this is not an obstacle. ⁠ In short Install VirtualBox from https //www.virtualbox.org https //www.virtualbox.org , without the Extension Pack. Switching on hardware virtualization If Task Manager shows “Virtualization Enabled” Exercise 7 virtuelle maschinen der rechner im rechner.html aufg 7 , skip this subsection. If it says “Disabled”, the hardware virtualization from subsection 3.4 virtuelle maschinen der rechner im rechner.html stufe 3 4 must be switched on in the firmware. A change in the firmware is an intervention in the boot chain. Back up the recovery key beforehand, as described in subsection 6.5 wie ein pc startet.html stufe 6 5 . In the firmware, change only the setting for virtualization and nothing else, not Secure Boot or the boot order either; Microsoft expressly advises changing only what you really need in the firmware. If you are unsure, leave the firmware without saving. Steps. Open the firmware via Settings System Recovery Advanced startup “Restart now” “Troubleshoot” “Advanced options” “UEFI Firmware Settings”. Depending on the manufacturer, the setting is called something like “Intel Virtualization Technology”, “Intel VT x”, “SVM Mode” or “AMD V” and is usually found under “Advanced”, “CPU Configuration” or “Security”. Set it to “Enabled”, save and restart. Afterward, Task Manager shows “Enabled”. ⁠ In short If hardware virtualization is off, you switch on only this one setting in the firmware, with the recovery key backed up. Creating a VM For the VM, you need the image ubuntu 26.04.1 desktop amd64.iso from https //ubuntu.com/download/desktop https //ubuntu.com/download/desktop , checked as in subsection 5.6 datentrager abbild und prufsumme.html stufe 5 6 . Then you create a new VM in VirtualBox. Steps. In VirtualBox, click “New”. The wizard asks, one after the other, for the following ⁠ Name and image. Enter a name, such as ubuntu labor , and select the checked ISO image. From it, VirtualBox recognizes the type and version of the system. ⁠ Skipping unattended installation. VirtualBox offers to install Ubuntu by itself. Decline depending on the version, you either check “Skip Unattended Installation” or clear the check box for unattended installation. It does not always work with new Ubuntu releases, and by hand, you see what happens. ⁠ Memory and processors. According to the vendor, Ubuntu 26.04 needs at least 6 GB of memory and a processor with two cores. Give the VM 6 GB 6 144 MB and 2 processors if your computer has 16 GB or more. ⁠ Hard disk. Create a new virtual hard disk with at least 25 GB. Keep the default that the file grows only with its contents. Whether the VM starts with UEFI or in the old BIOS mode makes no difference for Ubuntu; keep the default. On a computer with 16 GB, a VM with 6 GB still leaves 10 GB for Windows and its programs; that is enough. With 32 GB, you can also give the VM 8 GB, and 24 GB remain. On a computer with only 8 GB, a mere 2 GB would remain for Windows, and both systems would become painfully slow. There, it is better to use WSL 2, which takes memory as needed and releases it again. ⁠ In short A new VM with the checked image, without unattended installation, with 6 GB of memory, 2 processors and a 25 GB disk. The file of a new virtual hard disk initially contains only its management data. Only when the guest writes to a sector does VirtualBox allocate the space for it in the file. Sectors that have never been written to are read by the guest as zeros, without being stored anywhere. On Linux, the same principle exists for ordinary files in the experiments for this chapter, an image file the size of a 512 GB SSD that contained only a partition table took up just 40 KiB on the real disk. Installing Ubuntu in the VM When you start the new VM, it behaves like a newly bought computer with a DVD inserted its virtual firmware finds nothing on the empty hard disk and starts from the virtual DVD drive that holds the image. The Ubuntu installer appears. Steps. In the installer, you choose, one after the other, the language, accessibility, the keyboard layout and the internet connection; in NAT mode, the VM already has a connection. Then comes the choice between “Try Ubuntu” and “Install Ubuntu” here, in the VM, choose to install. For the type of installation, choose the simple option that uses the entire hard disk, then the user name, password and time zone. After the installation, the VM restarts; VirtualBox usually removes the image from the virtual DVD drive by itself in the process. The installer offers to erase the entire hard disk and install Ubuntu on it. On a real computer, this would destroy Windows with all its data. In the VM, it affects only the virtual hard disk, that is, the new, empty file from subsection 7.3 stufe 7 3 . The guest does not even see the host's SSD, so it cannot erase it either. ⁠ In short In the VM, you install Ubuntu quite normally, because everything the installer erases is the virtual hard disk. The first snapshot Right after the installation, the system is clean. You capture this state before you try out anything. Steps. Shut down Ubuntu in the VM. In VirtualBox, select the VM and open the “Snapshots” view via the menu next to its name. Create a new snapshot there and name it sauber . If you want to go back later, select it in the same view and restore it; in the process, VirtualBox offers to save the current state as a snapshot first. If you return to a snapshot, everything that the VM has saved since this snapshot is gone, including your own files. If you want to keep something, save it beforehand as a new snapshot or copy it out of the VM. ⁠ In short After the installation, create a snapshot “sauber”; you can return to it at any time, but you lose everything that came later. The terminal in the VM In Ubuntu, you open the terminal with the key combination Ctrl+Alt+T or via the app overview Show Apps , in which you type “Terminal”. There, as with WSL 2, you check the distribution and the kernel with cat /etc/os release and uname r . The distribution reports with the same lines as in subsection 2.3 drei wege zu einem eigenen linux.html stufe 2 3 . The kernel, however, is a different one than in WSL 2 in the VM, the kernel that Ubuntu itself builds for PCs is running. Its name does not contain microsoft ; for Ubuntu on desktop computers, it ends in generic . The VM is connected to the network in the NAT mode from subsection 3.6 virtuelle maschinen der rechner im rechner.html stufe 3 6 it can reach the internet, but it cannot be reached from outside. ⁠ In short Ctrl+Alt+T opens the terminal in Ubuntu; there, uname r shows Ubuntu's kernel. Exercises for Section 7 stufe 7 Set up VirtualBox, create a VM with Ubuntu 26.04, install Ubuntu in it and create the snapshot sauber . Check with cat /etc/os release and uname r in the terminal of the VM. Then create a file test.txt on the desktop of the VM, shut down the VM and return to the snapshot sauber . What do you expect before you start the VM again? Check it. After returning to the snapshot sauber , test.txt has disappeared. The file was created after the snapshot and was therefore in the differencing image, which is discarded when restoring. The VM starts in the state directly after the installation. In the terminal output of the VM, cat /etc/os release shows the same lines as in subsection 2.3 drei wege zu einem eigenen linux.html stufe 2 3 , and uname r shows a kernel whose name ends in generic and does not contain microsoft . Using the concepts guest, hypervisor and virtual hard disk, explain why choosing “Erase disk and install Ubuntu” in the VM does not endanger the files of Windows. Which file on the host does the guest actually change in the process? What would have to happen for the guest to be able to write to the host's SSD after all? The guest sees only the hardware that the hypervisor simulates for it. As its hard disk, it sees the virtual hard disk, and on the host, that is an ordinary file, in VirtualBox by default ubuntu labor.vdi in the folder VirtualBox VMs\ubuntu labor of the Windows user. When the installer “erases the whole disk”, the guest kernel writes new partitions and file systems to this virtual hard disk. Each of these write accesses is a privileged device access that the hypervisor traps and writes into this one file. The host's SSD with Windows is not a device of the VM; the guest does not even know that it exists. For the guest to be able to write to the host's SSD, you would have to assign the SSD to it explicitly as a device; VirtualBox can do that, but only via a setting for experts that you never use here. The guest could also get at individual files of the host if you share a folder of the host with it; this, too, happens only if you explicitly ask for it. Otherwise, the only remaining possibility would be a bug in the hypervisor itself that breaks the separation between guest and host.

A Linux that starts from a USB stick does not use the built in SSD, and yet you can create files and try out programs in it. This section explains how this works the system is in a write protected image, and everything that changes ends up in a layer in main memory. It also follows from this why everything is gone after switching off. What you need for this mounting Subsection 4.5 wsl 2 linux neben windows.html stufe 4 5 showed that Linux arranges all files in a single tree with the root directory / and shows drive C of Windows under /mnt/c . How do the contents of a storage device get to a place in this tree? Mounting means making a file system visible at a place in the directory tree from then on, the folder at this place shows the contents of the file system. The folder is called the mount point . Programs do not use a file system that is not mounted anywhere; they do not read or write any files there. The command lsblk lists the storage devices that the kernel sees, with their size and their mount point Linux names storage devices sda , sdb and so on. All four are virtual hard disks of the WSL 2 VM. The file system on sdd , the ext4 file from subsection 4.6 wsl 2 linux neben windows.html stufe 4 6 , is mounted at the root directory / and additionally at a second place; it contains the whole of Ubuntu. sda and sdb have no mount point in Ubuntu; WSL needs them for its own purposes outside the distribution. sdc contains no file system SWAP stands for an area to which the kernel can move parts of main memory, and the kernel uses it without mounting. Drive C is not in the list, because it is not a storage device of the VM; it comes from the Windows side via the file server from Figure 8 wsl 2 linux neben windows.html abb 8 and is mounted under /mnt/c . ⁠ In short A file system is mounted at a folder; no program uses what is not mounted anywhere. The live system A Linux should start from the stick, be fully usable and not touch the internal SSD. Still, you should be able to create files, and the system should appear fresh again after every start. Figure 11 abb 11 shows how a live system achieves this with two layers that the system places one on top of the other. The layers of a live system. At the bottom is the system as a compressed, write protected image from the stick, above it a writable layer in main memory. Together, they result in the directory tree that the programs see. The internal SSD is not mounted. A live system is an operating system that starts and runs entirely from a removable storage device without mounting the computer's built in storage devices. Its system is stored write protected on the removable storage device; all changes during the session end up in main memory. If you start an Ubuntu stick and choose “Try Ubuntu” in the installer, Ubuntu runs as a live system. You can browse the web, create files and use the terminal. The SSD with Windows remains untouched, and after a restart without the stick, Windows starts as before. ⁠ In short A live system runs from the stick and from main memory and leaves the internal SSD alone. The compressed image squashfs A complete Ubuntu with a browser, office programs and drivers takes up many gigabytes. So that it fits on a stick and is read quickly, it is stored compressed in a file. squashfs is a file system that stores its entire contents compressed in a single file and can only be read, not written to. It is created once, when the image is built. In the Ubuntu image, the system is stored in squashfs files in the folder casper . At startup, the live system mounts them, and from then on, it reads every program you start from the compressed image, unpacked piece by piece in main memory. Nothing in it can be changed. ⁠ In short squashfs is a compressed file system that can only be read. The reason lies in its structure. squashfs compresses the files in blocks, by default of 128 KiB each, and stores the compressed blocks one after the other without gaps. How much space a block then needs depends on its contents. If you change a few bytes in a file, its compressed block almost always becomes longer or shorter. Then it no longer fits in its old place, and all the following blocks, together with the references to them, would have to be moved. A file system that is never changed, on the other hand, can afford the densest arrangement, and that is exactly what you need for a system that is supposed to fit on a stick and remain unchanged. Writable file systems with compression exist too; for this, they leave space free between the blocks or write changed blocks to a new place and manage the space in a correspondingly more complex way. A file system in main memory tmpfs If the system itself cannot be written to and the SSD is off limits, a live system needs another place for everything that changes new files, changed settings, logs. tmpfs is a file system whose files are in main memory. It can be read and written to like any other file system. Its contents disappear as soon as it is unmounted or the computer is switched off. An ordinary Linux also uses tmpfs, for example for files that are needed only until the next restart. In WSL 2, for example, the folder /run is a tmpfs. How much main memory a tmpfs may take up at most is set when it is mounted; but it takes up only as much as its files actually need. ⁠ In short tmpfs is a file system in main memory, writable and volatile. Two layers on top of each other the overlay Now the live system has two file systems the system in the squashfs, which can only be read, and an empty tmpfs, which can be written to. But the programs should see a single directory tree that contains the system and in which you can nevertheless change everything. An overlay places two file systems on top of each other and shows them as one a lower, read only layer and an upper, writable layer. When a file is read, it first looks in the upper layer and, if the file is missing there, in the lower one. If a file of the lower layer is to be changed, it first copies the file to the upper layer and changes the copy there. If a file of the lower layer is deleted, it enters a marker in the upper layer that hides the file. The lower layer remains unchanged in every case. The lower layer is the squashfs of the system, the upper one a tmpfs. 1 You create the new file notiz.txt it is created only in the upper layer. 2 You change a settings file of the system the overlay copies it from the squashfs to the tmpfs and changes the copy; from now on, all programs see the changed version, because the upper layer takes precedence. 3 You delete a file of the system a marker is created in the upper layer, and the file can no longer be seen, although it is still present in the squashfs. After a restart, the tmpfs is empty, and all three changes have disappeared. ⁠ In short The overlay shows a read only and a writable layer as one tree; all changes end up at the top. When the boot loader starts the kernel, it additionally loads a small file system into main memory, the initramfs . In it runs a program that builds the layers before the actual system starts; in Ubuntu, it is called casper . It searches for the storage device on which the live system is located, mounts its squashfs files, creates a tmpfs and combines both into an overlay. It makes this overlay the root directory / of the system and hands over to the first program of the actual system. For all programs that start afterward, the live system looks like an ordinarily installed Linux. What happens when you switch off The behavior of a live system when it is switched off follows directly from the layers. The upper layer is in main memory, and main memory loses its contents without power. The lower layer was never changed. At the next start, the system is therefore exactly as it is on the stick. For this chapter, a very small live system, Alpine Linux version 3.24, was started from its image in a test VM. The list of mounted file systems shows the layers the boot medium with its ISO file system, read only ro , the root directory / as a tmpfs, and part of the system as a squashfs, also read only Here, the character at the beginning of the line is the prompt, because in this test VM you work as the administrator. In the same session, the program lsblk was also installed afterward from the internet. After a restart of the VM, both are gone Alpine puts the whole system into a tmpfs at startup and mounts only part of it as a squashfs; Ubuntu, on the other hand, as described in subsection 8.5 stufe 8 5 , places a tmpfs as an overlay over its squashfs files. The result is the same everything that changes during the session is in main memory. The same applies to programs that you install afterward in the live system they also end up in main memory and are gone after the restart. ⁠ In short After switching off, everything you changed in the live system is gone, and every start is fresh again. Persistence That a live system forgets everything is usually an advantage. But if you work with the same stick regularly, you sometimes want to keep your files and settings. For a live system, persistence means that it stores changes not in main memory but in an additional storage area on the stick, so that they survive the restart. In Ubuntu, this is a partition or file labeled casper rw , which the live system uses as the upper layer when it is started with the boot option persistent . The Windows program Rufus, with which you write images to USB sticks, offers a slider for the size of such a persistence partition when writing an Ubuntu stick. Ubuntu's guides do not describe this; Rufus itself has had to fix the function repeatedly for individual Ubuntu releases. Whether it works reliably with Ubuntu 26.04 is not certain. ⁠ In short Persistence turns the stick into a system that remembers, but in Ubuntu, it is a poorly maintained add on. With persistence, the stick loses exactly the properties that distinguish a live system it is no longer fresh at every start, and an error persists. In addition, all files are stored unencrypted on the stick, and if you lose it, you expose them to anyone who finds it. A USB stick is also neither fast nor durable for many small write operations. If you need a Linux for permanent work, you are better served by WSL 2 or a VM; the live stick is there for trying things out and for a clean restart. Exercises for Section 8 stufe 8 You are working in the Ubuntu live system without persistence. Which of the following is still there at the next start from the same stick? a A bookmark in the browser, b a file that you saved in your home folder, c a file that you saved on a second USB stick, d a file that you uploaded to your cloud storage, e a program that you installed afterward. Justify each answer with the layers. a Gone. The bookmark is stored in a file in the home folder, that is, in the upper layer in main memory. b Gone, for the same reason. c Still there. The second stick is a separate storage device that you mounted and wrote to directly; it does not belong to the overlay. d Still there. The file is on a server on the internet. e Gone. The program's files were written to the upper layer; the squashfs on the stick is unchanged. The lower layer of an overlay contains the files a , b and c ; the upper layer is empty. The following happens in sequence a is changed, b is deleted, d is newly created, d is changed. What is then in the upper layer, what is in the lower one, and which files do the programs see? What do they see after a restart? Step by step Changing a The overlay copies a to the upper layer and changes the copy there. Deleting b A marker is created in the upper layer that hides b . Creating d d is created only in the upper layer. Changing d The file is already in the upper layer and is changed there; no copy is needed. Afterward, the upper layer contains the changed copy of a , the marker for b and the changed file d . The lower layer contains a , b and c , unchanged. The programs see a in the changed version, c and d ; they do not see b . After a restart, the upper layer is empty The programs again see a in the original version, b and c , and d does not exist. A computer with 8 GB of memory is running the live system. You download a 5 GB file into your home folder. Why can the live system get into difficulties in the process, although the USB stick still has space and the internal SSD has 300 GB free? The home folder is in the overlay, and everything you save there ends up in the upper layer, that is, in the tmpfs in main memory. The 5 GB of the downloaded file therefore occupy 5 GB of main memory, in addition to what the running system, the browser and the download itself need. With 8 GB, main memory becomes scarce or runs full, or the tmpfs reaches the maximum size that was set when it was mounted. Then the download aborts with an error, or the whole system becomes sluggish. The free space on the stick does not help, because the live system without persistence writes nothing there; the lower layer is read only. The free space on the SSD does not help, because the SSD is not mounted. In the live system, you therefore save large files on a second USB stick or upload them directly to cloud storage.

This section sets up the third way Ubuntu 26.04 as a live system on a USB stick. Here, you write to a storage device and start the computer in an unusual way; that is why the risks and how to guard against them come first. The section assumes Sections 5 datentrager abbild und prufsumme.html stufe 5 , 6 wie ein pc startet.html stufe 6 and 8 das live system.html stufe 8 . The risks at a glance Almost everything that can go wrong with the live stick has one of two causes you write to the wrong storage device, or you change something in the boot chain. Table 4 tab 4 lists the individual dangers with their safeguards; the following subsections explain them. Table 4 The dangers of the live USB stick and how to guard against them. | Danger | Cause | Safeguard | | | | | | wrong storage device overwritten | the writing tool replaces the entire selected storage device | unplug other USB storage, recognize the stick by its size subsection 9.2 stufe 9 2 | | recovery key prompt | change to the boot chain | back up the key beforehand, use only the boot menu, Secure Boot on subsection 6.5 wie ein pc startet.html stufe 6 5 | | Windows data damaged | after “Shut down” with Fast Startup, Windows is at rest hibernated | “Restart” instead of “Shut down”, do not touch the Windows partitions subsection 9.3 stufe 9 3 | | Ubuntu installed by mistake | “Install Ubuntu” chosen instead of “Try” | only “Try Ubuntu” subsection 9.6 stufe 9 6 | | stick formatted | after writing, Windows offers to format the stick | close the message with “Cancel” subsection 9.5 stufe 9 5 | | trouble with other people's devices | computers of a university or employer | start only your own computers from the stick | ⁠ In short If you write to the right storage device and do not change the boot chain, you take hardly any risk with the live stick. Recognizing the right storage device The writing tool completely overwrites the storage device you specify, from the partition table to the last sector. If that is accidentally the internal SSD or an external hard disk with your backup, its data is lost. This is the greatest risk of the whole way. Windows shows all storage devices in the program “Disk Management”; you open it by right clicking the Start button and choosing “Disk Management”. Figure 12 abb 12 shows schematically what you see there when an 8 GB stick is plugged in. Windows Disk Management, schematically. Disk 0 is the internal SSD with the EFI system partition, drive C and the recovery partition; Disk 1 is the stick, a removable medium with 7.45 GB. Only Disk 1 may be the target of the writing tool. Unplug all other USB storage external hard disks, memory cards, other sticks. Then the writing tool cannot hit them. Use a stick with at least 8 GB whose contents may be erased. Back up beforehand everything you want to keep from it. Plug in the stick and check in Disk Management the stick is labeled “Removable” and has the size you expect according to subsection 5.1 datentrager abbild und prufsumme.html stufe 5 1 , that is, about 7.45 GB for 8 GB. The disk with drive C , the EFI system partition and the recovery partition is the internal SSD; its partitions must never be changed. Note the drive letter and the size of the stick, and compare both in the writing tool before you start. ⁠ In short Unplug other storage and recognize the stick by “Removable” and its size; only then write. Fast Startup in Windows On most computers, “Shut down” does not end Windows completely. This matters for starting from the stick, for two reasons. Fast Startup is a function of Windows that, when shutting down, ends the programs but writes the state of the Windows kernel and its drivers to a file on drive C and resumes from there at the next power on instead of starting anew. It is switched on by default in Windows and takes effect only when shutting down, not with “Restart”. Why “Restart” is the right way to the stick. After “Shut down” with Fast Startup, the firmware at the next power on often passes so quickly over the moment in which it responds to the key for the boot menu that you miss it. And drive C remains in a half used state, which Windows expects to find exactly like that when it resumes. If another system changed something there, the saved state and the disk would no longer match, and Windows could damage files. That is why Linux mounts a Windows partition that is at rest like this read only at most. “Restart”, on the other hand, ends Windows completely and leads immediately through the firmware, where the key for the boot menu reliably works. ⁠ In short Go to the stick via “Restart”, not via “Shut down”, and do not touch the Windows partitions in the live system. Downloading and checking the image For the stick, you need the same image as for the VM. Steps. This is how you download and check the image Download the file ubuntu 26.04.1 desktop amd64.iso , 6.48 GB, from https //ubuntu.com/download/desktop https //ubuntu.com/download/desktop . From https //releases.ubuntu.com/26.04/ https //releases.ubuntu.com/26.04/ , download the file SHA256SUMS into the same folder, usually “Downloads”. Open a PowerShell in this folder; in File Explorer, you do this by right clicking an empty area of the folder and choosing “Open in Terminal”. Then compare with the value from the fourth line of SHA256SUMS The answer must be True . Calculating takes a while for 6.5 GB. If it says False , download the image again and do not use it under any circumstances. ⁠ In short Download the image and SHA256SUMS from Ubuntu, compare the checksum and continue only if the answer is True . The writing tool An image is not copied but written subsection 5.4 datentrager abbild und prufsumme.html stufe 5 4 . There are dedicated programs for this. A writing tool is a program that writes an image sector by sector onto an entire storage device. In doing so, it replaces the partition table and all the data of the storage device; whatever was on it before is lost afterward. Figure 13 abb 13 shows a stick before and after writing. An 8 GB stick before and after writing the Ubuntu image, schematic and not to scale. Before a partition table and a FAT32 partition with files. After a new partition table from the image, the ISO file system with the system and a small EFI system partition; the rest of the stick remains unused. The old files can no longer be found. ⁠ balenaEtcher https //etcher.balena.io https //etcher.balena.io is the simplest tool and runs on Windows, macOS and Linux. By default, it does not even display system drives, and after writing, it checks whether every byte has arrived correctly. Operating it takes three steps “Flash from file” and select the image, “Select target” and select the stick, “Flash ” and confirm the prompt from Windows. ⁠ Rufus https //rufus.ie https //rufus.ie runs only on Windows and has more settings. Rufus follows the language of Windows; the names here are those of the English interface. After starting it, check in the “Device” field that the stick is listed there with its letter and its size. With “SELECT”, you choose the image; leave the other settings as they are and click “START”. Rufus then asks whether it may download missing boot files “Yes” and in which mode it should write the image; keep “Write in ISO Image mode”. Finally, it warns that all data on the drive will be destroyed. At this moment, check the drive once more, then confirm. After about ten minutes, “READY” appears. After writing, Windows often reports that you need to format the disk in a drive before you can use it. The reason is harmless Windows cannot read the partitions from the Linux image. Click “Cancel”, never “Format disk”, otherwise the freshly written stick is empty again. ⁠ In short A writing tool such as balenaEtcher or Rufus turns the stick into a copy of the image; everything that was on it before is gone. For this chapter, writing was simulated on an image file the size of an 8 GB stick, with the small Alpine Linux image from subsection 8.6 das live system.html stufe 8 6 . Before, the partition table contained a single FAT32 partition spanning the whole stick. Afterward, it contained the table from the image Partition 1 covers the entire image with the ISO file system; partition 2 lies in the middle of it and contains the boot files for UEFI. The remaining 7.4 GiB of the stick no longer belong to any partition. The old FAT32 partition is no longer entered; its files, insofar as they lay beyond the end of the image, have not yet been overwritten, but without their file system they can no longer be found. With Ubuntu, the layout is somewhat different, but the principle is the same. A third tool, Ventoy, sets up the stick once; afterward, you simply copy any number of images onto it as files. That is convenient, but in its default setting, Ventoy bypasses the Secure Boot check, and with its own key you permanently allow the computer to start arbitrary boot programs via Ventoy. For experienced users, this can make sense; for a first live stick, balenaEtcher and Rufus are enough. Starting from the stick “Try Ubuntu” Now you start the computer from the stick. Check the warning in subsection 6.5 wie ein pc startet.html stufe 6 5 beforehand if your drive is encrypted, the recovery key must be backed up. The installer on the stick can install Ubuntu on the internal SSD and, in doing so, erase Windows with all its data. Therefore, always choose “Try Ubuntu” and never “Install Ubuntu”. Even in the running live system, an icon for installing remains visible, depending on the version in the dock at the edge of the screen or on the desktop; do not click it. Steps. This is how you start Ubuntu from the stick Save all open files in Windows. Plug in the stick. In the Start menu, choose “Restart”, not “Shut down” subsection 9.3 stufe 9 3 . In the boot menu, choose the entry with the name of the stick. If it appears twice, take the one that begins with “UEFI”; the other one starts in the old BIOS mode. On the page “Try or install Ubuntu”, click “Try Ubuntu”. Then the Ubuntu desktop appears. If Linux now runs with graphics, Wi Fi and sound, your computer will also get along with an installed Ubuntu. For trying it out, Ubuntu uses only drivers that are available as open source software; some graphics cards therefore run more slowly than later in an installation. ⁠ In short “Restart”, boot menu, the “UEFI” entry with the stick, “Try Ubuntu”, never “Install”. The operating system manages the hardware; its core, the kernel, is the only part that runs in kernel mode. Programs run in user mode and get hardware services only via system calls. Linux is a kernel; a distribution such as Ubuntu 26.04 LTS turns it into a complete system and maintains it for five years as an LTS release. A virtual machine is a computer made of software. The hypervisor allocates hardware to it; thanks to hardware virtualization, the guest runs directly on the processor, and everything that would affect the real machine ends up with the hypervisor. A snapshot freezes the state; NAT lets the VM out, but nobody in. WSL 2 is a real Linux kernel in a small VM that Windows manages. Linux sees C under /mnt/c , and Windows sees the Linux files under \\wsl.localhost ; practice files belong in the Linux part. An image is an entire storage device in a file. The SHA 256 checksum proves that it is unchanged, but not that it is genuine; only a signature establishes that. At startup, the firmware loads the boot loader, and the boot loader loads the kernel; Secure Boot admits only boot programs with a valid signature. Windows device encryption depends on this chain, which is why you back up the recovery key before any intervention. A live system places a writable tmpfs in main memory as an overlay over a write protected squashfs; after switching off, everything is gone, and the internal SSD stays unmounted. With the live stick, almost all risks arise from a wrong storage device or from changes to the boot chain unplug other storage, recognize the stick by its size, “Restart”, boot menu, Secure Boot on, “Try Ubuntu”. On Windows, you get a Linux of your own to practice on in three ways with WSL 2 as a small VM alongside Windows, with a virtual machine in VirtualBox or as a live system from a USB stick. All three protect Windows because there is a boundary between the Linux you practice on and the Windows data the hypervisor for WSL 2 and the VM, and main memory instead of the SSD for the live system. It becomes dangerous only where you cross this boundary yourself, when writing to a storage device and when changing the boot chain, and what helps against this is a checked image, the correctly identified stick, the unchanged start via the boot menu and a backed up recovery key. One principle behind all the results. Almost everything in this chapter follows from one idea security comes from layers that protect a lower one from an upper one, and each layer is only as secure as the path through it. The kernel protects the hardware from the programs, the hypervisor the host from the guest, the signature check the boot chain from unknown programs, and the write protected layer the live system from A command line is not free text; it follows a few fixed rules. This section shows how the shell splits a line into words, which word names the command, which ones tell it what to work with and how, and how you pass a word that looks like an option as an ordinary word anyway. The command line Before the shell can run anything, it has to find out which parts the typed line consists of. There is a simple, fixed rule for this. Words, not letters. The shell does not read the line letter by letter as a whole; it first splits it at the spaces into separate pieces. Only then does it look at what the first piece means. Figure 5 abb 5 shows this for the line uname r . The shell splits the command line uname r at the spaces into the words uname and r . Only then does it look at what the words mean. A command line is everything you type after the prompt before you press Enter. The shell splits it at spaces into words ; several spaces in a row separate like a single one. uname r consists of the two words uname and r . echo Hallo German for “hello” also consists of two words, because the three spaces separate like a single one. uname r , by contrast, is a single word, because there is no space in it; the hyphen separates nothing. ⁠ In short The shell splits every command line into words at the spaces. The command Above all, a line to the shell has to say what is to happen. As in a short sentence, this most important part comes first. The first word of a command line is the command the name of what is to be run. The shell looks up only this word; it passes all the others on to the command. Upper and lower case matter uname and UNAME are different names to the shell. If the space is missing, two words become one, and the shell looks for a command with this long name. The first three lines consist of nothing but a command. uname names the operating system, whoami “who am I?” the user, hostname the name of the computer In the last two lines, the shell reports that it knows no command of this name once because of the capital letters, once because uname r without a space is a single word. For some typos, Ubuntu also suggests similar sounding commands; you do not need to install anything for this chapter. ⁠ In short The first word of the line is the command, and in its name every letter counts, including whether it is upper or lower case. The argument Many commands need more than their name Which file should be displayed, which text printed? This information is in the remaining words of the line. The shell passes on words, not spaces. The command echo simply writes out the words it receives, separated by one space each. With it, you can see exactly what the shell makes of a line. Figure 6 abb 6 shows this for a line with many spaces. The shell turns echo Hallo Welt into three words. echo receives only the two words Hallo and Welt and writes them with a single space between them. Every word of the command line after the command is an argument . The shell passes the arguments to the command in the order in which they appear. What an argument means is determined by the command itself. echo receives two arguments, the German words for “hello” and “world”, and writes them out. How many spaces there were between the words, echo never learns The command cat shows the contents of the files whose names it receives as arguments. The argument /etc/hostname names the file hostname in the system folder /etc ; the slash separates the folder from the name of the file. The file contains the name of the computer Upper and lower case matter in file names, too there is no file Hostname . The error message begins with the name of the command so that you know who is complaining. ⁠ In short The words after the command are its arguments; the shell passes them on in order, and the command decides what they mean. The shell passes a command a list of words, without the spaces between them. For echo Hallo Welt , the list is echo , Hallo , Welt ; the first element is the name under which the command was called. If the shell starts a program for this, it hands the list to the kernel with a system call, and the kernel places it in the new program's memory. The program never sees the line you typed, only this list. That is why echo cannot reproduce the many spaces, and that is why it is entirely up to the program whether it understands a word as a file name, a number or text. Different things can be behind the first word of a command line a program of its own on the disk, a command that the shell handles itself or a short name for a longer command. It is stored as a file on the storage device, like a photo or a letter, except that it contains instructions for the processor. A program file is a file that contains an executable program. You can also start it by this name, with the same result Nobody types this in everyday work; uname alone is enough. So the shell finds the file by itself. ⁠ In short Most commands are program files, files with an executable program in them. The search path When you type just uname , the shell has to find the right file by itself. Searching the entire storage device would be far too slow, and there could be several files with this name. A fixed list of folders. The shell does not search the entire storage device, only a short list of folders that contain programs, and always in the same order. Figure 10 abb 10 shows the search for uname . The shell searches for the command uname in the folders of the search path, one after another. In /usr/bin , it finds the program file uname and starts it; it no longer looks at the remaining folders. The search path is the list of folders in which the shell looks for a program file with the name of the command; it starts the first one it finds. On Ubuntu, it includes /usr/local/bin , /usr/bin and /bin , among others. The command which names the program file that the shell would find for a name in the search path. A builtin command is a command that the shell runs itself, without starting another program. Its program code is part of the shell, not of a file of its own. The command type , itself a builtin, tells you whether a name is a builtin command. The shell changes its own folder, and the prompt shows /etc . ⁠ In short The shell handles builtin commands itself; commands such as cd and exit , which change the shell itself, have to be built in. The kernel manages the current folder separately for each running program. The system call with which a program changes it is called chdir , and according to its description, it affects only the calling program itself. A newly started program inherits a copy of the folder of the program that started it, but it can never change that program's folder in return. The POSIX standard explicitly concludes from this that cd must always be built into the shell, because it affects the environment of the shell itself. For the same reason, exit , history and type are built in the first ends the shell, the second reads its list of typed commands, and the third asks what the shell would do with a name. Other commands are built in only for speed; see the next box. With the option a , type shows all locations of a name, not just the first So echo exists both as a builtin and as a file. The builtin version is faster because the shell does not have to start a new program for it, and it wins because the shell checks builtin commands before the search path. You still need the file some programs start other programs themselves, and they can start only files, not parts of a shell. POSIX therefore requires that standard commands such as echo , printf , pwd and test also exist as files; cd is exempt because a file with this name could achieve nothing. Older versions of the standard required a file for it, too; that is why some distributions, such as Fedora, still ship a file /usr/bin/cd , which of course cannot change the shell's folder either. Both /usr/bin/echo and /bin/echo appear because on today's systems, /bin is just a second name for the folder /usr/bin and both are in the search path; it is the same file. The alias If you ask type about ls on Ubuntu, you get a third answer, neither “builtin” nor a file So if you type ls , you do not get exactly ls at all. A shortcut that gets replaced. Like a text shortcut on a phone that replaces “omw” with “On my way ” as you type, the shell swaps certain command names for a stored text before it processes the line any further a picture for orientation . Figure 12 abb 12 shows the swap. The alias ls while reading the line, the shell replaces the first word with the stored text ls color=auto . Only then does it search for the command ls and find the program file. An alias is a name that the shell replaces with a stored text while reading a command line if the name stands at the start as a command. Only then does the shell search for the command at the front of the replaced text. Ubuntu stores a few aliases in every session. ls becomes ls color=auto so that the list appears in color, and ll becomes ls alF , a detailed list. Aliases apply only in sessions in which a person types; a program that starts ls itself gets the ordinary program file. There is no command ll as a file. It exists only as an alias in your session, and before the search, the shell turns it into ls alF , which the alias ls in turn makes into ls color=auto alF . ⁠ In short An alias is a shortcut that the shell replaces with a longer command before the search. What is behind a name type and which With type and which , there are two tools for finding out what is behind a command name. They do not always give the same answer, and the reason for this tells you a lot about the shell. How the shell resolves a name, as a decision chart first alias, then keyword, function and builtin command, and finally the search path. type knows all the steps because it is part of the shell; which is a program file of its own and sees only the search path. type is built into the shell and therefore knows everything the shell knows aliases, builtin commands and the program files in the search path. which , by contrast, is itself a program file, /usr/bin/which . As a program of its own, it sees only the folders of the search path, not the inside of the shell that started it. For builtin commands and aliases, it therefore finds nothing, or only the file that would never be used. Table 1 tab 1 compares the two. Table 1 type and which compared. Only type describes what really happens when you type the name. | Name | type answers | which answers | | | | | | uname | uname is /usr/bin/uname | /usr/bin/uname | | cd | cd is a shell builtin | nothing | | echo | echo is a shell builtin | /usr/bin/echo , which is not used when you type the name | | ls | ls is aliased to ls color=auto' | /usr/bin/ls , without the alias | | ll | ll is aliased to ls alF' | nothing | With t , type answers with a single word per name; with a , it names all locations in the order in which the shell checks them The word file stands for a program file. The first line of type a ls is the one that applies when you type the name. ⁠ In short type says what the shell does with a name; which only finds program files in the search path. For the first word of a line, bash proceeds in a fixed order. While still reading the line, it replaces an alias with its text. That is why the alias comes before all other steps. If the word is a keyword of the shell language, such as if , it processes it itself; type if answers if is a shell keyword . If someone has defined a function with this name in the session, a small command made of shell commands, it runs the function. This chapter does not define any. If it is a builtin command, it runs it. Only then does it search the search path. When it has found a name once, it remembers the location so that it does not have to search the next time. If the word contains a slash, such as /usr/bin/uname , it does not search at all but starts exactly this file. If it finds nothing, it reports command not found ; on Ubuntu, a small helper program then also checks whether a command with a similar name could be installed. It fits the picture that on Debian and Ubuntu, which is itself just a short file of shell commands that queries the folders of the search path; its manual page says explicitly that it searches only the search path. So if you want to know what really happens when you type a name, ask type , which the POSIX standard provides for exactly this purpose. Exercises for Section 3 stufe 3 Use type to find out what is behind these names, and assign each of them to one of the three kinds cd , ls , echo , pwd , type , uname , history , ll . Which of them also exist as program files? Check with type a . cd , echo , pwd , type and history are built in. ls and ll are aliases. uname is a program file. echo , pwd and, behind the alias, ls also exist as program files. Each file appears twice, under /usr/bin and under /bin , because both folders are in the search path and /bin is only a second name for /usr/bin . The first line for each name is the one that applies when you type it. Predict what which outputs for cd , ll , uname and echo , and check. For which names does which give a misleading answer, and why? For cd and ll , which outputs nothing cd is built in, ll is only an alias, and which , as a separate program, can see neither of them. For uname , the answer is correct. It is misleading for echo when you type it, the builtin version runs, not /usr/bin/echo . Equally misleading is which ls with /usr/bin/ls , because when you type it, the alias ls color=auto applies first. The reason is the same in both cases which searches only the folders of the search path and knows nothing about the inside of the shell that started it. Suppose there were a program file /usr/bin/cd that changes the current folder when it starts and then exits. Describe step by step what happens when you type /usr/bin/cd /etc ; the slash at the front makes sure that the shell starts exactly this file. Where is the shell afterward? Why would it not help if the program ran longer? The shell finds no alias and no builtin command, because the name contains a slash, and it starts the file /usr/bin/cd as a new program with the argument /etc . The program receives a copy of the shell's current folder, that is, /home/student . It changes its own current folder to /etc and exits. With that, its copy is gone as well. The shell shows the prompt again, and with ~ , because its own folder was never touched. A program that runs longer does not help either it could change its own folder as often as it likes, but it never reaches the shell's, because the kernel gives each running program a current folder of its own and the system call chdir affects only the calling program. For each command, decide whether it has to be built in, is built in only for speed or could just as well be a program file, and give your reasons a exit , b echo , c history , d uname , e type . a exit has to be built in. It is supposed to end the shell itself; another program could only end itself. b echo is built in only for speed. A program /usr/bin/echo does the same job, but it first has to be started for that. The builtin version saves this effort, which counts when there are many calls. c history has to be built in. The history is in the shell's main memory; no other program can get at this memory. At most, it could read the file .bash history , and that file is written only at the end of the session. d uname can be a program file without any problem, and it is one it asks the kernel for information about the system and needs nothing from the shell for this. e type has to be built in. It is supposed to say what the shell would do with a name, and for that it needs the shell's aliases and its list of builtin commands. A separate program such as which sees neither of them.

Nobody knows all the options of all commands, and nobody has to. Linux comes with instructions for almost every command, in three forms a short help from the program itself, the shell's help for builtin commands and a detailed manual with a search function. This section shows all three and when to use which. The short help Often you know exactly which command you need but have forgotten an option. Then a cheat sheet that you can read at a glance is enough. The short help is a brief description that a program outputs when you call it with the option help . It names the usage and the options, each with one line of explanation; then the program ends without doing anything else. Each line names a short option and its long form. The line Usage shows the usage uname , followed by any number of options. On other Linux systems, the wording is slightly different; the options are the same. ⁠ In short command help shows a program's options at a glance. Help for builtins Builtin commands are not program files. Usually, they also have no entry in the manual that the next subsection introduces man cd only answers No manual entry for cd . The shell itself carries their instructions. The builtin command help shows the instructions for the shell's builtin commands. With a name as an argument, it describes that command; with the option d , in a single line; without an argument, it lists all builtin commands. The first line of help cd shows the usage, the second one the purpose. Below them follow a good 30 more lines with all the details, which the chapter leaves out here. The usage contains optional parts in square brackets; the next subsection explains how to read them. ⁠ In short For builtin commands, you ask the shell help name . The manual page The short help is a cheat sheet. If you want to understand what exactly a command does, which files it reads and what its messages mean, you need the complete instructions. For this purpose, Unix systems have had a built in manual for more than fifty years, divided into individual pages. Always the same layout. Every page of the manual has the same structure so that you can quickly find your way around. Figure 14 abb 14 shows the structure using the page for uname . The structure of a manual page, using uname as an example a header line with the name and section number, then NAME, SYNOPSIS, DESCRIPTION, OPTIONS and more parts in a fixed order. A manual page , or man page for short, is the detailed description of a command, a file format, a system call or another part of the system, collected in the manual that every Linux comes with. The command man with the name as an argument displays it. The parts of a manual page always appear in the same order, although not every page has all of them ⁠ NAME the name and a one line description. ⁠ SYNOPSIS the usage. ⁠ DESCRIPTION what the command does, often in detail. ⁠ OPTIONS every option with an explanation. ⁠ EXIT STATUS how the command reports success or failure. ⁠ FILES, ENVIRONMENT which files and settings it uses. ⁠ EXAMPLES examples, unfortunately not on every page. ⁠ SEE ALSO related pages. If you call man uname , the page fills the window. This is how it begins in a window 81 characters wide; in a wider or narrower window, man wraps the lines differently The header line names the page and, in parentheses, the number of the part of the manual in which it appears; this is the topic of subsection 4.5 stufe 4 5 . Reading the usage. The line under SYNOPSIS uses a compact notation that also appears in short help texts. Figure 15 abb 15 shows it with two examples. Anything in square brackets may be left out. A vertical bar separates alternatives, of which you choose one a| all means “ a or all or neither”. ⁠ Three dots mean the preceding item may be repeated. OPTION ... stands for any number of options, including none. In the terminal, text printed in bold is to be typed exactly as shown; underlined text or text in capital letters such as FILE is a placeholder that you replace with something suitable, such as a file name. Two usage lines, read step by step uname a| all s| kernel name … and cat OPTION ... FILE ... . Square brackets mean “may be left out”, the vertical bar “choose one of them”, three dots “may be repeated” and capital letters “put in something suitable here”. ⁠ In short man name shows the complete instructions in a fixed layout; you read the usage under SYNOPSIS with the help of the characters , | and ... . On 3 November 1971, the first edition of the “UNIX Programmer's Manual” by Ken Thompson and Dennis Ritchie appeared. It was already divided into numbered parts, from part I with the commands through the system calls to the file formats, and every entry had the same format with name, usage and description. Even then, a square bracket in the usage meant “may be left out” and three dots meant “may be repeated”. The pages were made from plain text files with formatting commands mixed in, from which a program typeset the finished page, and it is still like that today every manual page is stored as a small, usually compressed text file with formatting commands in one of the folders /usr/share/man/man1 to man8 , and man typesets it when you call it, to fit the width of your window. Because the format has stayed the same for more than fifty years, you can read a manual page of today with the knowledge of back then. Not every page is easy the page for bash has more than 7 000 lines. The pager Even the short page for uname fills the window, and most manual pages are much longer. If man simply output a page, its beginning would scroll out of the top of the window before you could read it. That is why man does not display the page itself but passes it on to another program. A book you leaf through. As in a book, you only ever see one page, leaf forward and back and can search for a word a picture for orientation . The text stays as it is; only the part visible in the window moves. A pager is a program that shows a long text one screen at a time and lets you scroll and search in it. man passes every manual page to a pager; on Linux, this is usually the program less . Table 2 tab 2 lists the most important keys of less . After q , you are back at the prompt. Table 2 The most important keys in the pager less , in which man shows the manual pages. | Key | Effect | | | | | Space bar, Page Down | one screen forward | | b , Page Up | one screen back | | Arrow keys | line by line | | / word and Enter | search forward for word | | n or N | next or previous hit | | g or G | to the start or to the end | | h | help on all keys | | q | quit | You are looking for the option of uname that names the processor type, but all you remember is the word “machine”. Type man uname , then /machine and Enter. The pager jumps to the first hit and highlights it; it is already the line m| machine in SYNOPSIS. n jumps to the next hit, the explanation m, machine under OPTIONS. q ends the display. ⁠ In short man shows its pages in the pager less the Space bar pages forward, / searches, q quits. The sections of the manual The same name can refer to different things in the system. uname is a command, but it is also the name of the system call with which this command asks the kernel for its information. Both have a manual page, and the manual has to keep them apart. The manual as a shelf with numbered compartments. Under the name uname , there is one page in compartment 1 commands and one in compartment 2 system calls ; under passwd , one in compartment 1 and one in compartment 5 file formats . The manual is divided into numbered sections , one for each kind of content Table 3 tab 3 . You write a page together with its section as name number , for example uname 1 for the command and uname 2 for the system call. man with a number before the name shows the page from that section; without a number, it shows the first page it finds, searching in a fixed order that starts with section 1. Table 3 The sections of the Linux manual. For work on the command line, you mainly need 1, 5 and 8. | No. | Content | Example | | | | | | 1 | Commands for all users | uname 1 , ls 1 | | 2 | System calls of the kernel | uname 2 , chdir 2 | | 3 | Functions of program libraries | printf 3 | | 4 | Device files | null 4 | | 5 | File formats | passwd 5 , os release 5 | | 6 | Games | intro 6 | | 7 | Overviews and conventions | man pages 7 | | 8 | Commands for system administration | lsblk 8 | For a name, whatis lists the NAME line of every matching page, with its section; man f does the same passwd 1 is the command you use to change your password; passwd 5 describes the file /etc/passwd , in which the system records its user accounts. 1ssl is a subsection of 1 for the commands of the encryption program OpenSSL. You get the page from section 5 only with the number You type the command for this as man 5 passwd ; man passwd alone shows the page from section 1. ⁠ In short The manual has numbered sections; if a name occurs more than once, man 5 passwd selects the page from section 5. Searching the manual man helps only if you already know the name of a command. Often, though, you only know what you want to do show the free memory, change the computer's name. Then you need a search across all pages. apropos searches a database of all NAME lines. The keyword host name matches two lines; each names the page, section and short description. The command apropos searches the names and short descriptions of all manual pages for a keyword and lists the hits with their section. man k does the same. The search covers only the one line under NAME, not the whole text of the pages, and these lines are in English. You write a keyword that consists of several words in straight quotes so that it arrives as a single argument. The hits whose names begin with rust are a peculiarity of Ubuntu 26.04, which ships many core commands in a rewritten implementation; for your search, you read them like the page without rust . For the last line, there is no page whose short description contains the word. ⁠ In short apropos keyword finds manual pages whose short description contains the keyword. apropos does not read the manual pages themselves; with thousands of pages, that would be too slow. It searches a small database that contains only the name, the section and the NAME line of each page. The program mandb builds this database, and Ubuntu brings it up to date after every installation of new programs. This results in three reasons for an empty search the keyword appears in the text but not in the short description, as with disk usage ; it is in another language, German for example, while the descriptions are in English; or the database is not yet up to date. If a word does not help, try a related one, such as memory instead of RAM . Which help for what The three kinds of help complement one another. Which one fits depends on what you already know and what kind of command you are dealing with. Figure 18 abb 18 sums up the way to the right one. Which help for what if you do not know the name, you search with apropos . If the command is built in, you ask help . For a program file, help is often enough; man shows the complete instructions. You want to know how long the computer has been running and do not know a command for it apropos uptime or apropos running leads to uptime 1 . You have forgotten how cd jumps back to the previous folder type cd says “builtin”, so help cd . You are looking for the option of head that sets the number of lines head help shows it as the second entry in the list. ⁠ In short Name unknown apropos ; builtin help ; program file help for the overview, man for everything. Which option shows sizes in easily readable units such as K and M ? Try ls S /etc and compare it with ls /etc . After man ls , you type /size and press Enter, and you jump from hit to hit with n . Under OPTIONS, it says The easily readable units come from h , long form human readable Print human readable file sizes e.g. 1K 234M 56G . Use apropos to find one command each that a shows the computer's name, b shows the used and free main memory, c shows the storage devices as a list. Note down your keyword. Why does apropos festplatte festplatte is German for “hard disk” find nothing? a hostname . b free ; the keyword memory alone finds it too, but among more than a hundred other hits. c apropos "block devices" leads to lsblk 8 list block devices ; in Linux terminology, storage devices are called block devices. apropos festplatte reports festplatte nothing appropriate. , because apropos searches only the short descriptions, and they are in English. On an ordinary GNU system, the usage of head is head OPTION ... FILE ... . Which of the following lines match this form? a head b head /etc/hostname /etc/os release c head n 1 v /etc/hostname d head /etc/hostname n 1 . How do you read a| all in the usage of uname , and may you write uname a all ? a matches the options and the file names are both in square brackets, so they may be omitted; without file names, head then reads what you type. b matches FILE ... allows any number of file names. c matches two options, n with a value and v , then a file name. d does not match the form, which puts the options before the file names; under Linux, the line works anyway, because the option parsing also allows them after the file names. a| all means a or all or neither of them, but not both. uutils takes this literally GNU uname is more lenient and simply outputs all the information for gnuuname a all . So the usage describes what is sure to work everywhere.
