People who work a lot on the command line still type very little. The shell completes partly typed names, remembers every line, finds old commands again and knows keyboard shortcuts for interrupting, ending and editing. This section presents these aids and explains who handles the keys behind the scenes. Completion Long command and file names are tedious to type, and every typo leads to command not found or No such file . Yet the shell already knows the names it knows which commands exist and which files are in a folder. Completion with the Tab key. If the beginning is unique, the shell completes the name at once. If several names fit, it completes the common part, and pressing the key a second time shows all the possibilities. Completion finishes a partly typed word as soon as you press the Tab key. In the first word of a line, the shell completes command names; in the other words, mostly file names. If only one name fits, it writes it out in full; if several fit, it completes only the part they all have in common, and pressing the key a second time lists all the possibilities. Type unam and press the Tab key. There is only one command that begins like this, and the shell writes it out with a space after it You add r and press Enter. Then you type cat /etc/host and press the Tab key twice. Three files begin like this, so the shell cannot decide and shows all three; below them is your partly typed line, unchanged An n makes the beginning unique. Press the Tab key once more, then Enter The shell completed the rest of the file name, and a typo in it was impossible. ⁠ In short The Tab key completes command and file names; pressed twice, it shows all the possibilities. The history You type many commands several times, often with small changes. Instead of typing them again, you bring them back, because the shell has written down every line. The history as a numbered list in the shell's memory. With the Up arrow key, you move backward through the list. At the end of the session, the shell writes the list to the file ~/.bash history ; Ubuntu does not even record a line that begins with a space. The history is the numbered list of recently typed command lines that the shell keeps in its memory. The Up arrow key brings back the previous line, and each further press an older one; the Down arrow key goes forward again. The builtin command history shows the list. At the end of the session, bash writes the history to the file .bash history in your home folder, and the next session reads it back in from there. Ubuntu sets up the history so that the shell remembers the last 1 000 lines and the file keeps at most 2 000 lines. Two more default settings a line that is exactly the same as the previous one is not recorded again, and a line that begins with a space is not recorded at all. This session starts with an empty history. The third line begins with a space echo geheim “geheim” is German for “secret” is missing from the list; history itself is an entry, too. Pressing the Up arrow key twice brings back the second entry, ready for editing or running In your own terminal, the numbers are higher, because there the history also contains the lines of earlier sessions. Repeating lines with exclamation marks. The shell also knows shortcuts that refer to the history stands for the previous line, n for the entry with the number n . The shell writes out the substituted line before running it so that you can see what happens ⁠ In short The shell remembers every line in the history; the Up arrow key and history bring it back. Everything you type on the command line ends up in the history and, at the end of the session, as plain text in ~/.bash history . So never type a password or an access key as an argument. Programs that need a password ask for it themselves and do not display what you type; this input does not get into the history. The space at the start of the line is not reliable protection it works only because Ubuntu sets it up that way by default, and often not on other systems. Reverse search If the command you are looking for is a hundred lines back, the arrow key is too slow. Usually, though, you remember a piece of the command, such as its name. Reverse search with Ctrl+R. Each typed character narrows the search, and the shell shows the newest line of the history that contains what you typed. Another Ctrl+R jumps to the next older hit. The reverse search searches the history from the newest line to the oldest for the text you type; you start it with Ctrl+R. Each further character narrows the search, and each further Ctrl+R jumps to the next older hit. Enter runs the command found, an arrow key takes it over for editing, and Ctrl+G cancels the search. The history contains uname r , whoami , uname m and head n 1 /etc/os release . After Ctrl+R and the letters un , the shell shows the newest matching line A second Ctrl+R jumps to the older line that contains un Enter runs it as if you had typed it again If there is no older hit, the shell writes failed in front of the search and stays with the last one. ⁠ In short Ctrl+R searches backward in the history for what you type; Enter runs the hit. Interrupting with Ctrl+C Sometimes a command runs longer than expected or waits for something that never comes, or you realize in the middle of a line that you wanted something else. Then you need an emergency exit that almost always works. Two key combinations that do not arrive as ordinary characters. Ctrl+C becomes a request to the running program to stop immediately. Ctrl+D tells the reading program that no more input is coming. The key combination Ctrl+C asks the program that is currently running in the terminal to stop immediately; almost all programs then stop, and the shell shows the prompt again. If no program is running, Ctrl+C discards the partly typed line. When you press it, ^C appears in the window. The command sleep 30 does nothing for 30 seconds and then ends; it is ideal for trying things out. Here, it was interrupted with Ctrl+C after one second. After that, uname r was typed and, instead of Enter being pressed, discarded with Ctrl+C The discarded line was not run. ⁠ In short Ctrl+C interrupts the running program or discards the partly typed line. In almost all programs, Ctrl+C copies the selected text; in the terminal, it interrupts. There, copy and paste work with Ctrl+Shift+C and Ctrl+Shift+V , in Ubuntu's terminal as well as in Windows Terminal. Windows Terminal additionally copies with Ctrl+C, but only while text is selected; without a selection, it sends Ctrl+C to the running program. If you get used to the variant with Shift, you never interrupt anything by accident. Every Ctrl combination with a letter produces a control character from the ASCII character table, which dates back to the era of teleprinters. Ctrl+C produces the character with the number 3, which is called “End of Text” there; the capital letter C has the number 67, and Ctrl subtracts 64. This character goes from the terminal emulator into the pseudoterminal from subsection 1.2 terminal und shell.html stufe 1 2 . There, the kernel handles it before any program reads it it turns it into an interrupt message to the program that is currently running in the foreground of the terminal. Most programs then end immediately. Because the kernel does this, Ctrl+C works even with a program that no longer pays any attention to keys. The command stty a shows the assignment in the line intr = ^C ; “intr” stands for interrupt. This meaning in the terminal is older than the graphical interfaces in which Ctrl+C later came to mean copy. The end of input with Ctrl+D Some programs read what you type, line by line, until you tell them that nothing more is coming. A word cannot do this, because any word could be part of the input. It takes a key of its own for “end”. The key combination Ctrl+D at the start of a line tells the program that is currently reading that no more input follows. A program that reads until the end of input is then finished. The shell itself also reads input; Ctrl+D on an empty command line therefore ends the session like exit . cat without a file name reads what you type and prints each line again immediately. Here, Hallo and Welt were typed, each followed by Enter, and then Ctrl+D Each line appears twice once as you typed it, once as cat printed it. After Ctrl+D, cat was finished, and the shell showed the prompt again. A second Ctrl+D on this empty line ends the shell; it writes exit as a farewell ⁠ In short Ctrl+D tells the reading program “no more input”; on the empty command line, it ends the shell. Most commands in this chapter belong to a collection of core commands that every Linux system comes with. Ubuntu 26.04 ships them in a newly written implementation and additionally the previous one. This section shows how to tell the two apart, how to run the previous one and where they differ. The core commands coreutils uname , head , cat , date and ls are not individual pieces from different makers; they come from a shared collection. If you know this collection, you know which commands you can expect on any Linux system. Figure 29 abb 29 shows an excerpt. An excerpt from the collection of core commands, ordered by task commands for files such as ls and cp , for text such as cat and head , for information about the system such as uname , date and df . In all, there are over a hundred. The coreutils “core utilities” are a collection of over a hundred basic commands for files, text and system information, including ls , cat , head , cp , uname , date and df . The classic implementation comes from the GNU project and is called GNU coreutils. Every Linux distribution contains an implementation of the coreutils. Because the GNU implementation has been the standard for decades, countless sets of instructions, scripts and help forums are based on its behavior. With version , each of these commands reveals which collection it comes from. The copy command cp comes from GNU coreutils, version 9.7, packaged by Ubuntu. ⁠ In short The coreutils are the collection of core commands; the classic implementation comes from the GNU project. In 1983, the GNU project set out to write a free Unix like operating system, command by command. For a long time, the core commands were in three separate packages for files, for text and for the shell; in 2002, they were merged into the coreutils. Together with the Linux kernel, these programs form the core of the systems that Chapter 1, Section 1.5 /wissen/en/informatik/linux und kommandozeile/ein linux zum uben wsl virtuelle maschine live usb stick/betriebssystem kernel und distribution.html stufe 1 5 calls “GNU/Linux”, which is also why GNU/Linux appears at the end of uname a . uutils the rewrite in Rust If you ask ls for its version under Ubuntu 26.04, you get an unexpected answer It is not the GNU implementation that answers here, but a different one. Two toolboxes on an Ubuntu 26.04 system. Under the familiar names such as ls , cat and uname , the commands from uutils run; cp , mv , rm and df still come from GNU coreutils. Under names with the prefix gnu , all GNU implementations are ready to use. uutils coreutils , uutils for short, is a rewrite of the coreutils in the programming language Rust that is meant to behave like the GNU implementation. The open source project has existed since 2013. Ubuntu has used it for most core commands since release 25.10; in Ubuntu 26.04, only cp , mv , rm , df and true still come from GNU coreutils. Other distributions such as Debian, Fedora and Kali continue to use the GNU implementation. For almost all tasks, this makes no difference the commands have the same names, almost always understand the same options and deliver the same results. Differences show up mainly in the wording of help texts and error messages. uname and head from this chapter are uutils; df is GNU. ⁠ In short Ubuntu 26.04 uses uutils, a rewrite in Rust, for most core commands; version shows which implementation answers. The GNU coreutils are written in the programming language C. C gives the program full control over main memory, and a small mistake in handling it can crash a program or turn it into a security vulnerability. Rust checks while the program is being compiled that certain errors of this kind cannot occur. Canonical, the company behind Ubuntu, therefore justified the switch mainly with security and resilience; speed, it said, was not the main reason. New code, however, brings new bugs with it before the release of Ubuntu 26.04, an independent audit of uutils found over a hundred defects of varying severity, including security vulnerabilities, which have been fixed bit by bit since then. cp , mv and rm stayed with GNU for the time being because of bugs that were still open. uutils is a single program file of just over eleven megabytes that is registered in the system under over a hundred names /usr/bin/ls , /usr/bin/cat , /usr/bin/uname and many more all lead to it. How does it know whether it should play ls or date ? From the first word of the list it receives at startup, that is, the name under which it was called background box “The shell splits, the program interprets” in subsection 2.3 der aufbau einer befehlszeile.html stufe 2 3 . That is why ls version reports the name ls and uname version the name uname , although the same file answers. Such a program is called a multicall program. A copy of the file under a new, unknown name therefore does not work the program does not recognize the name and does not know which role to play. Running the GNU implementation Sometimes a set of instructions requires exactly the behavior of the GNU implementation, or you want to compare a surprising output. For this, you need to get at the GNU implementation without rebuilding the system. What differs The two implementations are meant to behave the same, and in ordinary work they do. If you look closely, however, you find differences in three places. Two programs work in the terminal window the terminal emulator draws characters and passes keystrokes on, and the shell reads command lines and has them run. In Ubuntu, the shell is bash, an ordinary program in user mode. The prompt shows the user, the computer and the current folder; $ stands for an ordinary user, for root. Each window has its own shell and therefore its own session. The shell splits a line at the spaces into words. The first one is the command, and the rest are arguments; options begin with or , short ones can be bundled, some require a value, and after every word is an ordinary argument. What a word means is decided by the program. A command is an alias, a builtin command or a program file in the search path; type tells you which, while which sees only the search path. Commands that change the shell itself, such as cd and exit , have to be built in. Help comes in three forms help for an overview, help for builtins, man for the complete manual page with a fixed layout and numbered sections; apropos finds pages by their short description. The Tab key completes, the history remembers every line, and Ctrl+R searches it. Ctrl+C interrupts, and Ctrl+D reports the end of input; while a program is running, the kernel handles both keys in the pseudoterminal before the program reads them. uname , whoami , id , date , uptime , free and df make up a fact sheet of the system. Ubuntu 26.04 ships most core commands as uutils; there, the GNU implementation is called gnu …. You talk to a computer that understands only text through the shell it reads a command line, splits it into words, finds the command as an alias, builtin command or program file and has it run. What the words are and what they mean is defined by each program itself, following common conventions for options and arguments; you can look it up at any time with help , help or man . Completion, history and keyboard shortcuts save typing, and just a few commands reveal the kernel, distribution, user, memory and disk space of your own system. One principle behind all the results. Almost everything in this chapter follows from one idea the shell mediates; it does not do the work itself. What this is about On Windows, files are stored on drives with letters, C for the hard disk, D or E for a USB stick, and you look for them with the mouse in File Explorer. In a Linux terminal, there are neither letters nor a mouse. Still, thousands of files are stored there programs, configuration settings, logs and your own texts and photos. This chapter pursues one question How does Linux organize its files, and how do you work with them when all you can do is type text? It shows how to find your way around with a few commands, how to view, create, copy, rename and delete files and where a Linux system keeps its programs and configuration. Then it looks underneath What actually is a file name, why can a file have two names, and why is there no trash in the terminal? Finally, you find files again whose location you have forgotten and measure how much space they take up. Afterward, you can move around confidently in any Linux system. How to work with this chapter. The sections build on each other, and every new term has its own subsection with an example. Expandable boxes contain background why something is the way it is and where it comes from and derivations; you do not need them to read on. Boxes marked “Caution” state rules that always apply to practical exercises. Try the exercises ★ to ★★★ yourself first; the solution expands right below each exercise.

Before you learn commands for files, you need a picture of what a file is and how Linux organizes many files. This section establishes three basic concepts the file, the directory and the one tree in which all directories hang. A byte is the smallest unit in which a computer stores data eight bits, that is, a whole number from 0 to 255 in detail Python, Chapter 2, Section 3.3 /wissen/en/informatik/programmieren/python/werte typen und variablen/zahlen im binarsystem.html stufe 3 3 . Open a terminal and type cat /etc/hostname . The command cat shows the contents of whatever follows as an argument; Chapter 2 /wissen/en/informatik/linux und kommandozeile/die shell erste befehle/die shell erste befehle.html already used it. The answer is the name of your computer, here labor German for “lab” . ⁠ In short You need the shell, the structure of a command line, the current folder with cd , the pager and the byte as a number from 0 to 255. The file A computer is supposed to keep things, even when it is switched off a letter, a vacation photo, a program. This requires a unit that you can put away, find again and open. A row of numbers with a name. You can picture a file as a strip of small boxes, each box holding a number from 0 to 255, with a name tag stuck on the strip. Figure 1 abb 1 shows the file from the example above in this way six boxes, with the letters that the numbers stand for below them. The file /etc/hostname as a sequence of six bytes. Each number stands for a character 108 for l , 97 for a and so on; the 10 at the end marks the end of the line. The name tag is not part of the bytes. A file is a sequence of bytes that is stored permanently under a name. What the bytes mean, whether text, image or program, is not determined by the system but by the program that reads the file. To the operating system, a file is therefore just a series of numbers with a length. Whether it contains a letter or a photo becomes apparent only to a program that interprets the numbers in its own way a text editor turns them into characters, an image viewer into colored dots. The command od short for “octal dump”, output as numbers shows the bytes of a file as numbers. The option An omits the position information at the start of each line, and tu1 requests each byte individually as a decimal number The file consists of exactly six bytes. The first five are the characters l , a , b , o , r ; each character is stored as a number, according to a fixed table. The 10 at the end is not a visible character but the character for “a line ends here”. cat sent the same six bytes to the terminal, and only the terminal turned them into the letters labor and a line break. ⁠ In short A file is a stored sequence of bytes with a name; what the bytes mean is decided by the program that reads them. An operating system could store files separately by kind, for example texts differently from images. Unix, the model for Linux, deliberately decided against this in the early 1970s a file is just a sequence of bytes, without any structure that the system would have to know. The only task of the file system is to store the bytes permanently and to return exactly the same bytes the next time they are read. As a result, every program can handle every file a program that counts or copies bytes works for letters, photos and programs alike, without understanding them. The price is paid by the program that reads the file it has to recognize for itself what it is dealing with. The directory A system with thousands of files needs order. In Chapter 2 /wissen/en/informatik/linux und kommandozeile/die shell erste befehle/die shell erste befehle.html , the means for this was called a folder. On Linux, the usual name is directory, and this name reveals how it works. A list of names. At its core, a directory is a list, similar to a telephone directory on the left is a name, on the right the reference to what belongs to it a picture for orientation . Figure 2 abb 2 shows the directory /usr as such a list. Each entry leads either to a file or to another directory, which is again a list. A directory as a list of entries. Each entry links a name to what belongs to it; here each entry of /usr leads to another directory, and the entry bin in turn opens a list that includes the file bash . A directory is a list of entries. Each entry links a name to a file or to another directory. “Directory” and “folder” mean the same thing; from now on, the chapter says directory. What Chapter 2 /wissen/en/informatik/linux und kommandozeile/die shell erste befehle/die shell erste befehle.html called the current folder is therefore a directory. The name of an entry is also simply called a file name, even if it leads to a directory. The command ls short for “list” shows the names that are entered in a directory The directory /usr contains ten entries. This short list does not reveal whether they lead to files or to directories. ⁠ In short A directory is a list that links names to files or to further directories. The directory tree and the root Because a directory can contain further directories, you get level upon level. So that every location can still be named unambiguously, this arrangement needs a fixed starting point. A tree that grows downward. The directories are drawn like a family tree at the top a single directory, below it the directories that it contains, below those their contents. Figure 3 abb 3 builds up a section of this tree level by level. The directory tree grows from top to bottom. At the very top is the root directory / ; every other directory hangs from exactly one directory above it. Shown is a section with /etc , /home/student , /tmp and /usr with bin , lib and share . At the end, /usr is highlighted one arrow up to / , three arrows down. The directories of a Linux system form a single directory tree every directory except one is entered under its name in exactly one other directory. The one directory that is not entered in any other is called the root directory ; it is written as a single slash / . Two words for positions in the tree come up all the time. The directory in which another one is entered is called its parent directory . Conversely, every directory that is entered in another one is a subdirectory of it. Thus /usr is the parent directory of /usr/bin , and /usr/bin is a subdirectory of /usr . At the end of Figure 3 abb 3 , the arrow up points to the parent directory of /usr and the arrows down point to its subdirectories every directory except the root has exactly one parent directory but any number of subdirectories. No drive letters. Windows gives each drive a tree of its own with its own beginning, C \ or D \ . Linux has exactly one tree, no matter how many storage devices are connected. Another storage device does not get a letter; instead, it is mounted on a directory of the tree, and its contents then appear below this directory Chapter 1, Section 8.1 /wissen/en/informatik/linux und kommandozeile/ein linux zum uben wsl virtuelle maschine live usb stick/das live system.html stufe 8 1 . This is how, under WSL 2, the Windows drive C appears under /mnt/c Chapter 1, Section 4.5 /wissen/en/informatik/linux und kommandozeile/ein linux zum uben wsl virtuelle maschine live usb stick/wsl 2 linux neben windows.html stufe 4 5 . Figure 4 abb 4 puts the two arrangements side by side. Left, Windows two drives, two trees, each with its own letter. Right, Linux under WSL 2 a single tree with the root / ; drive C hangs as a subtree under /mnt/c . ls / shows the entries of the root directory These are all the directories of the top level; every file of the system is stored somewhere below them. No entry is called C or D . The entry init exists only under WSL. ⁠ In short All directories hang in a single tree with the root / ; further storage devices are mounted instead of getting a letter. Unix introduced the single tree back in the 1970s, and Linux adopted it. The advantage a location in the tree always has the same name, regardless of which storage device it happens to be on. A program that looks for its configuration in /etc does not need to know whether /etc is on the first or the second hard disk; the system administrator can move a subtree to a larger storage device without a single name changing. With drive letters, the storage device would be part of every name, and a move would invalidate every reference that contains it. Windows inherited its letters from MS DOS, from the days of the floppy disk drives A and B . Incidentally, Windows can also attach a storage device to a folder instead of a letter, but this is not common there. There is no mouse in the terminal to point at a file. You name a file by writing down its route through the tree. This section shows where you currently are, how to write down such routes, from the top of the tree or from your own location, and how to move around with cd . The working directory Anyone moving around a large building has to know where they are standing before they can describe a route. The same is true in the directory tree. A location in the tree. You can imagine that you are standing in exactly one directory of the tree. From there, you see the entries of this directory, the way up to the parent directory and the ways down into the subdirectories. Figure 5 abb 5 marks this location and shows how it moves when you change directories. The working directory as a location in the tree. At first, the marker is in /home/student ; after cd /usr/bin , it jumps to /usr/bin , and each time pwd names the route from the root to the marker. The working directory of a running program is the directory in which it is currently working. If you do not give a command a location, it refers to this directory. For the shell, the working directory is exactly the current folder from Chapter 2, Section 1.4 /wissen/en/informatik/linux und kommandozeile/die shell erste befehle/terminal und shell.html stufe 1 4 . Every running program has a working directory of its own; that is why two terminal windows can be in different directories. The command pwd short for “print working directory” prints the shell's working directory. A freshly opened terminal is in your personal directory. This time, the box shows the full prompt so that you can see how it moves along pwd prints the full route; the prompt shows the same, except that it abbreviates /home/student as ~ . ⁠ In short The working directory is the location in the tree to which commands without a location refer; pwd names it. The path To name a file that is not in the working directory, you have to describe the route to it. There is a concise notation for this. Directions made of names. A route through the tree is a sequence of branches first into this directory, then into that one, then to the file. You write the names one after another and separate them with slashes. Figure 6 abb 6 reads the path /usr/bin/bash step by step. The path /usr/bin/bash , read step by step from the root directory into the entry usr , from there into the entry bin , and there to the entry bash . Each slash is a branch. A path is a sequence of names, separated by slashes / , that describes the route through the directory tree to a file or a directory. Every name except the last must denote a directory. The slash thus has two tasks at the beginning of a path, it stands for the root directory; between two names, it separates them. Windows uses the backslash \ as the separator; on Linux, that is a completely different character. The path /usr/share/doc means start in the root directory, go into its entry usr , in there into the entry share and in there into the entry doc . usr and share must be directories, otherwise the route could not continue; doc is the destination and here also a directory. ⁠ In short A path is a set of directions through the tree names, separated by slashes. The absolute path Some directions are meant to work everywhere, no matter where you currently are, like a complete postal address with street, house number and town. An absolute path begins with / . It describes the route from the root directory and therefore denotes the same location from every working directory. /etc/hostname , /usr/bin and /home/student are absolute paths. pwd always prints an absolute path, because only an absolute path states unambiguously where you are. cat /etc/timezone shows the computer's time zone. The absolute path leads to the same file from every working directory ⁠ In short An absolute path begins with / and is valid from everywhere. The relative path Absolute paths get long when you work deep in the tree. Directions from your own location are often shorter, like “second door on the left” in a building that you have already entered. Two routes to the same file /usr/bin/bash . The absolute path starts at the root. The relative path bin/bash starts in the working directory /usr ; from the working directory /home/student , the same relative path leads nowhere. A relative path does not begin with / . It describes the route from the working directory; which location it denotes therefore depends on where you currently are. A single name such as bash is the shortest relative path the entry bash in the working directory. Figure 7 abb 7 shows how the same relative path leads to different results from two locations. In /usr , bin/bash leads to the file /usr/bin/bash ; ls confirms this by repeating the name. In /home/student , there is no entry bin , so ls finds nothing and reports “No such file or directory”. ⁠ In short A relative path begins without / and is valid from the working directory. The special names . and .. With relative paths, you can only go down, into subdirectories. To get up, you need a name for the parent directory, and sometimes one for the directory you are standing in. Every directory contains two special entries . one dot denotes the directory itself, .. two dots its parent directory. In the root directory, .. denotes the root directory itself. In a path, .. works like any other name ../.. means “two levels up”, ../share means “one level up and then into share ”. The single dot seems superfluous, because ./bin and bin mean the same thing. However, it is needed when a command insists on a directory as an argument and the working directory is meant. Figure 8 abb 8 follows a series of steps upward. Steps up with .. from /usr/share/doc one level up to /usr/share , with ../.. two levels up to the root. Another step .. stays in / there is nothing above the root. The last cd .. reports no error; it simply stays in the root directory. ⁠ In short . is the directory itself, .. the parent directory; in the root, .. leads back to the root. Translating a path into a file is the kernel's task, not the shell's. Every program that wants to open a file passes the path to the kernel with a system call Chapter 1, Section 1.4 /wissen/en/informatik/linux und kommandozeile/ein linux zum uben wsl virtuelle maschine live usb stick/betriebssystem kernel und distribution.html stufe 1 4 , and the kernel goes through it name by name. If the path begins with / , the kernel starts in the root directory, otherwise in the program's working directory. Then it looks up each name in the directory reached so far. If a name is missing, the route fails with the message “No such file or directory”. If a name that is not the last one is not a directory at all, the route fails with “Not a directory”, because you cannot look up another name in a regular file The names . and .. always have their fixed meaning, regardless of how a file system stores them. Because all programs go through this one mechanism, all programs understand paths in the same way ls , cat and every text editor. The home directory and the tilde Every person who uses a computer needs a place of their own for their files, just as every roommate has a room of their own. Because you need this place all the time, it has an abbreviation. A user's home directory is the directory that belongs to them for their own files. On Linux, it is usually /home/ , so for the user student , it is /home/student . The home directory is the home folder from Chapter 2 /wissen/en/informatik/linux und kommandozeile/die shell erste befehle/die shell erste befehle.html ; a new terminal starts in it. As an ordinary user, you may essentially create and change files only there; you may read most of the system's directories, but not change them. The abbreviation for it is the tilde ~ if it is at the beginning of a word, the shell replaces it with the path of your home directory before it starts the command. That is why it works with every command. ~/fotos then means /home/student/fotos , and ~root means “the home directory of the user root ”. In the middle of a word, the tilde remains an ordinary character. The command echo simply prints its arguments Chapter 2, Section 2.3 /wissen/en/informatik/linux und kommandozeile/die shell erste befehle/der aufbau einer befehlszeile.html stufe 2 3 . It therefore shows what the shell made of the tilde before echo started The directory /home/student/fotos does not have to exist for this; the shell only replaces text. The home directory of root is not under /home ; it is /root . ⁠ In short The home directory is your own place in the tree; ~ at the beginning of a word stands for its path. Changing the directory cd With paths, you can now describe any location. To work there without writing out the path every time, you change the working directory. The builtin command cd short for “change directory” makes the directory that its argument denotes the shell's new working directory. Without an argument, it changes to the home directory; with the argument , it changes back to the previous working directory. The argument may be an absolute or a relative path. On success, cd prints nothing; the new prompt shows the new location. Only cd states where it has changed to, to be on the safe side. Figure 5 abb 5 already shows how the marker of the working directory jumps. cd switches back and forth between the last two locations. The last two attempts fail /etc/hostname is a file, not a directory, and Etc does not exist in the home directory. The message begins with bash cd because the shell itself runs the command. ⁠ In short cd changes the working directory cd path goes there, cd goes home, cd goes back, cd .. goes one level up. ls is the command people type most often at the command line it shows what is in a directory. With a few options, it also reveals hidden entries, the type of each entry, size and age. Along with it come the rules for which names a file may have at all. The command ls Section 1 dateien verzeichnisse und der verzeichnisbaum.html stufe 1 already used ls to show the names in /usr and / . Here, the focus is on exactly what it does with its arguments. The command ls prints, for each directory given as an argument, the names of its entries, sorted by name, and for every other file its name. Without an argument, it shows the working directory. If you name several directories, ls puts the name of the directory and a colon before each list. If an argument does not exist, ls reports this and continues with the others. In a terminal, ls arranges the names in columns to save space. The directories appear in alphabetical order, not in the order in which they were typed. For the file /usr/bin/bash , ls only repeats its name this is the confirmation that it exists. ⁠ In short ls lists the entries of directories; for a regular file, it gives its name. The hidden file Many programs store configuration files in the home directory. If these files appeared with every ls , your own files would get lost among them. That is why there is a convention that keeps such files out of the normal listing. Figure 9 abb 9 shows a directory that looks empty without an option. The same directory /etc/skel listed twice. Without an option, the list stays empty; with a , . , .. and three files whose names begin with a dot appear. The files were there all along. A hidden file is a file or directory whose name begins with a dot. ls shows such entries only with the option a short for “all” ; A shows them as well but leaves out . and .. . “Hidden” only means not in the ordinary list. Anyone who is otherwise allowed to read the file can read it; there is nothing secret about it. The directory /etc/skel contains the files that Linux copies into a new user's home directory when it creates the user Without an option, the directory looks empty. With a , three configuration files of the shell appear, along with the two special entries from subsection 2.5 das arbeitsverzeichnis und pfade.html stufe 2 5 ; so these are real entries of every directory. Copies of the three files are also in your home directory; ls a ~ shows them alongside further hidden files. ⁠ In short A name with a dot at the start makes a file invisible to the ordinary ls ; ls a shows everything. A hidden file has no special attribute that would be stored in the system. There is only the rule that ls and many other programs skip names that begin with a dot. Graphical file managers follow it as well and have a switch such as “Show Hidden Files”. Windows is different there, “hidden” is an attribute that you can give to or take from each file individually, regardless of its name. On Linux, you make a file visible by renaming it. The type of an entry ls F In the ordinary list, a directory and a file look the same. But if you want to move around the tree, you have to be able to tell them apart. With the option F long form classify , ls appends a character to each name that reveals the type of the entry / for a directory, for an executable file, that is, a program, and a few other characters for rarer types. Regular files get no character. The character is not part of the name; ls only adds it in the display. Ubuntu also colors the names in the terminal, directories blue and programs green, for example; but the characters from F work without colors as well, for instance in a transcript or in this chapter. All entries of /usr are directories. /usr/bin/bash is a program, the shell itself. ⁠ In short ls F marks directories with / and programs with . The long format ls l Often you want to know more than the name How big is a file, when was it last modified, is it a directory? For this, the long format gives each entry a line of its own. A line of ls l , taken apart column by column type of the entry, permissions, a number, owner, group, size in bytes, the time the contents were last modified and name. This section explains the type, owner and group, the size, the time and the name. With the option l short for “long” , ls prints each entry on a line of its own with seven pieces of information type and permissions, a number, owner, group, size in bytes, the time of the last modification of the contents and name. Figure 10 abb 10 takes such a line apart. The details The first character gives the type. A stands for a regular file , that is, a file with contents such as a text or a program; a d stands for a directory. There are further letters for rarer types. Many files of a Linux system are text that you can read directly configuration files, logs, instructions. This section explains what makes a file a text file and shows the tools with which you view files in full, page by page, at the beginning or at the end, measure them and determine their type. What you need for this the text file The tools in this section work with lines and characters. For this, it must be clear how lines and characters are contained in the bytes of a file. Characters as numbers. Subsection 1.2 dateien verzeichnisse und der verzeichnisbaum.html stufe 1 2 showed that every character is stored as a number. The rule by which Linux today translates characters into bytes is called UTF 8. For the letters without accents, the digits and the usual punctuation marks, UTF 8 needs exactly one byte per character. For umlauts, accents and other scripts, it needs two to four bytes; the Ä , for example, becomes the two bytes 195 and 132. A text file with two lines as a sequence of bytes. After each line comes the byte 10, the line end; an umlaut takes two bytes. Below, the same bytes as a program shows them as text. A text file is a file whose bytes represent nothing but characters. It is divided into lines at the end of each line is the invisible character line end , the byte with the value 10, which programs often write as \n . So what is called a line is everything up to and including a line end. Figure 13 abb 13 shows a small text file as bytes. A file that does not consist only of characters, such as a photo or a program, is by contrast called a binary file. od c shows each byte as a character; the line end appears as \n The file has a single line with 13 characters and the line end, 14 bytes in total. ⁠ In short A text file consists only of characters; each line ends with the byte 10. Showing the entire contents cat For a short file, it is enough to write the entire contents to the terminal at once. The simplest command in this section does exactly that. The command cat reads the files given as arguments in turn and writes out their bytes unchanged, one after the other. The name comes from “concatenate”, to chain together with several arguments, cat joins the contents byte by byte, without putting anything in between. For long files, cat is impractical, because the beginning rushes past the top edge of the window. Because each of the two files ends with a line end, the contents appear on two lines. ⁠ In short cat writes out the contents of files one after the other; for short files, this is the quickest look inside. cat also writes the bytes of a program or photo to the terminal. For the terminal, some of these bytes are control commands; afterward, it may show nothing but strange characters. The command reset , which you type blind and send with Enter, gets you out of this state, as does a new window. So do not blindly output a file whose contents you do not know with cat . Reading page by page less It is better to read a long file like a book, page by page, with the option of paging back and searching for a word. The pager from Chapter 2, Section 4.4 /wissen/en/informatik/linux und kommandozeile/die shell erste befehle/hilfe finden.html stufe 4 4 does exactly that. If less receives a file as an argument, it shows the file's contents page by page. It does not change the file and does not load it all at once; that is why it opens even very large files immediately. In less , the same keys apply as for the manual pages Chapter 2, Section 4.4 /wissen/en/informatik/linux und kommandozeile/die shell erste befehle/hilfe finden.html stufe 4 4 . If less notices that a file is not a text file, it asks before showing it. Type less /usr/share/common licenses/GPL 3 . The first screen of the license appears, with the file name at the bottom. Type /Distribution and Enter, the search from Chapter 2 /wissen/en/informatik/linux und kommandozeile/die shell erste befehle/die shell erste befehle.html less jumps to the first place with this word and highlights it. With q , you are back at the prompt, and the file is unchanged. ⁠ In short less file shows a file page by page, with paging and search, without changing it. Beginning and end head and tail For many files, only one piece is of interest the head with a heading or the end, where the newest entries of a log are. A file as a stack of lines. head n 3 highlights the first three, tail n 2 the last two; the lines in between stay gray. The command head writes out the first lines of a file, the command tail the last ones. Without an option, it is ten lines each; with the option n and a number, you set how many. You already know head n 1 from Chapter 2, Section 6.1 /wissen/en/informatik/linux und kommandozeile/die shell erste befehle/das system erkunden.html stufe 6 1 . Figure 14 abb 14 shows which lines the two commands pick out of the same file. The file /etc/passwd contains one user of the system on each line; the user created last is far down. The third line of the license is empty; you see two lines of text and an empty line. In the user list, the fields are separated by colons; you can recognize the name student and the home directory /home/student . Without n , head shows ten lines. /etc/os release has thirteen ⁠ In short head shows the beginning, tail the end of a file, ten lines each or as many as n says. Counting wc How long is a file? Depending on the purpose, this means lines, words or bytes. One command delivers all three numbers at once. wc counts three things in a small text the line ends, the words, that is, sequences of characters between whitespace, and the bytes. Each number appears in its own column. The command wc short for “word count” prints three numbers for each file named the number of lines, counted as the number of line ends, the number of words, that is, of the character sequences between spaces, tabs and line ends, and the number of bytes. With l , w or c , it prints only lines, words or bytes. Several files get one line each, and at the end there is a sum with the word total . Figure 15 abb 15 counts the three quantities in a small text. The license has 674 lines, 5644 words and 35 149 bytes; ls lh showed 35K for it, rounded up from 34.3 KiB. On the test computer, there are 28 user accounts. /etc/hostname has the six bytes from subsection 1.2 dateien verzeichnisse und der verzeichnisbaum.html stufe 1 2 . ⁠ In short wc counts lines, words and bytes; l , w , c select one of the numbers. Determining the file type file Because the system does not record what is in a file, and because the extension is only part of the name, you need a tool that recognizes the type of a file by its contents. The command file examines each file named and describes what it contains, such as text, an image in a particular format, a program or a directory. It judges by the contents, not by the name. First, file checks whether it is dealing with a special type such as a directory. Then it compares the first bytes with a long list of known signatures, and only at the end does it check whether the bytes form text. The first check that matches provides the answer. Figure 16 abb 16 shows the middle step. How file recognizes a file it reads the first bytes and compares them with known signatures. For /usr/bin/bash , the bytes 127, E , L , F match the signature for programs; for the Ubuntu logo, the bytes 137, P , N , G match the signature for PNG images; the file name does not matter. /etc/passwd is text from the ASCII character set, that is, only characters with one byte each. /usr/bin/bash is a program in the ELF format, the format for programs on Linux, compiled for 64 bit processors of the x86 64 family; the name has no extension, and file recognizes it anyway. The image is a PNG graphic with 187 by 72 pixels. With that, you also have the tool for the caution box in subsection 4.2 stufe 4 2 before you output an unknown file with cat , you ask file whether it contains text. ⁠ In short file determines the type of a file from its contents, regardless of name and extension. Many file formats begin with a fixed sequence of bytes, a kind of signature called a magic number. Programs in the ELF format begin with the byte 127 and the letters E , L , F ; PNG images with the byte 137 and the letters P , N , G . od c shows this; it writes bytes that are not printable characters as octal numbers, that is, in base 8 instead of 10 , The option N4 reads only the first four bytes. file has a collection of thousands of such markers, together with rules for which further bytes it should evaluate, such as the image size for PNG. There is a practical reason why the marker is at the very beginning a program only has to read a few bytes to know whether it can do anything with the file. The kernel itself also checks the first bytes when a program is started, before it runs it. Creating a directory mkdir If you want to keep things in order, you first create directories one for recipes, one for photos. There is a command of its own for this. The command mkdir short for “make directory” creates a new, empty directory for each argument. The parent directory must already exist, and the name must not already be taken in it. A new directory is not completely empty from the start, it contains the entries . and .. . A directory that has only these two counts as empty. One call may create several directories. The second attempt to create rezepte German for “recipes” fails because the name is taken. The terse form reflects the state of uutils version 0.8 in Ubuntu 26.04; later versions may bring their messages in line with GNU. With intermediate directories mkdir p. If you want to create several levels at once, mkdir fails because the parent directory is still missing. The option p short for “parents” also creates missing intermediate directories and reports no error if a directory already exists. Figure 17 abb 17 shows how one level after another comes into being. mkdir fotos/urlaub/2026 fails because urlaub is missing. mkdir p creates urlaub and then 2026 ; the directories that are already there are left untouched. Under Ubuntu 26.04, the first message currently does not even name the path; the GNU implementation writes cannot create directory ‘fotos/urlaub/2026’ No such file or directory . In both cases, the meaning is a directory is missing along the way. With p , it works, and rezepte/kuchen and rezepte/suppen are created in passing. ⁠ In short mkdir creates directories; with p , it also creates all missing levels above them. Creating an empty file touch Sometimes you need a file before you write anything into it, for example as a placeholder for a list that you are about to fill. The command for this actually has a different main task; Figure 18 abb 18 shows both. touch on a new name creates an empty file with 0 bytes. touch on an existing file leaves the contents unchanged and only sets the clock of the last modification to now. The command touch sets the time of the last modification and of the last access of each file named to the current time. If the file does not exist yet, it creates it as an empty file with 0 bytes. touch never changes the contents of an existing file, even if its name suggests otherwise. With the option t , you can enter any time instead of the current time, written as YYYYMMDDhhmm . The new file belongs to you student and has 0 bytes. First, touch enters the evening of the previous day, then the current time again. The size stays 0. Under GNU, the option d with a time such as "2026 11 09 18 30" does the same; however, uutils version 0.8 in Ubuntu 26.04 interprets such a time as UTC and therefore shifts it in winter in Germany, the result is one hour later. This is a bug in this version that may disappear with an update. t behaves the same in both implementations. ⁠ In short touch creates an empty file or, for an existing one, only sets the modification time to now. Linux keeps track of several times for each file. The modification time, which ls l shows, belongs to the last write of the contents. The access time belongs to the last read; so that not every read triggers a write to the storage device, Linux usually updates it only if it is older than the modification time or older than one day. A third time, the status change time, advances with every change to the file's administrative information, such as the permissions or the name; it cannot be set back, not even with touch . Many file systems also store the creation time. Backup programs use the modification time to copy only what has changed since the last time; with touch , you can therefore make them believe that a file is new. The text editor nano An empty file is only the beginning; now text should go into it. A graphical program such as Windows Notepad does not exist in the terminal, but there are editors that run in the terminal window itself. A text editor is a program with which you create and change text files; it stores only the characters, no font and no formatting. nano is a simple text editor that runs in the terminal and constantly shows the most important shortcuts at the bottom edge. You start it with nano file . If the file exists, nano shows its contents; if it does not, nano starts with an empty page and creates the file only when you save. You type as in any editor; the arrow keys move the cursor. The commands work through shortcuts that nano lists at the bottom there, the character ^ stands for the Ctrl key, M for the Alt key. Under Ubuntu 26.04, these lines are in English as long as the system language is English. Figure 19 abb 19 shows the structure of the window. The nano window as a diagram at the top, a title bar with program and file name an asterisk means “unsaved” ; in the middle, the text with the cursor; at the bottom, a status bar for messages and two lines with shortcuts. One after another, the shortcuts for saving and for quitting light up. You need these shortcuts all the time ⁠ Ctrl+O saves “Write Out” ; nano asks for the file name at the bottom, and Enter confirms it. ⁠ Ctrl+X quits nano; if the text is unsaved, nano first asks whether it should save it Y for yes, N for no . ⁠ Ctrl+K cuts the line the cursor is on, Ctrl+U pastes it back in. ⁠ Ctrl+F searches for a word, Ctrl+G shows the help. You simply give nano the path as an argument. ⁠ In short nano file opens a text editor in the terminal; Ctrl+O saves, Ctrl+X quits. Many servers have no graphical desktop, and over a network connection, you often reach the computer only through a terminal. An editor that runs in the terminal works there just as it does at your own desk. nano is available on almost every Linux and is easy to use. You do not only work with files; you also rearrange them making a backup copy, changing a name, throwing away what is old. This section shows the commands for this, warns about their pitfalls and introduces patterns with which one command affects many files at once. All examples run in the practice directory ~/linuxk3 . Copying cp Before you rework a file, it is a good idea to keep the old version. For that, you need a second, independent file with the same contents. Figure 21 abb 21 shows what “independent” means here. After cp einkauf.txt einkauf alt.txt , there are two files with the same contents. If one of them is changed afterwards, the other stays as it was the copy is independent. The command cp short for “copy” copies a file cp source target creates a new file with the same contents under the name target . If target is an existing directory, the copy lands in it under the old name. If you name several sources, the last argument must be a directory. If a file target already exists, cp overwrites it without asking; its old contents are then lost. The option i short for “interactive” makes cp ask first; v short for “verbose” reports each copy. The first line creates a copy under a new name, the second a copy in rezepte under the old name. The last one fails with three arguments, cp expects the target to be a directory neu.txt , and it does not exist. With i , cp asks whether it should overwrite einkauf alt.txt ; n and Enter leave the file alone, y would have overwritten it. Without i , the second command overwrites without comment; v at least says what happened. ⁠ In short cp source target creates an independent copy and overwrites an existing target without asking; i asks first. Copying directories cp r A backup often has to cover a whole directory, with all its subdirectories and files. Without a special option, however, cp refuses to touch directories. cp r rezepte sicherung twice in a row sicherung is German for “backup” . The first time, sicherung does not exist yet it is created as a copy of rezepte . The second time, sicherung already exists the copy lands inside it as sicherung/rezepte . With the option r short for “recursive” , cp copies a directory together with everything in it, level by level. If the target does not exist yet, it becomes the copy; if the target is an existing directory, the copy lands in it. “Recursive” means that cp does the same thing again for each subdirectory until no level is left. The behavior at the target follows the same rule as for files and still surprises many people, as Figure 22 abb 22 shows. Without r , cp omits the directory and says so. The first cp r creates sicherung with the same contents as rezepte . The second time, sicherung already exists, so another copy lands in it as sicherung/rezepte . ⁠ In short cp r copies whole directories; if the target already exists, the copy is created inside it. A copy gets a new timestamp and belongs to whoever made it. For a backup, this is impractical, because later you want to see when the original was last changed. The option a short for “archive” copies recursively like r and keeps the timestamps, the permissions and, as far as allowed, the owner. So if you want to back up a directory, you usually use cp a . Moving and renaming mv A file is to get a better name or move to another directory. On Linux, both are the same operation, and there is a single command for it. Figure 23 abb 23 shows why. mv changes only entries. When renaming, the entry gets a new name; when moving, it disappears from one list and appears in another. The data of the file stay where they are. The command mv short for “move” gives a file or a directory a new name or a new location mv source target renames source to target . If target is an existing directory, mv moves the source into it and keeps its name. Afterward, the old name no longer exists. mv overwrites an existing file target without asking, just like cp ; here, too, i asks first. Unlike cp , mv needs no option for directories. The first line renames. The second moves, because sicherung is a directory. The fourth renames the directory sicherung together with its contents to archiv , because archiv does not exist yet; if there were a directory archiv , sicherung would land in it. ⁠ In short mv renames or moves, depending on whether the target is an existing directory; an existing target is replaced without asking. A directory is a list of entries subsection 1.3 dateien verzeichnisse und der verzeichnisbaum.html stufe 1 3 . There is a single system call for this, and the kernel as a rule carries it out in such a way that even a crash in the middle leaves no half finished state afterward, there is either the old name or the new one. That is why a file of many gigabytes is moved just as quickly as an empty one. It is different when the source and the target are in different file systems, for example on two storage devices. Then the kernel cannot move an entry from one list to the other, and mv copies the data like cp a and then deletes the original. That takes as long as a copy. Deleting rm What you no longer need should go. If you come from Windows, you expect a Recycle Bin from which you can retrieve mistakes. On the command line, there is none; Figure 24 abb 24 compares the two ways. Two ways to get rid of a file. At the top, the Trash of a graphical desktop the file is only moved into a special directory and can be restored. At the bottom, rm the entry disappears from the directory, and there is no way back. The command rm short for “remove” removes the named files from their directories, immediately and usually without asking. There is no command that undoes this. Without a further option, rm leaves directories alone. rm i asks before each file, rm v reports each deleted one. For Linux, an rm without asking is the normal case whoever types the command is expected to know what they are doing. What rm removes is gone. Before every rm , check the name, ideally with ls and exactly the same argument; the Tab key prevents typos. Back up important files with cp beforehand. The copy in rezepte has disappeared without any message. rm cannot remove a file that does not exist, and it does not touch a directory without an option. rm names the type of the file, a regular file, and waits. The answer n leaves the shopping list where it is. ⁠ In short rm deletes files immediately and permanently; rm i asks first. Graphical desktops on Linux have a trash, too. It is not part of the kernel but a convention between the file managers moving a file “to the trash” means moving it into the directory ~/.local/share/Trash/files and writing a small text file with the original path and the time into ~/.local/share/Trash/info . From this, the file manager can put the file back in its old place. So a trash is an mv , not a deletion. rm does not know this convention; it really deletes. Deleting directories rmdir and rm r Sooner or later, you also want to get rid of directories. There are two ways to do this a careful one that removes only empty directories and a thorough one that takes everything with it. The command rmdir short for “remove directory” removes a directory only if it is empty. rm with the option r removes a directory together with everything in it, level by level and without asking. The option f short for “force” additionally makes rm never ask and stay silent about missing files. That is why the line rm rf appears in many instructions, and it is the most dangerous command in this chapter one wrong path, and a whole subtree is lost. rmdir refuses because archiv contains files; rm r removes it with everything in it. rmdir removes the freshly created, empty directory leer German for “empty” without an error message. ⁠ In short rmdir deletes only empty directories, rm r whole subtrees without asking. Before every rm r , have ls or tree show you what is underneath, and type the path with the Tab key. Never give rm r a path that begins with / unless you know exactly why. If you are unsure, use rm ri and answer each question individually. Removing a directory can affect far more data than a single file. The system call that removes a directory therefore requires it to be empty, that is, to contain only . and .. ; otherwise it fails. rmdir is only a thin wrapper around this call. rm r , on the other hand, walks through the tree itself from the bottom up it first deletes all the files in a directory, then the now empty directory, and so on up to the topmost one. So the safeguard in the kernel remains in place; rm r merely satisfies it by doing the preparatory work itself. A pattern is a word of the command line that contains one of the characters , ? or . Before the command starts, the shell replaces it with all matching names, sorted by name. Here stands for any sequence of characters, even none, ? for exactly one arbitrary character, abc for exactly one of the characters in the brackets, 0 9 for exactly one from a range and abc for exactly one character that is not in the brackets. A pattern acts like a sieve through which the names of the directory fall a picture for orientation . It catches names that begin with a dot only if it begins with a dot itself; so hidden files stay hidden here, too. What matters is who does the work the shell, not the command. ls never gets to see the pattern, only the finished list of names, as if you had typed them one by one. That is why patterns work with every command that takes file names as arguments. strand ?.jpg does not match strand 10.jpg , because 10 is two characters; strand .jpg matches it. bn selects all names that begin with b or n . strand 1 requires a character after strand that is not a 1. Because echo merely repeats its arguments, it shows the list that the shell has made from a pattern echo received two arguments, not the pattern. In the same way, you can move all the mountain photos berg is German for “mountain”, strand for “beach” into a directory of their own mv received three arguments, berg 1.jpg , berg 2.jpg and berge ; the last one is a directory, so the two photos move into it. ⁠ In short Patterns with , ? and … select many names at once; the shell replaces them with the matching names before the command starts. If you want to delete all the text files in a directory, you type rm .txt . If a space slips in between and .txt , two words result matches all names in the directory, and rm deletes all the files among them before it complains about a missing file .txt . In / , there are a good twenty directories with short, puzzling names. They follow a plan that is the same on almost all Linux systems. If you know it, you know on any unfamiliar system where the programs, the configuration and the logs are. This section goes through the most important directories. The standard for the directory structure For programs to find their parts on every Linux, all distributions have to agree on fixed locations. This agreement is written down. The top level of the directory tree, colored by purpose programs and libraries /usr , /opt , configuration /etc , users /home , /root , variable data /var , /tmp , booting /boot , mount points /mnt , /media and directories that the kernel creates /dev , /proc , /sys , /run . The Filesystem Hierarchy Standard , FHS for short, specifies which directories a Linux system should have and which kind of files belongs in which of them. The current version, 3.0, appeared in 2015; today it is maintained by freedesktop.org, a joint project of open source developers. The major distributions largely follow it, though not always in every detail. Table 2 tab 2 lists the top level directories; Figure 26 abb 26 arranges them by purpose. Table 2 The top level directories according to the FHS. | Directory | Contents | | | | | /usr | Programs, libraries and data that come with the system | | /etc | Configuration of the whole system, almost exclusively text files | | /home | Home directories of the users | | /root | Home directory of root | | /var | Data that change during operation, such as logs in /var/log | | /tmp | Temporary files, writable for everyone | | /boot | Kernel and files for booting the system | | /dev | Devices as files | | /proc , /sys | Information from the kernel about running programs and devices | | /run | Information since the last boot, in main memory | | /mnt , /media | Mount points for further storage devices | | /opt | Add on programs that are not part of the distribution | | /srv | Data for services that the computer offers to others | | /bin , /sbin , /lib | Formerly separate directories for the most important programs and libraries; today found under /usr | For a tour, cd , ls l , file and less are enough change into a directory, look at the entries, check the type of an interesting file and read a text file. You cannot destroy anything along the way, because as an ordinary user, you may only read in the system's directories. Where even that is forbidden, Linux reports “Permission denied”, and you simply move on. ⁠ In short The FHS specifies which directory is there for what; that is why all Linux systems look alike in their basic outline. Programs and libraries /usr The largest part of a Linux system is the programs it comes with. They are collected in one subtree. The directory /usr contains the programs, libraries and unchanging data that come with the distribution. The programs are in /usr/bin , programs for system administration in /usr/sbin , libraries in /usr/lib and data such as manual pages and documentation in /usr/share . A library is a file with program parts that many programs share instead of each containing them itself. You know /usr/bin as the location of the program files from Chapter 2, Section 3.1 /wissen/en/informatik/linux und kommandozeile/die shell erste befehle/arten von befehlen.html stufe 3 1 ; on the test computer, it holds more than a thousand entries. Two further locations are intended for software that does not come from the distribution /usr/local for programs that the system administrator installs by hand, and /opt for larger add on programs, often from companies, that bring everything along in a subdirectory of their own. man1 to man8 are the eight sections of the manual from Chapter 2, Section 4.5 /wissen/en/informatik/linux und kommandozeile/die shell erste befehle/hilfe finden.html stufe 4 5 ; the other directories contain translations, de , for example, the German ones. ⁠ In short Under /usr is everything that the distribution brings along in programs and fixed data; your own add on software belongs in /usr/local or /opt . The FHS sorts files by two questions. First do they change during operation? Programs and manual pages change only when someone installs new software; they are called static. Logs, queues and intermediate results change constantly; they are called variable. Second could several computers share them? A program is the same on every computer, the configuration of one particular computer is not. The division follows from both questions | | shareable | tied to one computer | | | | | | static | /usr , /opt | /etc , /boot | | variable | /var/mail | /var/run , /var/lock | The benefit /usr can be on a write protected storage device or be provided over the network for many computers, and a backup mainly has to cover /etc , /home and parts of /var . Configuration /etc Every system is set up a little differently a different host name, a different time zone, different users. These differences are kept in a single place. The directory /etc contains the configuration that applies to the whole system. Almost all files in it are text files that you can read and, with administrator privileges, change in a text editor. You already know three files from /etc /etc/hostname with the host name, /etc/timezone with the time zone and /etc/passwd with the list of users. Many programs have a file of their own in /etc , whose name often ends in .conf , or a subdirectory of their own. With a pattern from subsection 6.6 kopieren verschieben loschen.html stufe 6 6 , you find files with a common beginning Besides hostname , there is hosts , a list of host names and their addresses on the network, and host.conf , which controls how names are looked up. All three are text files; less shows them. ⁠ In short /etc is the place for the configuration of the whole system, in the form of text files. The users /home and /root The personal files of the people who use a computer do not belong among the programs. They get a subtree of their own. The directory /home contains a home directory for each ordinary user, named after that user. The home directory of root is kept apart from it in /root . Because /root is directly under the root directory, the administrator can reach their files even when /home is on a separate storage device that is not mounted at the moment. Other users' home directories are usually not readable, or only to a limited extent. On the test computer, there is a single ordinary user. This user may not look into /root . ⁠ In short The users live in /home/ , root lives in /root . Variable data /var and the logs While the system is running, data are created all the time programs record what they have done, queues fill up, intermediate results are stored. These data need a place that is allowed to grow. The directory /var short for “variable” contains data that change while the system is running. An important part of it is /var/log with the log files files to whose end a program continuously writes what happens, each entry with the date and time. Because new entries are always appended at the bottom, you usually read a log from the end with tail the last lines are the most recent. Some logs only root may read, because they contain information about logins and other sensitive events. dpkg.log is written by the program that installs and removes software on Ubuntu. Each line begins with the date and time. Files with the extension .gz are older, compressed logs that take up less space. ⁠ In short /var takes in everything that changes during operation; the logs are in /var/log . Temporary files /tmp Many programs briefly need a file, for example for an intermediate result that nobody needs once they have finished. There is a shared place for this. The directory /tmp is intended for temporary files. Every user may create files there; when the system restarts, the contents may disappear. On the test system, Ubuntu 26.04 under WSL 2, /tmp is in main memory, as a file system of type tmpfs Chapter 1, Section 8.4 /wissen/en/informatik/linux und kommandozeile/ein linux zum uben wsl virtuelle maschine live usb stick/das live system.html stufe 8 4 ; when the computer is switched off, the contents are gone. Other systems put /tmp on the storage device and empty it at boot. Files that are to survive a restart belong in /var/tmp . Your own files that you want to keep go in neither place but in your home directory. Both belong to root , and the permissions end in a t instead of an x ; this has to do with the fact that everyone may write there. The size of /tmp is not 4096 but 140 a file system in main memory calculates the size of a directory differently from one on a storage device. ⁠ In short /tmp is a shared place for short lived files; what is to stay belongs in the home directory. Devices as files /dev Programs have to talk to devices to hard disks, to the terminal, to random number generators. On Linux, they need no special commands for this; devices look like files, as Figure 27 abb 27 shows. Device files are doors to the kernel. A program reads from /dev/zero , /dev/urandom or /dev/sdd by the same means as from a regular file; behind the door, however, what answers is not stored contents but a driver in the kernel. A device file is an entry in the directory tree behind which there are no stored contents but a device that a driver in the kernel manages. Reading from it or writing to it means talking to this device. The device files are in /dev . ls l marks them with letters of their own c for a device that delivers data character by character, b for one that works in blocks, like a storage device. Instead of a size, there are two numbers with which the kernel selects the driver and the device. Four device files are particularly well known /dev/null swallows everything written into it and delivers nothing when read; /dev/zero delivers any number of null bytes; /dev/urandom delivers random bytes; /dev/sdd is, on the test computer, the storage device on which the Linux is installed. /dev/null has zero bytes when read. Only zeros come out of /dev/zero , and different numbers each time out of /dev/urandom ; yours will look different. Only root and the group disk may read /dev/sdd , because anyone who reads the storage device directly sees all the files on it. ⁠ In short In /dev , devices appear as files; you read and write them with the same tools as regular files. One of the basic ideas of Unix is this almost everything a program works with appears as a file in the one tree. This has a tangible advantage. A program needs only a handful of system calls, namely open, read, write and close, and with them it can process regular files and devices alike. In the example, od did not know that it was reading from a random number generator; for od , /dev/urandom was a file like any other. The common naming is just as important because devices have names in the tree, the same paths and permissions apply to them as to files. The principle has limits, since some devices, such as network cards, have no entry in /dev on Linux; as a guiding principle, it still shapes the system today. The kernel as a file system /proc and /sys How long has the computer been running, which processor is in it, how large is the storage device? The kernel knows this information. So that you can query it without a special tool, it provides it as files. Figure 28 abb 28 shows how such a file comes about. A file that exists only when it is read. cat /proc/uptime asks the kernel; only at that moment does it create the line of text with the uptime and hand it back. This file is on no storage device. A virtual file system is a file system whose files are not on any storage device; the kernel creates their contents at the moment a program reads them. /proc is such a file system with information about the kernel and about every running program, /sys one with information about devices and drivers. In /proc , every running program has a directory whose name is a number. Besides these, there are files such as /proc/version with the version of the kernel, /proc/uptime with the uptime in seconds and /proc/cpuinfo with information about the processor. According to ls l , /proc/version has the size 0 and still delivers a long line the contents are created only when it is read. The first number in /proc/uptime is the uptime in seconds, here 46.5; the second counts how long all processor cores together have been idle. The pattern 0 9 selects all entries that begin with a digit one directory per running program.
