Sooner or later, you no longer know where a file is, or space is running low and you look for what is using it. This section shows find , which searches a subtree by name, type, size and age, and du , which adds up the space used. Searching with find ls shows what is in a directory; ls R and tree show whole subtrees. But if you are looking only for certain files, you do not want to read thousands of lines; you want a selection. How find works it enters the starting directory and goes through each entry, descends into each subdirectory and then returns. At each entry, it checks the conditions; whatever meets them is printed. The command find walks through the subtree below each given starting directory, entry by entry and level by level. For each entry, it checks the conditions that follow the starting directories, the so called tests, and prints the path of every entry that passes all tests. Without tests, it prints every entry. The paths begin with the starting directory, exactly as you typed it. The order is the one in which the entries are stored in the directories; it is not sorted. Figure 37 abb 37 shows the route through the tree. find begins with the starting directory itself, descends into kuchen , returns, takes the link zettel.txt along and descends into suppen . ⁠ In short find start tests walks through a subtree and prints the paths of the entries that pass all tests. Searching by name name Usually you remember part of the name the file ended in .txt , or “strand” appeared somewhere in it. For this, there is a test that understands patterns. Two ways to type the same pattern. Without quotes, the shell replaces .txt with the matching names in the working directory before the command even starts, and find gets a wrong condition. With quotes, the pattern reaches find unchanged, and find tests it against every name in the whole subtree. The test name pattern passes if the name of an entry, that is, the last part of its path, matches the pattern; the pattern follows the same rules as in subsection 6.6 kopieren verschieben loschen.html stufe 6 6 . The test iname does the same but does not distinguish between uppercase and lowercase letters. Here it is not the shell that applies the pattern but find , and it does so to every name in the subtree it walks through. For the pattern to reach find , you have to put it in quotes; otherwise the shell replaces it beforehand with names from the working directory, as Figure 38 abb 38 shows. The starting directory . is the working directory ~/linuxk3 . The links aktuell.txt and zettel.txt are found as well, because name checks only the name, not the type. iname finds the beach photos, although the pattern is typed in uppercase letters. The working directory contains three names ending in .txt aktuell.txt , einkauf.txt and zettel.txt . The shell replaced the pattern with these three, and find received name aktuell.txt einkauf.txt zettel.txt . It does not know what to do with the extra einkauf.txt , and it even guesses correctly that a pattern without quotes is to blame. ⁠ In short name "pattern" searches by name; the quotes make sure that find , not the shell, applies the pattern. Searching by type type Sometimes you are not looking for a particular file but for all directories of a subtree or all symbolic links, for example to find dangling ones. The test type type passes if an entry is of the given type f for a regular file, d for a directory, l for a symbolic link, b and c for device files. The letters correspond to those in the first column of ls l , except that f instead of stands for the regular file. Eight directories, including the starting directory, and four symbolic links. The link urlaub points to a directory but is counted as a link; find does not follow symbolic links but looks at the links themselves. ⁠ In short type f , type d and type l select regular files, directories or symbolic links. Searching by size size When space is running low, you look for the big chunks. Conversely, empty files help you track down forgotten placeholders. How size rounds files of 0, 32, 1024 and 1025 bytes on a number line, above them their size in whole KiB, rounded up. size 1k requires less than 1 and matches only the empty file; size 2k matches everything up to 1024 bytes. The test size n compares the size of an entry with n ; +n means greater than n , n less than n , and n alone exactly n . A letter after the number gives the unit c for bytes, k for 1024 bytes, M for , G for ; without a letter, the old unit of 512 bytes applies. Before comparing, find rounds the size up to whole units. Rounding up is a trap. A file with 32 bytes counts as 1 KiB, because a unit that has been started counts in full. size 1k requires “less than 1 KiB” and therefore matches only empty files, not all files under 1024 bytes as you might expect. Figure 39 abb 39 shows the rounding on the number line. The placeholders for the photos and the hidden settings file are empty; find always shows hidden entries as well. size 1k returns exactly the same as size 0 . Only size 2k also finds the recipes and the shopping list with their few dozen bytes, 32 to 59 on the test computer. If you are looking for files under 1024 bytes, the safest way is to write size 1024c . ⁠ In short size +n and size n search by size; because find rounds up to whole units, you use bytes c for exact limits. Searching by age mtime, mmin and newer “The file from yesterday” is often the only thing you remember about a file. find can search for that, too, using the time of the last modification of the contents. Figure 40 abb 40 shows how it counts the age. A time axis that reaches from now to the left into the past, divided into whole days of 24 hours. mtime 1 marks the most recent day, mtime +7 everything that lies at least eight whole days back; the cheesecake from October 1 is far to the left. The test mtime n compares the age of the last modification in whole days of 24 hours with n ; partial days are dropped, and +n and n mean more and less, as with size . mmin n does the same in minutes. newer file passes if an entry was modified later than the given file. So mtime 1 means “changed in the last 24 hours”, and mtime +7 means “at least eight whole days ago”, because an age of seven days and a few hours counts as 7 and is not greater than 7. With newer , you can create a reference file and later find everything that has changed since then. With touch t , the cheesecake gets a modification time in October Only the cheesecake is older than seven whole days; the other two recipes were changed in the last hour. Only the apple cake was changed after the reference file merker German for “marker” . Backup programs work on the same principle. ⁠ In short mtime and mmin search by age in whole days or minutes, newer by comparison with another file. Combining tests and processing matches A search becomes really useful only when you combine conditions regular files that end in .txt and are no older than a week. And often you want to do more with the matches than display them. If several tests follow one another, an entry must pass all of them. A in front of a test negates it. The option maxdepth n directly after the starting directories limits the search to n levels below the starting directory. What find does with a match is determined by an action ; if none is given, it is print , which prints the path. Two more actions are useful ls prints each match in a form similar to ls l , and delete deletes it. The test samefile file goes with Section 8 inode und links.html stufe 8 it finds all names of the same inode, that is, all hard links of a file. With maxdepth 1 , find stays in /etc itself and does not descend into any of its 91 subdirectories. The second search returns all regular files whose name does not end in .jpg . For samefile , the shopping list needs a second name delete deletes everything that passes the tests without asking, and if you are in the wrong directory or a test is too broad, it hits much more than intended. So always run the same line without delete first and check the list. delete belongs at the end of the line if it comes before the tests, find deletes every entry before it checks it. The trial run shows exactly the two files that are to go; the same line with delete removes them, and a second trial run finds nothing more. ⁠ In short Tests in a row must all pass, negates one, maxdepth limits the depth; use delete only after a trial run without it. Besides the silent “and”, find also knows an “or” o . Because “and” binds more strongly, you often need parentheses, and you must protect them from the shell, for example with a backslash find . \ name " .jpg" o name " .png" \ finds both kinds of images. find evaluates the tests from left to right and stops as soon as the result is certain; that is why the order matters, and that is why a delete at the beginning deletes everything. Because find walks through the whole subtree for every search, it can take a long time on large storage devices. Some systems also have the command locate , which searches a list of all paths that is usually rebuilt once a day much faster, but without the files that have been added since the list was last built. Measuring disk usage du df tells you how full an entire file system is. If you want to free up space, you need to know which directory is using it. The command du short for “disk usage” adds up, for each given directory and each subdirectory in it, the space that the files occupy on the storage device, in units of 1024 bytes. With s , it prints only the total for each argument, with h human readable units like ls h . du counts the space used, not the number of bytes in the contents. A file system allocates space in blocks, usually of 4096 bytes each with ext4; a file always occupies whole blocks, even if the last one is only partly used. A file with 32 bytes therefore occupies 4 KiB. With apparent size , du instead counts the bytes of the contents, like ls l . A file with several hard links is counted only once by du . The space of the directory rezepte , added up the directory itself 4 KiB, kuchen with two recipes KiB, suppen with one KiB, the symbolic link 0. Together KiB. kuchen occupies 12 KiB one block for the directory itself and one each for the two recipes. With its own block, rezepte comes to 24, as Figure 41 abb 41 calculates. fotos occupies 16 KiB, namely four directories of one block each; the empty photo files occupy nothing. 32 bytes of contents, but a whole block of 4096 bytes occupied. stat showed the same in subsection 8.1 inode und links.html stufe 8 1 Blocks 8 counts in old units of 512 bytes, and . ⁠ In short du sh shows how much space a directory occupies; whole blocks are counted, which is why even a tiny file occupies 4 KiB. A file system could manage every byte individually, but then it would need a huge list for each file stating where its bytes are. Instead, it divides the storage device into blocks of equal size and records in the inode only which blocks a file occupies. Large blocks keep this administrative data small and make reading large files fast, but they waste space with small files; 4096 bytes are a compromise that matches the page size with which the processor manages main memory. This also explains why du and df do not always agree du counts up what the files of a subtree occupy, while df asks the file system for its administrative data. A deleted file that a program still has open is no longer found by du , because it has no name; df , however, continues to report its space as used until the program closes it subsection 8.4 inode und links.html stufe 8 4 . A file is a stored sequence of bytes, a directory a list of entries. All directories hang in a single tree with the root / ; further file systems are mounted on directories instead of getting a drive letter. A path describes a route through the tree absolute from / , relative from the working directory. . is the directory itself, .. the parent directory, ~ the home directory; pwd shows your location, cd changes it. ls shows entries, with a also hidden ones, with F their type, with l type, permissions, link count, owner, size and time, with h human readable sizes. File names may contain anything except / and the null byte and distinguish between uppercase and lowercase. cat , less , head , tail and wc show and measure text files; file determines the type of a file from its first bytes, not from the extension. mkdir p , touch and nano create; cp , cp r and mv copy and move, overwriting without asking; rm , rm r and rmdir delete permanently. The shell replaces patterns with , ? and … with matching names before the command starts. The FHS organizes the system programs in /usr , configuration in /etc , users in /home , variable data in /var , temporary files in /tmp , devices in /dev , information from the kernel in /proc and /sys . A directory entry connects a name with an inode, which contains all the other information. A hard link is another name for the same inode, a symbolic link a file containing a path; rm removes only a name, and the data disappear with the last one. lsblk , findmnt and df show storage devices, mount points and usage; find searches by name, type, size and age, and du counts the blocks used. Linux organizes all files in a single tree in which every location has a path and every additional storage device is mounted on a directory; the FHS defines which directory is for what. With paths and a few commands, you move through this tree, view files, create, copy, move and delete them, select many at once with patterns and find them again with find . What this is about One program lists files, another counts lines, a third sorts. Each of them can do exactly one thing on its own. But many everyday questions at the computer need several steps How many programs are there in a directory? Which kinds of fruit are on a long list, each named only once? How do you keep the result of a command instead of just watching it scroll past in the window? And how do you tell whether a command worked without reading its messages? This chapter pursues one question How do you get small programs to work together so that they jointly solve a task that none of them can manage alone? It shows the paths by which data gets into a running program and out again, how to connect these paths to files and to other programs and how to make the next command depend on whether the previous one succeeded. The process So far, this series has spoken of the “running program”. That is no longer enough as soon as the same program runs several times if you open two terminal windows and start the editor nano in both, two instances of the same program work side by side, each with its own file and its own position in the text. Such a single instance needs a word of its own. As a picture for orientation a recipe in a cookbook corresponds to the program. Every time someone cooks from the recipe, a cooking session begins with its own pots, its own ingredients and its own state of how far along it is; two people can cook from the same recipe at the same time without getting in each other's way. Figure 1 abb 1 shows the same for a program. A program file on the storage device and two processes that were started from it. Each process has its own memory, its own open files and its own working directory. When a process ends, only the process disappears; the program file remains. A process is a program that is currently being executed, together with everything that belongs to exactly this execution its own area in main memory, the files it has opened and its working directory. The kernel keeps each process separate from all others. It gives each process a number, the process ID . A program is therefore a file stored on the storage device; a process comes into being only when the program is started, and it disappears when the program ends. For every program that the shell is to run, it starts a new process and waits until that process ends. A builtin command, by contrast, the shell runs itself, without a new process. In the early years of Unix, all programs wrote their messages to standard output. That was already a nuisance when you had the output written to a file error messages then sat in the middle of the data, and you saw nothing of them on the screen. The shell needs a new process for every program, and it sets up the redirection at exactly the moment when this process already exists but the new program is not yet running in it. The decisive steps are three system calls With fork , the kernel creates an almost exact copy of the shell process, with a number of its own. The copy inherits the open descriptors, including 0, 1 and 2, which lead to the terminal. In the copy, the shell opens the target file, for with the instruction to empty it; the file gets the lowest free number, say 3. Then it puts this file on descriptor 1 with the system call dup2 and closes 3 again. Now descriptor 1 of the copy leads to the file, while descriptor 1 of the actual shell still leads to the terminal. With exec , the copy loads the desired program, say ls , in place of the shell code. The open descriptors are kept. ls starts running, writes to descriptor 1 as always, and the bytes end up in the file. Meanwhile, the actual shell waits until the new process ends. Unix splits creating a process fork and loading a program exec into two steps precisely for cases like this between the two steps, the shell can set up what the future program starts with, such as where its descriptors lead, without the program needing a single line of code for it. And because a terminal and a file look the same to a program subsection 1.7 prozesse und ihre drei strome.html stufe 1 7 , redirection works with every program. What works for output also works for input the shell can connect the standard input of a program to a file or give it a few lines of text that are written directly in the command line. So far, the output of a program has led to the screen or into a file. This section connects the standard output of one program directly to the standard input of another. It explains the pipe, the programs that are suited to such connections, chains of many programs, a branch that captures an intermediate result and the principle by which Unix programs are built. The pipe How many programs are there in /usr/bin ? ls can list them, and wc l can count lines. With what Sections 2 ausgaben umleiten.html stufe 2 and 3 eingaben umleiten.html stufe 3 have shown, this works by way of an intermediate file That is three commands and a file that you have to delete again afterward. It would be more convenient to plug the standard output of ls directly into the standard input of wc . Figure 14 abb 14 shows this connection. The pipe ls /usr/bin | wc l Both processes are running at the same time. What ls writes to descriptor 1 collects in a buffer in the kernel, from which wc reads through descriptor 0. At the end, wc writes the number 1018 to the screen. A pipe connects the standard output of one process to the standard input of another. The notation command1 | command2 tells the shell to start both programs at the same time, each in a process of its own, and to connect descriptor 1 of the first to descriptor 0 of the second. The bytes pass through a buffer in the kernel, not through a file. The character | is called a vertical bar; on a US keyboard, you type it with Shift and the backslash key, on a German keyboard with AltGr+<. As with a redirection, the two programs notice nothing of the connection ls writes to descriptor 1, and wc reads from descriptor 0. The same number as by way of the intermediate file, with a single command and without a file. On your computer, the number depends on what is installed. The shell connects the pipe before it carries out the redirections of the individual commands. If the first command itself has a redirection, such as ls liste.txt | wc l , this redirection therefore takes effect after the pipe and wins descriptor 1 then leads into the file, and nothing comes through the pipe. A pipe connects only descriptor 1 to descriptor 0. Standard error of the first program still leads to the screen. If it is to go through the pipe as well, you write 2 &1 as the last redirection before the | . bash has the short form |& for this; it works exactly as if 2 &1 stood after all redirections of the first command, immediately before the | . Figure 15 abb 15 shows both cases. Top, ls /gibtsnicht | wc l The message from ls goes through descriptor 2 past the pipe to the screen, nothing comes through the pipe, and wc counts 0. Bottom, with |& Descriptor 2 also leads into the pipe, and wc counts the message as one line. On the first call, wc counts zero lines, because nothing came through the pipe; the message appears on the screen. On the second, the message came through the pipe, and wc counts it as one line. This is exactly why standard error is separate messages are not supposed to end up in the data of the next program. ⁠ In short command1 | command2 connects the standard output of the first program to the standard input of the second; both run at the same time, and the messages still go to the screen. connects a program to a file, | to another program. If you type ls wc , you do not start wc ; instead, the output of ls goes into a file named wc . If a file of that name already existed there, it would be overwritten In a directory full of programs such as /usr/bin , the same typo made as root Chapter 2, Section 1.4 /wissen/en/informatik/linux und kommandozeile/die shell erste befehle/terminal und shell.html stufe 1 4 could destroy a program of the system. A pipe is a buffer in the kernel with two ends, one for writing and one for reading; on Linux, it usually holds 65 536 bytes. The shell creates the pipe before it starts the two programs and gives each process the matching end as descriptor 1 or 0, respectively. After that, the kernel manages the traffic if the buffer is empty, the reader waits until bytes arrive; if it is full, the writer waits until the reader has made room. In this way, both programs run at the same time, and even a huge output never needs more than this small buffer. Once the writer has closed its end, for example because it is finished, and the buffer is empty, the next read request returns zero bytes the reader sees the end of the stream. Conversely, if a writer wants to write into a pipe that nobody reads anymore, the kernel ends it with an interrupt message Chapter 2, Section 5.4 /wissen/en/informatik/linux und kommandozeile/die shell erste befehle/schneller arbeiten vervollstandigung verlauf tastenkurzel.html stufe 5 4 . That is why the following pipeline ends, even though the command yes writes lines containing y without end head stops after three lines and thereby closes the read end; at the next attempt to write, the kernel ends yes . The idea is older than Unix. In 1964, Doug McIlroy wrote in a memo at Bell Labs that it should be possible to connect programs like a garden hose, screwing in another segment when the data is to be processed in another way. It was put into practice only in 1972 or 1973, when Ken Thompson added the system call for the pipe to Unix in a single night; the sources give different years. The first notation still used the same characters as redirection and lasted only a few months; then came the vertical bar. Dennis Ritchie saw the stroke of genius in the fact that a pipeline consists of exactly the programs that you use individually every day anyway. The filter Not every program fits behind a pipe. wc fits, because it reads its standard input when it does not get a file name. ls , on the other hand, never reads its standard input; whatever you send it through a pipe never arrives. Programs of the first kind have a name of their own. Figure 16 abb 16 shows four of them on the same input. Four filters, the same input the seven lines of the fruit list. sort sorts them, head n 2 keeps the first two, grep Apfel keeps only the lines with Apfel , and uniq changes nothing here, because no two equal lines are directly next to each other. A filter is a program that reads data from its standard input, transforms it and writes the result to its standard output. Most filters read files instead if you give them their names as arguments. This chapter uses the following filters, each of them here only in its simplest form sort sorts the lines; head n number keeps the first lines Chapter 3, Section 4.4 /wissen/en/informatik/linux und kommandozeile/dateien verzeichnisse und pfade/dateien ansehen.html stufe 4 4 ; wc counts lines, words and bytes Chapter 3, Section 4.5 /wissen/en/informatik/linux und kommandozeile/dateien verzeichnisse und pfade/dateien ansehen.html stufe 4 5 ; grep word keeps only the lines in which word occurs; uniq keeps only one of several equal lines that are directly next to each other; tr replaces characters subsection 3.3 eingaben umleiten.html stufe 3 3 . ls , echo , mkdir , cp and rm are not filters they do not read any data from their standard input. uniq has kept all seven lines, because nowhere in the fruit list are two equal lines directly next to each other. Here sort gets no file name; the fruit list arrives through the redirection from subsection 3.1 eingaben umleiten.html stufe 3 1 , and the result goes through a pipe to head ⁠ In short A filter reads its standard input, transforms it and writes the result to its standard output; that is why it fits behind a pipe. The pipeline How many different kinds of fruit are on the list? This takes three steps sort the lines so that equal ones are next to each other, delete the repetitions and count the remaining lines. Each step is a filter, and the filters can be plugged together one after the other like the stations of an assembly line. Figure 17 abb 17 shows the assembly line with the intermediate result after each station. The pipeline sort obst.txt | uniq | wc l as an assembly line. Under each pipe is what is flowing through it after sort the seven sorted lines, after uniq the four kinds and at the end the number 4. A pipeline is a sequence of commands connected by | . The shell starts all commands at the same time, each in a process of its own, and connects the standard output of each command to the standard input of the next. The standard output of the last command leads where it would have led without a pipeline; it can be redirected like any other. To the shell, a single command without | is also a pipeline, one with only one stage. The order of the stages matters uniq compares each line only with the one directly before it, so sort has to bring equal lines together first. The first pipeline shows the four kinds, each once. The second appends wc l and answers the question with a number. Without sort , uniq would have deleted nothing, as the example in subsection 4.2 stufe 4 2 showed, and wc l would have counted 7. The simplest way to bring a file to the start of a pipeline is to give its name to the first filter as an argument, as in sort obst.txt , or to use < . The notation cat obst.txt | sort also works, but it starts one more process that only passes the data on. ⁠ In short A pipeline lines up filters like the stations of an assembly line; each station works with what the previous one delivers. The branch tee Sometimes you want to keep an intermediate result of a pipeline and still process it further, for example save the list of kinds and count them at the same time. This would not work with , because then nothing would arrive at the next filter anymore. What is needed is a branch in the line, as Figure 18 abb 18 shows. tee as a T piece in the line What arrives from the left flows on unchanged to the right to the next filter and at the same time down into the file sorten.txt German for “kinds” . The command tee reads its standard input and writes everything it reads both to its standard output and to every file named as an argument. It creates these files or empties them first; with the option a , it appends. The name comes from the T piece in plumbing, called a tee , which splits one stream into two paths. wc l counted the four lines that tee passed on; the same four lines are in sorten.txt . ⁠ In short tee file passes its input on unchanged and at the same time writes a copy into the file. The Unix philosophy Why is there no program “count kinds of fruit”, but three small ones that you have to connect? Behind this way of building lies a principle that has shaped the tools of Unix and Linux since the 1970s. The Unix philosophy is a principle for building programs. Each program should do one thing well. Programs should read and write text, without unnecessary extras, so that the output of every program can become the input of another. You solve new tasks by connecting existing programs instead of writing a big new one. The advantage shows as soon as the question changes. Connected in new ways, the same small programs answer completely different questions for which nobody has written a program of its own. How often is Apfel on the fruit list, and how many entries does the shopping list have? grep searches, wc counts; neither of the two knows anything about fruit or shopping. For this to work, filters write only their data and no headings or notices in between that the next filter would take for data. ⁠ In short Small programs that do one thing well and read and write text can be connected into ever new tool chains. In 1978, Doug McIlroy and two colleagues wrote down a few rules of style in the foreword to a collection of papers on Unix; to this day, they are regarded as the core of the Unix philosophy. In essence, they say Each program should do one thing well; for a new task, it is better to build a new program than to overload an old one with additional features. You should expect the output of every program to become the input of another one that does not even exist yet; therefore, no extraneous information in the output, no input formats with rigid columns or made of binary data, and no program should insist on getting its input in a dialog with a person. Many peculiarities that came up in this chapter follow from this into a file, ls writes one name per line and no columns; messages go into a stream of their own; and the programs are small enough to be combined in one line. The common language is text in lines every program that reads lines and writes lines can be connected to every other program of this kind. Every command ends either with success or with failure, and the next step often depends on which. This section shows how a process leaves behind a number when it ends, how you query it and what the different numbers mean. The exit status Whether a command worked can often be read from its messages. That is enough for a person, but not for the shell it should be able to make the next command depend on it without interpreting texts that differ from program to program and from language to language. This requires a simple, uniform answer from every process. Figure 19 abb 19 shows where it comes from. A process ends and leaves behind a number. The kernel passes it on to the shell, which has been waiting for the end; the shell remembers the number, and echo ? . Before the shell executes a command line, it replaces ? writes out this number. The first ls succeeded; its output went to /dev/null . The second failed with exit status 2. The last echo 300 = 256 + 44 ? returns the number of the most recently ended command. If you think of truth values, you might expect 1 to stand for “it worked”. With the exit status, it is the other way around, and there is a simple reason for this there is exactly one kind of success but many kinds of failure. With 0 for success, all other numbers remain free to distinguish different errors. That only 0 to 255 are possible is due to the path the number takes. When a program ends, it does pass an arbitrary integer to the kernel, but on Linux, only its lowest byte, that is, eight bits, arrives at the waiting shell; this corresponds exactly to the remainder of division by 256. The waiting shell learns the number through a system call with which a process waits for the end of a process that it started. What the nonzero numbers mean “Failure” can mean different things a search found nothing, or the file that was to be searched does not even exist. A program that knows more than one kind of failure can distinguish them with different numbers. Figure 20 abb 20 shows this with the search program grep . Three outcomes of a search with grep q The word occurs in the file, exit status 0; it does not occur, exit status 1; the file is missing, exit status 2. Only in the third case is there a message. Which nonzero number means which failure is determined by each program itself; the manual page describes it in its EXIT STATUS part Chapter 2, Section 4.3 /wissen/en/informatik/linux und kommandozeile/die shell erste befehle/hilfe finden.html stufe 4 3 . Many programs report every failure with 1. Programs that distinguish several kinds usually use 1 for a “no” result or a minor error and 2 for a serious error or an incorrect call. The option q short for quiet makes grep output nothing and answer only with its exit status; it still writes error messages, though. grep distinguishes three cases. The 1 is not an error in the strict sense but the answer “does not occur”; only the 2 reports that the search was not possible at all. cat reports every failure with 1. In the previous subsection, ls ended with 2 because a file that had been explicitly asked for did not exist; it reports minor problems with 1. ⁠ In short The nonzero number says which failure it was; what it means is stated in the program's manual page. The shell's numbers 126, 127 and 128 + n Sometimes a program never gets to leave a number behind the command does not exist, the file cannot be executed, or the process is aborted in the middle of its work. For these cases, the shell itself puts in numbers that are worth remembering. Figure 21 abb 21 places them on the number line. The number line of the exit status from 0 to 255 0 for success, the small numbers for errors reported by the program itself, 126 and 127 for commands that could not start and, from 129 upward, aborts by an interrupt message, such as 130 for Ctrl+C. The shell itself sets an exit status in three cases 127 if the command does not exist; 126 if the file does exist but cannot be executed as a program; if the process was ended by the interrupt message with the number . Each kind of interrupt message has a number. The message that Ctrl+C triggers Chapter 2, Section 5.4 /wissen/en/informatik/linux und kommandozeile/die shell erste befehle/schneller arbeiten vervollstandigung verlauf tastenkurzel.html stufe 5 4 has the number 2; a process aborted with Ctrl+C therefore leaves behind . A command gibtsnicht exists neither as a builtin nor in the search path. Next, the shell is to execute the directory /etc /etc exists, but a directory is not a program. Finally, sleep 10 waits ten seconds; type Ctrl+C before they are up The terminal shows Ctrl+C as ^C . sleep was ended by message number 2, so . ⁠ In short 127 means “not found”, 126 “not executable”, and means “ended by interrupt message ”, such as 130 after Ctrl+C. The kernel tells the waiting shell exactly how a process ended either by itself, with a number from 0 to 255, or by an interrupt message, with the number of that message. With the exit status, the shell can decide whether to continue. This section shows how to write several commands in one line simply one after another, only on success, only on failure or in combination. Finally, it clarifies which exit status a pipeline has in which several processes end. One after another the semicolon Sometimes you want to send off several commands at once without waiting for the prompt after each one. The notation command1 ; command2 first runs command1 , waits until it ends and then runs command2 , regardless of the exit status with which command1 ended. The exit status of the whole line is that of the last command. The semicolon therefore acts like the Enter key between two lines. Spaces around the semicolon are allowed but not necessary. Although ls failed, the second echo runs. ⁠ In short The semicolon runs commands one after another without paying attention to whether they succeed. If the output of several commands is to go into the same file, you do not have to redirect each one separately. Curly braces combine them into a group, and a redirection after the group applies to all the commands in it The shell is strict here after { there must be a space, and the last command before } also ends with a semicolon. The exit status of the group is that of its last command. Only on success && Often the second step makes sense only if the first one worked a file should be copied into a directory only if the directory exists; the old list should be replaced only if the sorting worked. The notation command1 && command2 is an AND list the shell runs command2 only if command1 ended with exit status 0. The exit status of the AND list is that of the last command executed. The name fits the whole list succeeds only if the first AND the second command succeed. If the first one already fails, the result is settled, and the shell skips the second. If you know Python, you will find the same idea there in and Python, Chapter 3, Section 1.8 /wissen/en/informatik/programmieren/python/entscheidungen und schleifen/bedingungen vergleiche und logische operatoren.html stufe 1 8 ; in the shell, however, the exit status decides, and 0 counts as success. In the first case, mkdir p succeeded, so cp ran. In the second, cp failed, and the echo did not run; kopiert German for “copied” does not appear. The solution to the truncation trap from subsection 2.7 ausgaben umleiten.html stufe 2 7 becomes safer with && the original file is replaced only if sort succeeded; if it fails, mv does not run, and the old list stays intact. ⁠ In short command1 && command2 runs the second command only if the first one succeeded. Only on failure || You need the counterpart for the case that something goes wrong then a message should appear or a fallback should take over. Figure 22 abb 22 shows both operators side by side as railroad switches. Two switches that are set by the exit status of the first command. Left, && at 0, the way leads to the second command, otherwise past it. Right, || at a nonzero number, the way leads to the second command, at 0 past it. The notation command1 || command2 is an OR list the shell runs command2 only if command1 ended with a nonzero exit status. The exit status of the OR list is that of the last command executed. Here, too, the name fits the list succeeds if the first OR the second command succeeds. If the first one already succeeded, the second is no longer needed. Mangoes are not on the list, grep q ends with 1, and the message appears “Keine Mangos da.” is German for “No mangoes here.” . Kiwis are on it, grep q ends with 0, and the shell skips the echo . ⁠ In short command1 || command2 runs the second command only if the first one failed. && and || in one line With both operators together, you can write “if …, then …, else …” in one line. This works almost always, but not always, and the borderline case is one of the most common traps in the shell. Figure 23 abb 23 shows all the paths through such a line. The paths through a && b || c as a decision tree. If a fails, c runs. If a succeeds, b runs; if b also succeeds, the line is done. But if b fails, c runs as well the path marked in red, which is easy to overlook. && and || have equal precedence and are evaluated from left to right. a && b || c therefore means first a && b as a whole, then c if this whole failed. So c runs if a fails, and also if a succeeds and b fails. Here the line behaves like “if, then, else”, because echo practically always succeeds. There are apples, so cat ran. It failed, so grep … && cat … failed as a whole, and the shell also ran the echo . The message “Keine Äpfel.” German for “No apples.” is wrong. ⁠ In short a && b || c is an “if, then, else” only if b cannot fail; otherwise c also runs after a failed b . The exit status of a pipeline In a pipeline, several processes end, and each leaves behind its own exit status. A pipe delivers data to standard input. Some programs, however, do not read their standard input but expect file names as arguments. This section shows how to turn a list of names from a pipe into arguments, how to manage this with names that contain spaces and how find passes its matches to a command itself. Stream or argument If a pipe delivers a list of file names, it seems natural to pass it straight on to rm or wc . That goes wrong, and in two different ways. Figure 26 abb 26 shows why a process receives data through two separate ways in. Two separate ways into a process the shell fixes the arguments at the start; standard input is a stream that flows afterward. With echo probe2.txt | rm , the name arrives in the stream, and the argument list of rm stays empty. With echo einkauf.txt | wc l , wc reads the name as one line of data. A pipe connects streams, not arguments. What comes through the pipe is in the standard input of the next program and never in its argument list. A program that does not read its standard input sees none of it; a filter treats it as data, not as file names. rm does not read its standard input, got no argument and complains that the name is missing. wc l read its standard input and counted one line in it, namely the line einkauf.txt ; it never opened the file itself. That file has five lines. ⁠ In short What comes through a pipe is input, not an argument; programs without input do not see it, and filters take it for data. The command xargs So between the pipe and the program, a translator is missing that takes the words from the stream and appends them to the program as arguments. Figure 27 abb 27 shows it at work. xargs as a translator the words einkauf.txt and obst.txt come from standard input. xargs appends them to the command line wc l and starts wc l einkauf.txt obst.txt as a new process. The command xargs reads its standard input and splits it into words at spaces, tabs and line ends. Then it starts the command that follows it as arguments and appends these words at the end as additional arguments. Without a command, it uses echo . xargs started wc l einkauf.txt obst.txt ; wc opened both files and counted their lines. Only together with find Chapter 3, Section 10.1 /wissen/en/informatik/linux und kommandozeile/dateien verzeichnisse und pfade/dateien finden und platz messen.html stufe 10 1 does xargs show what it is good for the list of names comes into being during the search, and nobody has to type it. find writes each match on a line of its own; xargs turns all the lines into arguments for a single call of wc l . The order is the one in which find comes across the entries. ⁠ In short xargs command turns the words of its standard input into arguments for the command. Batches xargs n and the argument list limit Some commands take only one argument at a time, and no command tolerates arbitrarily many the kernel has an upper limit for all the arguments of a program start together. xargs can therefore divide the words into batches and start the command several times. Figure 28 abb 28 shows this. Three words, two ways to divide them into batches. Top, without n one call with all three words. Bottom, with n 1 three calls with one word each. The kernel limits how many bytes all the arguments of a program start may have together; getconf ARG MAX shows this argument list limit . xargs keeps to it on its own and starts the command as often as necessary. With n number , it passes at most number words per call. Besides the arguments, a few further pieces of information that every program receives at its start also count toward the limit. If a program start fails because of the limit, the shell reports “Argument list too long”. With n 1 , xargs started echo Obst three times, each time with one word; without n , it started it once with all three. That is bytes, exactly 2 MiB. The thousand names from /usr/bin need only a small part of it; with hundreds of thousands of files, however, the limit is reached quickly. ⁠ In short There is an upper limit for the arguments of a program start; xargs distributes the words over several calls on its own, and with n in batches of a fixed size. When loading a program with exec , the kernel copies all the arguments into the memory of the process, namely into the area that the program also uses for its ongoing work, the so called stack. So that enough room remains for this work, the arguments may occupy at most a quarter of the stack on Linux. On the test system, the stack is 8 MiB in size; a quarter of that is 2 MiB, exactly the value that getconf ARG MAX shows. If you set the stack larger, you may also pass more arguments, though not arbitrarily many. Names with spaces the null byte as a separator xargs separates the words at spaces. A file name like mein foto.jpg German for “my photo.jpg” falls apart into two words, and xargs passes two names, neither of which exists. What is needed is a separator that never occurs in file names. Figure 29 abb 29 shows the difference. Top xargs splits at spaces and line ends; ./mein foto.jpg becomes the two wrong names ./mein and foto.jpg . Bottom null bytes stand between the names, and xargs 0 splits only there; both names stay whole. The action print0 of find writes a null byte, that is, the byte with the value 0, after each match instead of a line end. The option 0 makes xargs split its input only at null bytes; spaces and line ends then belong to the name. This always works, because a file name may contain any character except the slash and the null byte Chapter 3, Section 3.7 /wissen/en/informatik/linux und kommandozeile/dateien verzeichnisse und pfade/den inhalt eines verzeichnisses anzeigen.html stufe 3 7 . The null byte can therefore never stand in the middle of a name. In the first attempt, ls got three names, two of which do not exist. In the second, it got the two correct ones; ls added the quotation marks itself when displaying them, so that you can see that the space belongs to the name. Without 0 , xargs also interprets quotation marks and the backslash in its input as characters meant to prevent splitting. A name with a single apostrophe therefore throws it off completely xargs took the apostrophe for the start of a quoted section whose end is missing, and did not even start ls . With print0 and 0 , this problem does not occur either. ⁠ In short With find print0 and xargs 0 , the null byte separates the names, and spaces remain part of the name. With rm , splitting at spaces can become dangerous if splitting alte liste.txt German for “old list.txt” produces the word liste.txt , rm deletes a file of that name, if there is one, and it is a completely different file from the one intended. Anyone who passes matches from find to rm therefore always uses print0 and 0 and tries the command with ls instead of rm beforehand. The way without a pipe find exec find can also pass its matches to a command itself, without a pipe and without xargs . Chapter 3, Section 10.6 /wissen/en/informatik/linux und kommandozeile/dateien verzeichnisse und pfade/dateien finden und platz messen.html stufe 10 6 already showed actions such as print and delete ; another one starts any command you like. The action exec command {} \; of find starts the command once for each match and puts the name of the match in place of {} . The action exec command {} + collects the names like xargs and starts the command as rarely as possible, with many names at once; here {} must stand directly before the + . The semicolon at the end needs a backslash in front of it without it, the shell would take it for the semicolon from subsection 6.1 befehle verketten.html stufe 6 1 and would not pass it on to find at all. Because find passes the names directly as arguments, without sending them through a stream, spaces cause no problems. With \; , ls ran twice, each time with one name, and wrote each name on a line of its own. With + , it ran once with both names, sorted them and put them side by side. ⁠ In short find … exec command {} + passes the matches directly as arguments to a command, names with spaces included; with \; instead of + , one at a time. Some programs insist on file names and do not read standard input, or they are supposed to get two inputs at once. For this, bash knows another notation, process substitution < command starts the command with its standard output in a pipe and puts in its place a file name under which the read end of this pipe can be reached. wc counted two “files”, /dev/fd/63 and /dev/fd/62 . These are descriptors 63 and 62, which the shell opened for the two pipes and which wc inherited; ls l shows that a pipe is behind such a name. Here the basic idea that everything is a file pays off wc opens a name and reads, without knowing that a program is writing at the other end. A process is a running execution of a program with its own memory, its own open files and its own number. The shell starts a new process for each program. Every process has three standard streams standard input descriptor 0 , standard output for results 1 and standard error for messages 2 . In the terminal, all three lead to the terminal; a descriptor is the number by which the process refers to an open file in its requests to the kernel. Redirections connect descriptors to files before the program starts empty and write , append , 2 standard error , 2 &1 copy of a descriptor , & both , < input , <<ENDE and <<< text as input . /dev/null swallows everything. Redirections take effect from left to right, hence file 2 &1 . The shell empties the target file before the start, so never command file file . A pipe connects the standard output of one program to the standard input of the next; a pipeline lines up filters such as sort , uniq , grep , head and wc , and tee branches off a copy. Messages go past the pipe. What this is about You type a line and press Enter. By the time a program starts, quite a lot has already happened to this line. Usually you notice none of it, but sometimes you notice something strange a command is supposed to show the file mein bericht.txt German for “my report.txt” and complains about two files that do not exist. A program is in the current directory, ls shows it, and yet it cannot be started. A setting you have just made has disappeared again in the next terminal window. This chapter pursues one question What does the shell do with a command line before it starts a program, and what does it give the program to take along? It shows which parts of a line the shell replaces and how to prevent this deliberately, how to remember values and pass them on to programs, how the shell finds a program in the first place and how settings outlast the end of a session. Afterward, you can predict which arguments a program really receives, and you can explain the surprises above. How to work with this chapter. The sections build on each other, and every new term has its own subsection with an example. Expandable boxes contain background why something is the way it is and where it comes from and derivations; you do not need them to read on. Boxes marked “Caution” state rules that always apply to practical exercises. Try the exercises ★ to ★★★ yourself first; the solution expands right below each exercise.

The expansions from Section 1 expansion muster klammern und tilde.html stufe 1 replace text according to fixed rules. This section introduces expansions that insert values the value of a variable, the output of a command and the result of a calculation. The shell variable Some pieces of information you need in several commands in a row a long path, a name, a result. Instead of typing them again each time, you would like to remember them under a short name. As a picture for orientation a drawer with a label. The label shows the name, and in the drawer lies a note with text. You can exchange the note at any time, and whoever names the name gets the text that is currently inside. Figure 6 abb 6 shows such a drawer. A shell variable as a drawer. The assignment wohnort=Hamburg puts the text Hamburg into the drawer with the label wohnort German for “place of residence” . In echo Ich wohne in wohnort with the contents of the drawer before echo starts. A shell variable is a name under which the running shell stores a text, the value of the variable. You create a variable or change its value with an assignment of the form NAME=value ; there is no space before or after the equals sign. The name consists of letters without umlauts or other accents, digits and the underscore, and it does not begin with a digit; uppercase and lowercase letters are different. If NAME and NAME or ? from Chapter 4 /wissen/en/informatik/linux und kommandozeile/strome umleitung pipes und exit status/stroeme umleitung pipes und exit status.html is a special parameter that the shell sets itself; it is inserted in the same way. The builtin command unset removes a variable. In {datei}1.jpg end the name before the 1 . After unset , wohnort is empty, and here, too, there is no error message. ⁠ In short {NAME} marks off the name; an unknown variable yields empty text. The curly braces can do more than just mark off the name. { NAME} inserts the number of characters of the value There are many more forms, for example for cutting off extensions; the bash manual describes them in the part “Parameter Expansion” man bash . Command substitution Sometimes you do not know a value in advance, but a command can output it how many files are in the directory, who is logged in, on which day of the week a date falls. You would like to insert this output directly into another command line. Figure 8 abb 8 shows how the shell does this. Command substitution in echo Angemeldet ist whoami . Only then does echo start. Command substitution command inserts the output of a command into the command line, without the line ends at the end. Older guides write command substitution with two backquotes, the grave accent that leans to the left command . This form still works, but it is considered outdated. It is hard to tell apart from the apostrophe, and with it, nested command substitutions need additional backslashes; with expression computes the expression in the double parentheses with integers and inserts the result as text. Allowed are, among others, + , , times , / divided by , % remainder of the division , to the power of and parentheses; multiplication and division come before addition and subtraction. / drops the remainder. In the expression, you refer to variables by their name; a … is not a pattern but the multiplication sign. Spaces are allowed in the expression. Three rolls at 45 cents each and two liters of milk at 119 cents each how much does that cost in euros and cents? Because the shell knows only integers, you calculate in cents Figure 9 abb 9 checks the calculation step by step. In summe / 100 , there is no 3 \cdot 45 + 2 \cdot 119 = 135 + 238 = 373 3 \cdot 100 + 73 = 373 7/2 7/2 3 4 … calculates with integers and inserts the result; / drops the remainder, % returns it. The shell calculates with integers of fixed size, as the processor handles them directly; the standard for Unix shells requires signed integers for this. It does not know numbers with decimal places, it reports a division by zero as an error, and on the test system the numbers have 64 bits. The largest is ; one more, and the result jumps into the negative without warning For numbers with decimal places, you use a different tool, such as Python Python, Chapter 2 /wissen/en/informatik/programmieren/python/werte typen und variablen/werte typen und variablen.html . For the shell itself, integers are usually enough it counts files, lines and repetitions. After the expansions, the shell splits some results into words once more. That is the reason for the surprise with mein bericht.txt from “What this is about”. This section shows when the shell does this, how you use quotes and the backslash to control what it may change and in which order all the steps of expansion take place. Showing arguments one by one printf echo writes its arguments with one space between each of them. From the output, you cannot tell whether it received one argument with a space in it or two arguments. For this section, however, you need exactly that the boundaries between the arguments. Figure 10 abb 10 shows a tool that makes them visible. printf " %s 
" eins zwei printf applies its format to the first remaining argument and writes eins with a line end. Because one argument is still left, it applies the format a second time and writes zwei . Each line of the output is one argument. The builtin command printf writes text according to a format, its first argument. In the format, %s stands for the next argument and 
 for a line end. If arguments are still left after the pass through the format, printf applies the format again. With the format " %s 
" , printf therefore writes each argument in square brackets on a line of its own. The quotes hold the format together as one argument and protect the square brackets and the backslash from the shell, just like the quotes around the pattern in find name " .txt" in Chapter 3, Section 10.2 /wissen/en/informatik/linux und kommandozeile/dateien verzeichnisse und pfade/dateien finden und platz messen.html stufe 10 2 ; this section shows exactly what they do. The four spaces between eins and zwei German for “one” and “two” only separate two words; when writing, echo puts a single space between them. printf shows the two arguments as two lines. ⁠ In short printf " %s 
" writes each argument in brackets on a line of its own and thus makes visible which arguments a command receives. Word splitting Two observations do not fit together at first. The shopping list has four lines, but echo datei with the value mein bericht.txt . Parameter expansion inserts the value, one word with a space in it. Then word splitting splits this result at the space into two words, and ls receives two arguments. Below, ls " ' and ' , there are a space, 	 for the tab and 
 for the line end. Older shells used these characters to split every word of a line, including typed ones. Today's standard for Unix shells restricts word splitting to the results of expansions; its rationale explicitly names security as a reason, too. You can change IFS , for example to a colon; in the interactive shell, however, this affects every following command, so it is better to leave it alone there. Quoting Expansion and word splitting are usually wanted, but sometimes not a file name should remain one word, a pattern should reach find unchanged, a dollar sign should be a dollar sign. So you need a way to tell the shell please take these characters literally. Quoting means marking characters of a command line so that the shell takes them literally instead of giving them a special meaning. The three basic means for this are single quotes, double quotes and the backslash. Variables live in the shell; programs run in processes of their own. This section clarifies which values a program receives from the shell when it starts the environment. It shows how to add a variable to the environment, why a started program receives only a copy and cannot pass anything back and how to give a single command a setting of its own. What you need for this processes and bash c A process has its own memory and its own working directory; the kernel keeps processes separate from one another. For every program, the shell starts a new process; it runs a builtin command itself. That is why cd has to be built in Chapter 4, Section 1.2 /wissen/en/informatik/linux und kommandozeile/strome umleitung pipes und exit status/prozesse und ihre drei strome.html stufe 1 2 ; Chapter 2, Section 3.3 /wissen/en/informatik/linux und kommandozeile/die shell erste befehle/arten von befehlen.html stufe 3 3 . bash c '…' starts another bash that runs the text in the quotes as a command line Chapter 4, Section 5.1 /wissen/en/informatik/linux und kommandozeile/strome umleitung pipes und exit status/der exit status.html stufe 5 1 . Between single quotes, the shell inserts nothing; between double quotes, it inserts values with obst , looks up obst itself and finds nothing. At the bottom with double quotes the shell inserts the value before the start, and the child already receives echo Obst Apfel . In the first line, the single quotes prevent the shell from replacing obst before the start; the child no longer has to look anything up. In neither case did it receive the variable itself. ⁠ In short A process that another process starts is its child process; it does not automatically receive the shell's variables. The environment Almost every program needs certain information where the home directory is, what the user is called, in which language messages should appear. For this, there is a fixed path from process to process. As a picture for orientation every program receives two notes when it starts, one with its arguments and one with general settings; Figure 16 abb 16 shows both. What a process receives when it starts on the left, the argument list, here printenv HOME USER ; on the right, the environment, a list of entries of the form NAME=value such as HOME=/home/student and LANG=C.UTF 8 . printenv picks out the entries for its arguments from the environment. The environment of a process is a list of texts of the form NAME=value that the process receives when it starts, in addition to its arguments. Each program decides for itself which entries it takes into account. The command printenv writes the environment, one line per entry. With names as arguments, it writes only their values; if a name is missing from the environment, it writes nothing and ends with exit status 1. HOME names the home directory, USER the user, SHELL the shell that starts at login and LANG the language setting. The variable obst is not in the environment of printenv , even though the shell knows it. Tilde expansion also uses such an entry for a tilde without a user name, the shell inserts the value of HOME , which it received in its own environment when it started. ⁠ In short The environment is a list of entries NAME=value that every process receives when it starts; printenv shows it. The environment variable export So the shell knows variables that do not end up in the environment of its children. If a program is to receive a value, you have to tell the shell to pass it on. Figure 17 abb 17 shows what this changes in the shell. The shell holds variables, and some of them carry a mark for passing on. export obst puts the mark on obst as well. When a child starts, the shell writes exactly the marked variables into its environment; variables that are not marked stay in the shell. An environment variable is a shell variable that is marked for passing on; the shell writes all marked variables into the environment of every child process. The builtin command export marks a variable export NAME marks an existing one, export NAME=value assigns and marks in one step. Variables that the shell finds in its environment when it starts are marked from the beginning. That is why every program knows HOME and USER the shell itself already received them in its environment and passes them on. A habit prevents mix ups the system's environment variables have names in uppercase letters, and you write your own variables in lowercase, as in this chapter. The same line as in subsection 4.2 stufe 4 2 now finds a value, because obst is in the environment of the child shell. printenv now sees the variable too. ⁠ In short export marks a shell variable as an environment variable; every child receives it in its environment. export n NAME takes the mark away again; the variable stays in the shell, but children no longer receive it. unset NAME removes the variable entirely. Inheritance as a copy If a child receives its environment, the reverse question arises what happens when the child changes a value? Does the change reach the shell? Figure 18 abb 18 shows the sequence of events. Inheritance of the environment as a timeline. At the start, the child receives a copy of the shell's environment, with obst=Apfel . The child changes its copy to obst=Birne . The way back to the shell is crossed out when the child ends, its copy disappears, and the shell still has obst=Apfel . A child process receives a copy of its parent process's environment when it starts. Whatever it changes in its variables afterward changes only its copy; none of it gets back to the parent process. Likewise, a later change in the parent process no longer reaches a child that is already running. The child shell changed obst and even exported a new variable. None of this arrived at the shell. An export in the child affects only the child's own children. From this follows a rule that often comes as a surprise no program that you start can change the variables of your shell, not even a second shell. It is the same separation that requires cd to be built in. ⁠ In short A child inherits a copy of the environment; it can change the copy but cannot pass anything back. On Linux, a new process comes into being in two steps, which Chapter 4, Section 2.1 /wissen/en/informatik/linux und kommandozeile/strome umleitung pipes und exit status/ausgaben umleiten.html stufe 2 1 already described for redirections. With fork , the kernel creates a copy of the parent process with its own memory; the environment lies in this memory and is therefore copied along. With exec , the child process then loads the new program; in doing so, it passes on the environment, in the case of a shell the list of its exported variables, as texts NAME=value , and the kernel places them in the memory of the new program. From this moment on, there are two separate lists in two separate memories. The kernel keeps the memories of the processes separate an ordinary program cannot write into the memory of another, and there is no system call that changes the environment of the parent process. That this is intended was already stated in the guide with which Stephen Bourne introduced his shell in 1978 for an invoked program, copies of the exported variables are made, and changes to them do not affect the invoking shell. A program should not be able to change the state of whoever invoked it unless the caller explicitly asks for it. As a picture for orientation the child receives a photocopy and not the original; what it writes on its copy does not appear on the original. A variable for one command only Sometimes only a single command is to get a different setting. One example is the time zone the environment variable TZ determines in which time zone programs such as date show the time. If it is not set, the system's time zone applies. If you want to know what time it is in Tokyo right now, you do not want to change the setting of the whole shell for that. Figure 19 abb 19 shows how the shell solves this. TZ=Asia/Tokyo date the shell gives the child date a copy of its environment and appends the entry TZ=Asia/Tokyo . The environment of the shell itself stays without TZ ; the next command no longer receives the entry. If one or more assignments NAME=value come before the command name, they go only into the environment of this one command. The shell itself keeps its variables as they were. Such assignments take effect only after the shell has expanded the remaining words of the line; a tier' b bash c "echo Tier HOME' . In particular, explain why c shows a value but a does not. a The single quotes pass the text unchanged to the child shell; it looks for tier among its variables and finds nothing, because tier is not exported. b The shell inserts Katze before the child even starts. c Here, too, it is the child shell that does the replacing, but HOME is an environment variable the shell found it in its environment when it started itself, so it is marked, and the child receives it in its environment. Afterward, it is in the environment of every child. The assignment before the command applies only to this one child; the shell keeps hallo . The last child shell changes and exports gruss , but only in its own copy. The explanation when a program starts, it receives a copy of the environment in its own memory. This section shows that an environment variable lies behind it, by which rules the shell searches, why a program in the working directory does not simply start and how to change the search path. What you need for this search path and kinds of commands The search path is the list of directories in which the shell looks for a program file with the name of the command; it starts the first one it finds. The variable PATH How does the shell know which directories belong to the search path? The answer is an environment variable that you can read and change like any other. Figure 20 abb 20 shows how its value becomes a list. The value of PATH is one single text. The colons in it separate the directories; read from left to right, they give the order in which the shell searches. The environment variable PATH contains the search path as text the directories, separated by colons, in the order in which the shell searches them. An empty entry, that is, two colons in a row or a colon at the beginning or at the end, stands for the working directory. The standard for Unix shells lists the empty entry only as a leftover from old times; anyone who means the working directory should write . . Because PATH is an environment variable, every child receives the search path of its parent process. The value is long. So that each directory stands on a line of its own, tr replaces each colon with a line end; head shows the first nine The first eight entries come from Ubuntu's default settings; /usr/lib/wsl/lib and the many Windows directories that follow it under WSL 2 are appended by WSL. Because /bin is a second name for /usr/bin , the shell finds some programs twice type a names all matches in the order of the search. The first one is started the alias from Chapter 2, Section 3.4 /wissen/en/informatik/linux und kommandozeile/die shell erste befehle/arten von befehlen.html stufe 3 4 leads to ls , and the shell finds it in /usr/bin . The builtin command command v answers more briefly for each name, it writes only what the shell would start, the path for a program and the name for a builtin command. ⁠ In short PATH is the search path as text, the directories separated by colons and in the order of the search. Command search With PATH , the rules of the search can be stated completely, including the case in which the name already contains a path. If the command name contains no slash, the shell, after checking for an alias, keyword, function and builtin command Chapter 2, Section 3.5 /wissen/en/informatik/linux und kommandozeile/die shell erste befehle/arten von befehlen.html stufe 3 5 , goes through the directories from PATH from left to right and starts the first executable file with this name; it remembers the path it found for later. If it finds none, it reports the error and sets exit status 127. If the command name contains a slash, the shell does not search at all but starts exactly the file that the path designates. Figure 21 abb 21 summarizes the way from the name to the started program as a decision tree. Command search as a decision tree. First question does the name contain a slash? Yes the shell starts exactly this file. No is it an alias, a keyword, a function or a builtin command? Then the shell handles it itself. Otherwise, it goes through the directories from PATH from left to right as soon as it finds the program, it starts it and remembers the path; if it finds nothing, it reports “command not found” and sets exit status 127. echo alone would be the builtin command. With the path /usr/bin/echo , the shell instead starts the program file of the same name, without searching. ⁠ In short Without a slash, the shell searches in PATH and takes the first match; with a slash, it starts exactly the named file. So that it does not have to go through all the directories on every call, bash creates an entry in a table for every program it finds. The builtin command hash shows this table, and for a remembered program, type says “is hashed”. If you move a program after the shell has remembered it, the shell keeps trying the old location and reports that the file does not exist there; only hash r empties the table, and the search starts anew. Every new assignment to PATH empties it as well. A program in the working directory ./ If you put a program of your own in a directory that is not in the search path, the shell does not find it, even though it is right in front of you. For an experiment, you need a program. With the usual default settings, cp gives the copy the permissions of the original, including the indication that the file may be started as a program; a copy of tree is therefore again a program that can be started. At the bottom, ./meinbaum the slash turns the name into a path, and the shell starts the file in the working directory directly. Without a path, the shell does not find meinbaum . With ./ in front, it is a path relative to the working directory Chapter 3, Section 2.5 /wissen/en/informatik/linux und kommandozeile/dateien verzeichnisse und pfade/das arbeitsverzeichnis und pfade.html stufe 2 5 , and the program draws the tree that brace expansion created in subsection 1.6 expansion muster klammern und tilde.html stufe 1 6 ; tree counts the starting directory too. You start a program that is not in any directory from PATH with a path that contains a slash ./program in the working directory, otherwise with an absolute or relative path. This applies to the uutils implementation in Ubuntu 26.04 most core commands there are one single multicall program that recognizes from the name it was called by which command it is supposed to be Chapter 2, Section 7.2 /wissen/en/informatik/linux und kommandozeile/die shell erste befehle/zwei fassungen der grundbefehle gnu und uutils.html stufe 7 2 . A renamed copy of it no longer knows what to do The GNU implementation gnudate is a program of its own and also works under a new name; on systems with GNU coreutils, such as Debian, this also applies to date itself. For experiments of this kind, you therefore use a standalone program such as tree . ⁠ In short The working directory is not part of the search path; you start a program there with ./ . It used to be different. In the guide to the Bourne shell from 1978, the shell searches the current directory first by default, then /bin and /usr/bin , and the example there begins PATH with a colon, that is, with the working directory. Today, the working directory is missing from the default settings of the distributions; since its version 2.24 from 2016, the program library glibc, on which almost all Linux programs are built, also no longer searches it when it starts other programs and PATH is missing. The manuals give hardly any reasons for this. Reasoning it out yields two. First, a command should mean the same program everywhere ls is /usr/bin/ls in every directory, no matter where you are. If the working directory were in the search path, the meaning of a command would depend on which files happen to be there. Second, it would be dangerous. If someone put a program named ls in a directory that others also enter, such as /tmp , then anyone who typed ls there would start this foreign program, and with their own permissions. If the working directory were at the end of the search path, the real ls would win, but a program named after a typo, such as sl , would still run. The small effort of typing ./ is the price for commands that always mean the same thing. Changing PATH For your own programs, ./ becomes tedious in the long run, and from another directory you would have to type the whole path. It is more convenient to add the directory with your own programs to the search path. Because PATH is a variable, this works with an assignment. With an assignment before the command, the changed search path applies only to this one command PATH the old search path; a colon stands between them. Afterward, everything is as before. For the whole session, you create a directory of your own for programs and put it at the front of the search path An export is not necessary, because PATH was already in the shell's environment when the shell started and is therefore marked subsection 4.4 umgebung und vererbung.html stufe 4 4 . type reports that the shell has remembered the path. The change applies until the shell ends. The assignment builds the new value from the old one parameter expansion inserts the previous text for PATH HOME/linuxk5/bin PATH and puts the new directory in front of it with a colon; the old entries remain and move back one place. At the bottom, PATH=/gibtsnicht German for “doesnotexist” the old text does not appear in the assignment, and the list consists only of this one entry. Always append new directories to the old value, as above with PATH" puts a directory of your own at the front of the search path; at the front means priority, and the old value must be kept. Everything that you have set up in a shell so far disappears with it. This section shows which files the shell reads every time it starts, how to set up variables, the search path and aliases in them permanently and how to make a changed file take effect immediately. The startup file A new shell starts almost from scratch it receives the environment of its parent process, nothing else. It does not know a variable that you have not exported The option i makes the new bash an interactive shell, like the shell you type into. Even so, it does not know wohnort . And yet every new shell has the aliases ll and la from Chapter 2, Section 3.4 /wissen/en/informatik/linux und kommandozeile/die shell erste befehle/arten von befehlen.html stufe 3 4 . It must get these settings from somewhere every time it starts. Figure 24 abb 24 shows where from. The start of an interactive bash. Before the first prompt appears, the shell reads the file ~/.bashrc line by line and runs each line as if it had been typed, among them alias ll='ls alF' and alias la='ls A' . A startup file is a text file with commands for the shell that the shell reads and runs when it starts, as if you had typed the lines. If you start a new interactive bash in a terminal, it reads the file ~/.bashrc in your home directory. The ending “rc” short for “run commands” is common on Unix for files with startup commands; the dot at the beginning makes the file a hidden file. On Ubuntu, bash first reads the file /etc/bash.bashrc , which applies to all users. Ubuntu creates a ~/.bashrc with sensible default settings for every new user. grep shows the lines of the file that contain alias l , with their number in front. There is one exception, however if bash starts without a terminal over a network connection, for example because someone sends a single command from another computer, it does read ~/.bashrc .
