Now you can define your own and know where they are kept permanently. The builtin command alias name='text' defines an alias if name is the first word of a command, the shell replaces it with text . unalias name removes the alias, and alias without arguments shows all of them. Aliases apply only in the shell in which they were defined, and only in interactive shells. The single quotes hold the text together as one word and prevent the shell from replacing anything in it already when the alias is defined; a tilde in the text is replaced only each time the alias is used. What this is about A lot of everyday data comes as plain text the runs of a running club, the transactions of a bank account as a file from online banking, weather readings, the entries of a log that a program writes line by line. Often you have a simple question about such a file. Who ran most often? Which run was the longest? How many kilometers does a run cover on average? Which lines come from a particular week? This chapter pursues one question How do you answer such questions on the command line without writing a program of your own? It shows small tools that select lines, cut out columns, sort, count, transform and calculate, and a notation with which you search not for fixed words but for the form of a text. Afterward, you can analyze a file with many lines in a few steps, and you know why the tools sometimes behave differently than you would first expect. How to work with this chapter. The sections build on each other, and every new term has its own subsection with an example. Expandable boxes contain background why something is the way it is and where it comes from and derivations; you do not need them to read on. Boxes marked “Caution” state rules that always apply to practical exercises. Try the exercises ★ to ★★★ yourself first; the solution expands right below each exercise.

Record and field After every run, a running club writes down when, who, how far and how long someone ran. On paper or in a spreadsheet program, this would be a table with rows and columns. A text file, however, knows no boxes, only characters and line ends. Figure 1 abb 1 shows how a table still fits into a text file. At the top, a small table with the columns date, name, distance in kilometers and time in minutes. Below, the same values as text each row of the table becomes a line of the file, and the values of a row stand one after the other, separated by commas. The commas light up, then the four values of the line 2026 11 02,Ben,10.5,62 get their numbers 1 to 4. A record is a line of a text file that contains the values of one table row. Its individual values are called fields ; they stand one after the other in a fixed order. Between any two fields there is an agreed character, the separator . The fields of a record are counted from the left, starting with 1. Whoever writes the file decides which character separates; common choices are the comma, the semicolon, the colon and the tab. A separator must not occur in the values themselves; otherwise it would no longer be clear where a field ends. The fields with the same number in all records together form a column . In the record 2026 11 02,Ben,10.5,62 , three commas separate four fields. Field 1 is the date 2026 11 02 , field 2 the name Ben , field 3 the distance 10.5 in kilometers and field 4 the time 62 in minutes. Decimal numbers are written with a decimal point, the way most programs write them; with a decimal comma, as in 10,5 , the comma could not be told apart from a separator. The user list /etc/passwd from Chapter 3, Section 4.4 /wissen/en/informatik/linux und kommandozeile/dateien verzeichnisse und pfade/dateien ansehen.html stufe 4 4 also consists of records; there, a colon separates the seven fields. ⁠ In short A line with the values of a table row is a record; its values are the fields, separated by a separator and counted from the left. The CSV file and its header line For tables in text form, there is a format that almost every program can read and write, from spreadsheet programs to online banking. In this format, you now create the running log that the chapter works with until the end. A CSV file is a text file in which each line is a record and the comma separates the fields. The name stands for “comma separated values”. Often the first line contains the names of the columns instead of values; it is called the header line . The header line is meant for people and for programs that address columns by their names. The tools in this chapter treat it like any other line; where it gets in the way, you remove it beforehand. You create the running log with a here document from Chapter 4, Section 3.2 /wissen/en/informatik/linux und kommandozeile/strome umleitung pipes und exit status/eingaben umleiten.html stufe 3 2 . Type the first line, then the ten lines of the table and finally ENDE German for “end” ; the shell shows a before each continuation line The file laeufe.csv German for “runs” has a header line, datum,name,km,minuten German for “date,name,km,minutes” , and nine records nine runs by Anna, Ben and Clara between 2 and 9 November 2026. The date has the form year month day so that it sorts correctly as text. ⁠ In short A CSV file is a table as text with one record per line and commas between the fields; the first line often names the columns. There is no binding standard for CSV, only a description that appeared in 2005 as RFC 4180 and records widespread practice. According to it, a field that itself contains a comma, a quotation mark or a line end may be enclosed in double quotes, for example "Berg, Anna" . The simple tools in this chapter do not know this rule; for them, every comma is a separator. For files with such fields, there are dedicated programs that understand CSV completely. Spreadsheet programs set to German often separate with semicolons when saving as CSV, because there the comma is the decimal separator. So if you analyze a CSV file from someone else, first look into it with head to see which separator it uses and whether fields are enclosed in quotes. Replacing and deleting characters tr Sometimes a single character gets in the way everywhere in a file a carriage return at the end of every line, commas where another program expects semicolons, lowercase letters where uppercase letters are wanted. Chapter 4, Section 3.3 /wissen/en/informatik/linux und kommandozeile/strome umleitung pipes und exit status/eingaben umleiten.html stufe 3 3 already used tr to turn lowercase letters into uppercase letters. Figure 6 abb 6 shows the rule by which it does this. tr a z A Z as a mapping at the top, the characters of the first set a b c … z side by side, below them those of the second set A B C … Z ; arrows connect the characters at the same position. A text runs through character by character each character that occurs at the top is replaced by its counterpart at the bottom; digits and commas pass through unchanged. The command tr reads its standard input character by character and writes it out changed. tr set1 set2 replaces each character that stands at a certain position in the first set with the character at the same position in the second set. tr d set deletes all characters of the set; tr s set squeezes several identical characters of the set in a row into one. You write a set as a sequence of characters, such as ',;' , with ranges such as a z or with names such as lower for all lowercase letters and digit for all digits. tr itself understands the notations \n for the newline, \t for the tab and \r for the carriage return. So that the shell changes none of this, the sets are enclosed in single quotes. Digits, dots and hyphens occur in no set and stay as they are. tr does not accept file names; the file comes in with < or through a pipe. A file name as a third argument leads to a message With d , tr also solves the problem from subsection 1.4 textdaten datensatze felder und zeilenenden.html stufe 1 4 it deletes every carriage return from the Windows file. You compare the result with cmp , which compares two files byte by byte, outputs nothing if they are the same and reports exit status 0 gleich is German for “equal” the cleaned up file linux.csv is byte for byte the same as the first three lines of the running log. ⁠ In short tr replaces characters according to two sets, deletes them with d or squeezes repetitions with s ; tr d '\r' removes Windows line ends. The ä stays lowercase, even with the names of the sets. On the test system, tr works byte by byte, in the uutils implementation as well as in the GNU implementation, whose manual states this explicitly. In UTF 8, an ä consists of two bytes that are not letters on their own, so tr finds nothing in them to replace. For the digits, commas and ASCII letters that this chapter is mostly about, this does not matter. Who ran most often, which run was the longest? For questions like these, you put the lines in order and count identical ones. This section shows how sort compares lines, how it sorts numbers and individual columns, why the order depends on the language setting and how to count identical lines with uniq . How sort compares the character order In Chapter 4, Section 4.2 /wissen/en/informatik/linux und kommandozeile/strome umleitung pipes und exit status/pipes und filter.html stufe 4 2 , sort put the lines of a list in order. With words, the result looks like a dictionary; with numbers, sometimes it does not. To predict the result, you need to know how sort compares two lines. The command sort reads all lines of its input and writes them out in order. It compares two lines character by character from the left; the first character in which they differ decides, according to the order of the characters. If one line is the beginning of the other, the shorter one comes first. With r , sort reverses the order. Under the language setting of the test system, which Chapter 5, Section 1.3 /wissen/en/informatik/linux und kommandozeile/wie die shell eine befehlszeile liest expansion quoting variablen umgebung/expansion muster klammern und tilde.html stufe 1 3 mentioned in connection with the order of file names, the order of the characters is the order of their numbers. In it, among other things, the digits come before the uppercase letters, these come before the lowercase letters, and umlauts such as ä come after them. Python compares strings the same way Python, Chapter 3, Section 1.3 /wissen/en/informatik/programmieren/python/entscheidungen und schleifen/bedingungen vergleiche und logische operatoren.html stufe 1 3 . 10 and 100 begin with 1 , 9 with 9 ; the 1 comes before the 9, so both come before the 9. 10 is the beginning of 100 and comes first. In the running log, every record begins with a digit, the header line with the letter d ; digits come before letters, which is why the header line ends up at the end. The runs themselves are in date order, because a date of the form year month day sorts correctly character by character. r simply turns the same order around. ⁠ In short sort compares lines character by character from the left according to the order of the characters; that is why 10 comes before 9 . Sorting numerically sort n For distances and minutes, the character order is wrong a run of 10.5 km is longer than one of 5 km, even though 1 comes before 5 . Figure 9 abb 9 puts the two ways of comparing side by side. At the top, sort compares the texts 10.5 and 5.0 character by character the very first character decides, 1 is less than 5 , so 10.5 comes first. At the bottom, sort n reads a number at the beginning of each line and compares the numeric values 5.0 is less than 10.5, so 5.0 comes first. With the option n , sort reads a number at the beginning of each line, with an optional minus sign and an optional decimal point, and compares the lines by the value of this number. A line that does not begin with a number counts as the number 0. If the values are equal, the character order of the whole line decides. abc has no number at the beginning, counts as 0 and ends up between and . The difference is especially clear in the column of distances; paste s d' ' puts the result into one line to save space Without n , the two digit distances come first and km from the header line comes last; with n , it is the other way around km counts as 0, and the distances are in the order of their values. ⁠ In short sort n compares the number at the beginning of the line by its value; lines without a number count as 0. Sorting by a column t and k In the running log, the distance is not at the beginning but in field 3. You could cut it out with cut , but then the date and the name would be lost. What you want is to sort the whole records by a single field. Figure 10 abb 10 shows the idea. The records of the running log one below the other; in each line, field 3, the distance, has a colored background the key. sort t, k3,3n compares only these highlighted pieces, as numbers. The whole lines move to their new places until the distances grow from top to bottom; for the three runs of 5.0 km, the whole line decides. t and a character set the separator at which sort splits the lines into fields. k A,B makes the fields from number to number the sort key sort compares only this piece of the line. Letters such as n or r directly after the specification, as in k3,3n , apply only to this key. If ,B is missing, the key extends to the end of the line. Several k are compared one after the other; if all keys are equal, the whole line decides. So k3,3 means “from field 3 to field 3”, only this one field. Without t , a new field begins where spaces or tabs follow another character; these spaces belong to the new field. The header line has the text km in field 3, counts as 0 and comes first. The three runs of 5.0 km have the same key; among them, the whole line decides, that is, the date. In descending order and cut down to three lines, this gives the leaderboard The longest run was Ben's half marathon of 21.1 km. Ordered by name and, for each name, the longest runs first; tail n +2 removes the header line beforehand The first key orders by name, the second, only within identical names, by distance, in descending order. ⁠ In short sort t, k3,3n sorts whole lines by the value of field 3; further k decide in the case of a tie. Without an end, a key extends to the end of the line. You notice this only when the values of the field are equal With k2 , sort compares pieces such as Anna,12.0,70 and Anna,5.0,27 ; after Anna, , the 1 decides against the 5 , a text comparison of the distance. With k2,2 , all four keys Anna are equal, and the whole line, that is, the date, decides. With numbers, this is especially treacherous k2n instead of k2,2n makes everything from field 2 to the end of the line the key for the numeric comparison, and the manual of the GNU implementation explicitly warns that this rarely does what you expect. If you mean a single field, write k2,2 . The option debug underlines in each line the piece that sort uses as the key. The locale The same file can come out sorted differently on two computers. This is not due to sort but to the language setting, which has so far come up only in passing. It determines which language's rules are used to handle text. The locale , the language setting, is a set of rules for a language and a country. Among other things, it determines which bytes together form a character, which characters are letters, in which order characters are sorted and which character is the decimal separator. A program learns it from environment variables, above all from LANG and LC ALL ; if LC ALL is set, it takes priority. A locale has a name such as de DE.UTF 8 for German in Germany with UTF 8. Two special ones are called C and C.UTF 8 they sort by the numbers of the characters and are the same everywhere. You can use only locales that are installed on the system; locale a shows them. WSL starts Ubuntu with C.UTF 8 , and nothing more is installed on the test system; POSIX is a second name for C . With this setting, sort sorts uppercase letters before lowercase letters and the umlaut to the end. f treats lowercase letters like uppercase letters; LC ALL=C before the command forces the setting C for this one call C and C.UTF 8 both order by the numbers of the characters; that is why the first and the last line are the same. On a computer with a German desktop, de DE.UTF 8 is usually set. According to the documentation of the GNU tools, sort sorts like a dictionary there case and umlauts count only when the letters are otherwise the same, and the list would come out as a, A, ä, b, B, Z. This is not verified here, because this locale is missing on the test system. ⁠ In short The locale determines how sort orders; C and C.UTF 8 order by character numbers, and LC ALL=C sort makes a result the same on every computer. The locale also determines which character sort n reads as the decimal separator; this is how the manual of the GNU implementation describes it. Under de DE.UTF 8 , it is a comma, and the dot separates thousands there, as in 1.050 . The GNU implementation of sort n then reads a distance such as 10.5 as 105; on the test system, this cannot be shown, because this locale is missing. If you sort files with a decimal point, you therefore write LC ALL=C sort n . The same is advisable in anything that is supposed to deliver the same result on different computers. The option debug names the rules by which sort is currently comparing As of the uutils implementation in Ubuntu 26.04 under C.UTF 8 , it reports a simple comparison of the bytes, the GNU implementation the rules of C.UTF 8 . Both result in the same order, because in UTF 8 the bytes of the characters follow the same order as their numbers. The dashes under each line are the underlining of the key, here the whole line. Identical adjacent lines uniq Chapter 4, Sections 4.2 /wissen/en/informatik/linux und kommandozeile/strome umleitung pipes und exit status/pipes und filter.html stufe 4 2 and 4.3 /wissen/en/informatik/linux und kommandozeile/strome umleitung pipes und exit status/pipes und filter.html stufe 4 3 showed that uniq removes repetitions only if sort has brought identical lines together beforehand. With an option, removing turns into counting. Figure 11 abb 11 shows how uniq works and why it depends on neighbors. uniq c reads a stream of names, line by line from the top. Next to the stream, there is a single note with the previous line and a counter. If the new line is the same, the counter grows; if it is different, uniq writes out the counter and the note and starts over. With the unsorted sequence Anna, Ben, Clara, Anna, every line therefore comes out with 1; with the sorted sequence Anna, Anna, Anna, Anna, Ben …, the counts 4, 3 and 2 result. The command uniq compares each line of its input with the line directly before it and, of several identical lines in a row, writes out only one. With c , it puts in front of each output line how often it occurred in a row. d outputs only lines that occurred several times in a row, u only those that stood alone. Nowhere in the running log are two identical names one below the other, so uniq counts each line on its own. After sort , identical names stand together, and the counters are right Anna ran four times, Ben three times, Clara twice. Only the distance 5.0 occurs more than once. All other values stand alone, including km from the header line. ⁠ In short uniq combines identical lines that stand directly one below the other; c counts them, d and u select repeated or single ones. uniq reads its stream exactly once from front to back and remembers only one line, the previous one. It needs no more than that to recognize identical neighbors, and that is why its memory requirement depends only on the length of a line, not on the number of lines. It can output each line as soon as the next one is different, and it even works behind tail f with a stream that never ends. Finding identical lines in arbitrary places, by contrast, would mean remembering all previous lines. This work is left to sort , which has to read everything anyway the smallest line may be at the very end, so sort cannot output any line before it has seen the last one. For large inputs, the GNU implementation sorts pieces in memory, stores them in temporary files and merges them afterward. Neither the standard for Unix shells and their tools nor the manuals explicitly justify the restriction to neighbors; the reasoning above is a derivation of our own from the way the two tools work. Counting frequencies sort, uniq c, sort rn The question “What occurs how often, and what occurs most often?” comes up so often that a fixed sequence of tools has become established for it. Figure 12 abb 12 shows what the three steps do with the column of distances. The nine distances of the running log, unsorted. sort orders them and pushes the three values 5.0 together into a block; the other six values stand alone. uniq c turns each block into a line with its length in front once 3 5.0 , six times a 1. sort rn orders these lines by the number, and 3 5.0 moves from the middle to the top. The pipeline sort | uniq c | sort rn turns a list of values, one per line, into a table of the different values with their frequency, the most frequent first. The first sort brings identical values together, uniq c counts them, sort rn orders by the count in descending order. The second sort needs n , because the lines now begin with a number; uniq c indents them to the right, and sort n skips leading spaces. First the header line goes, then the names are cut out, then comes the frequency table. With field 3 instead of field 2 and head n 1 at the end, the same pipeline asks for the most frequent distance If you need only the different values without a count, you can write sort | uniq more briefly sort u writes out only one of several identical lines. ⁠ In short sort | uniq c | sort rn counts how often each value occurs and puts the most frequent one at the top; sort u delivers only the different values. Three small tools round off the toolbox one numbers lines, one generates sequences of numbers, and one shows how two files differ. Numbering lines nl When you talk to others about a file, you want to be able to point to lines “There is a typo in line 7.” For that, you need the numbers in front of the lines. The command nl writes out each line of its input with a running number in front of it, separated by a tab. Without an option, it numbers only lines that are not empty; with ba , it numbers all of them. The name stands for “number lines”. The numbers are right aligned in a column six characters wide. Without an option, an empty line gets no number printf has turned the empty argument '' into an empty line. Without an option, nl skips it when counting; with ba , it does not. ⁠ In short nl puts line numbers in front of the lines; it counts empty lines only with ba . Generating sequences of numbers seq For trying things out, you often need a sequence of numbers the days of a month, the numbers from 1 to 100, kilometer marks 0.5 apart. The brace expansion from Chapter 5, Section 1.6 /wissen/en/informatik/linux und kommandozeile/wie die shell eine befehlszeile liest expansion quoting variablen umgebung/expansion muster klammern und tilde.html stufe 1 6 can do this only with whole numbers, and it happens before variables are substituted. A program that writes numbers to its standard output has neither of these limitations. Figure 13 abb 13 shows how it forms a sequence. A number line from 0 to 10. seq 1 4 10 sets a mark at 1 and jumps 4 further to 5 and to 9; the next jump would land at 13, beyond the 10, and stays gray. Below it, seq 0 0.5 2 with marks 0.5 apart up to exactly 2. The command seq writes a sequence of numbers, one per line. seq end counts from 1 to end , seq start end from start to end , seq start step end in steps of the given size. The sequence ends with the last number that does not exceed end . s sets a separator other than the line end, w pads with leading zeros to equal width. With a step of 0.5, seq writes all numbers with one decimal place. The last sequence ends at 9, because 13 would be above 10. Chapter 5, Section 3.9 /wissen/en/informatik/linux und kommandozeile/wie die shell eine befehlszeile liest expansion quoting variablen umgebung/worttrennung und quoting.html stufe 3 9 showed that {1.. n ⁠ In short seq start step end writes a sequence of numbers, also with decimal numbers and with limits from variables. Finding differences diff Two versions of a file look almost the same an older and a newer one, your own and one from the internet. Comparing them line by line by eye is tedious and error prone. Figure 14 abb 14 shows what a tool reports instead. On the left, the first five lines of the running log; on the right, the same five lines with a lowercase b in ben . Identical lines are connected by gray lines. Only line 3 differs, Ben versus ben ; it lights up on both sides. Below that appears the message from diff 3c3 , the old line with < , three dashes, the new line with . The command diff compares two text files line by line and outputs what you would have to change in the first one to get the second one. Each change begins with a line of line numbers and a letter a for add, c for change, d for delete. Below it are the affected lines of the first file with < in front of them and those of the second with . The exit status is 0 for identical files, 1 for differences and 2 for an error. To the left of the letter is the line number in the first file, to the right the one in the second; a range is written with a comma, 6,10 . If the files are identical, diff writes nothing. For the comparisons, create two shorter files kurz.csv German for “short” with the first five lines of the running log and klein.csv German for “small” , in which, in addition, every uppercase B is written in lowercase neu.csv from subsection 1.6 textdaten datensatze felder und zeilenenden.html stufe 1 6 has one run more than laeufe.csv 10a11 after line 10 of the first file, add what is line 11 in the second. Now the running log against its first five lines 6,10d5 lines 6 to 10 of the first file are to be deleted; after that, it matches the second one up to that file's line 5. Finally, the two short files 3c3 line 3 is to be changed; the three dashes separate the old version from the new one. ⁠ In short diff a b uses a , c and d to show which lines you would have to add, change or delete in a to get b ; the exit status tells whether there are differences. With u , diff writes a more detailed format that developers use to exchange changes The header lines name both files with their modification time. @@ 1,5 +1,5 @@ means five lines starting at line 1 in both files. Lines with are removed, lines with + are added, and lines with a space at the beginning are included for orientation. The program patch can apply such a diff to another copy of the first file. This is how developers send each other changes instead of sending whole files. In Chapter 4 /wissen/en/informatik/linux und kommandozeile/strome umleitung pipes und exit status/stroeme umleitung pipes und exit status.html , grep picked out lines with a word. This section shows what grep does exactly and how its most important options invert a search, count, number, restrict it to the matches and extend it to whole directories. Lines with a search text grep From a long file, you often want only the lines that contain something specific all of Clara's runs, all messages of a program on a particular day. After the options, the command grep receives a search text as its first argument and then files. It writes out every line of these files in which the search text occurs anywhere and leaves out the others. Without files, it reads its standard input. Its exit status is 0 if at least one line matched, 1 if none matched and 2 for an error. Case matters clara is a different search text from Clara . Chapter 4, Section 5.2 /wissen/en/informatik/linux und kommandozeile/strome umleitung pipes und exit status/der exit status.html stufe 5 2 showed how to use the exit status of grep q , which produces no output, for decisions. With a lowercase c, grep finds nothing, writes nothing and reports exit status 1. ⁠ In short grep searchtext file writes the lines that contain the search text; the exit status tells whether there were any. The name comes from the text editor ed , which was used to edit files in the early years of Unix. There, the command that outputs all lines with a particular content was called g/re/p g for “global”, all lines, re for the search expression and p for “print”. Around 1973, Ken Thompson turned this one command into a small program of its own that you can use with any file and after any pipe, entirely in the spirit of the Unix philosophy from Chapter 4, Section 4.5 /wissen/en/informatik/linux und kommandozeile/strome umleitung pipes und exit status/pipes und filter.html stufe 4 5 . Inverting, counting, numbering i, v, c and n Often the question is put a little differently from “which lines contain the word” Which ones do not contain it? How many are there? Where in the file are they? Figure 15 abb 15 shows how four options change the same search. The running log with its ten lines and the search text Anna . Without an option, the four lines with Anna light up. v inverts now the other six light up. c replaces the lines with their count, 4. n puts in front of each matching line its number 2, 5, 7 and 10. i ignores case in the comparison. v inverts the selection and writes the lines in which the search text does not occur. c writes only the number of lines instead of the lines themselves. n puts in front of each output line its number in the file and a colon. v also delivers the header line, because Anna does not occur in it either. The numbers with n count the header line as line 1. As a filter, grep fits at the beginning of a pipeline. Which distances did Anna run? ⁠ In short i ignores case, v gives the other lines, c their count, n adds line numbers. Outputting only the match o grep normally writes the whole line. Sometimes, however, only the piece that matched is of interest, for example to count how often something occurs rather than in how many lines. Figure 16 abb 16 shows the difference. The line Anna und Anna German for “Anna and Anna” with two matches for Anna . grep c counts lines and reports 1. grep o picks out the two matches and writes each on a line of its own; wc l counts these lines and reports 2. With the option o , grep writes, instead of the whole line, only the pieces that match the search text, each on a line of its own. If the search text occurs several times in a line, several output lines result. One line, two matches. With a fixed search text, every match looks the same; o then serves mainly for counting. ⁠ In short grep o writes only the matching pieces, one per line; with wc l , you thus count matches instead of lines. Searching in many files r and l Where was Clara's run again, in which file? With several files or a whole directory tree, grep must also say where a line comes from. Figure 17 abb 17 shows how it goes about this. A small directory tree the practice directory with a few files and the subdirectory archiv with november.csv . grep r Clara visits every file, including the one in the subdirectory; each matching line appears on the right with the file path and a colon in front of it. With l , the output shrinks to one line per file with a match. If grep receives more than one file, it puts the file name and a colon in front of each output line. With r , it searches all files in the given directories and their subdirectories. With l , it writes, instead of the lines, only the names of the files in which it found something, each one once. With several files, c counts for each one separately. For r , create a subdirectory with a copy . is the working directory; rl names all files below it in which Clara occurs, including the list of names from subsection 2.3 spalten ausschneiden und zeichen ersetzen cut tr und paste.html stufe 2 3 . grep r goes through the files in the order in which they are stored in the directory, unsorted like find in Chapter 3, Section 10.1 /wissen/en/informatik/linux und kommandozeile/dateien verzeichnisse und pfade/dateien finden und platz messen.html stufe 10 1 ; the sort after it makes the list easy to read. If you have solved the exercises in the practice directory, the list also names their files, such as probe.csv . ⁠ In short With several files, grep names the origin of each line; r searches whole directory trees, l names only the file names. Exercises for Section 5 stufe 5 a How many runs did Ben have? b Output all runs that are not Anna's, without the header line. c In which line is the run of 7 November? a Three lines with Ben. b grep v Anna also lets the header line through; a second grep v with a word from the header line removes it. A tail n +2 in front would work just as well. c Line 8, counting the header line. Predict which of the two numbers is larger, grep c 0 laeufe.csv or the number that grep o 0 laeufe.csv | wc l returns, and give your reasons. So far, grep has searched for fixed words. But many questions concern a form a date from a particular week, a time under 30 minutes, a number with a decimal point. This section introduces the notation used to describe such forms, and its first building blocks any single character, a selection of characters and the positions at the beginning and at the end of a line. The regular expression How do you find all runs that took longer than 99 minutes? There is no fixed search text for this; 128 is only one of 900 three digit numbers. What is needed is a description such as “a comma, then three digits, then the line end”, and a tool that compares every line with this description. A string here is simply a sequence of characters, such as a word, a number or a whole line. A regular expression is a text that describes a set of strings. It consists of ordinary characters, which stand for themselves, and of special characters with a meaning of their own. A line matches a regular expression if a contiguous piece of it belongs to this set; this piece is called the match . The search text of grep has always been a regular expression; so far, it consisted only of ordinary characters. The name “regular expression” is often shortened to “regex”. The expression Clara contains only ordinary characters. It describes a set with exactly one string, Clara . The line 2026 11 03,Clara,7.2,41 matches, because its piece from position 12 to 16 is exactly this string; that is the match. This is exactly how grep Clara laeufe.csv worked in subsection 5.1 suchen mit grep.html stufe 5 1 . Many special characters of regular expressions also mean something to the shell , ? , , . The expression ,2 0 9 finds a match at ,21 ; with at the end of an expression the position after the last character, directly before the line end. So ^d matches only lines that begin with d, ,28 only empty lines. The word comes from the picture of an anchor that fastens the expression to one end of the line. Without , the two runs under 30 minutes remain. The file has no empty lines. Both files contain the line with ,28 . In windows.csv , however, the carriage return from subsection 1.4 textdaten datensatze felder und zeilenenden.html stufe 1 4 still stands between 28 and the line end. The last character of the line is therefore not an 8 , and with at the end of the line; both match positions, not characters. A character, a selection, a position with these, you can write expressions of fixed length. This section adds repetitions, groups and alternatives, shows the two notations in which they exist and explains three peculiarities which match wins, why an expression checks only the form and how regular expressions differ from file name patterns. Any number of times the star Numbers have different numbers of digits, names different numbers of letters. An expression therefore needs a way to say “any number of these”. A star after an ordinary character, a dot or a bracket expression matches any number of repetitions of it in a row, including none at all. So a matches the empty string, a , aa , aaa and so on. . matches any sequence of characters; it is the usual way to write “and anything in between”. The first expression requires, from the start to the end, any number of a's and then a b; b alone matches with zero a's. The second looks for lines in which 5.0 follows somewhere after Anna . a matches in every line, even in b , because every line contains the empty string, that is, zero a's. An expression that consists of nothing but one element with a star therefore searches for nothing; only anchors or fixed characters next to it give it a hold. ⁠ In short x means “any number of x, including none”; . matches any sequence of characters. The extended form grep E For “at least one digit” or “exactly three digits”, there are special characters of their own. An attempt without preparation goes wrong, though Without an option, grep finds nothing; with E , it finds the run of 128 minutes. There are two notations for regular expressions; Figure 22 abb 22 shows how they read the same text differently. This group appears four times, three times with a dot. The expression is correct, but hardly readable anymore; for such checks, you are better off with a tool that calculates with numbers. From there, the longest match wins, up to the last a in Clara . b n matches at every position, if need be with zero n's. grep selects lines, tr replaces single characters. Often, however, you want to transform whole pieces of a line a date into German notation, commas into semicolons, two fields swapped. This section shows a tool that edits lines as they pass through, substitutes with regular expressions, selects and deletes lines and, if needed, changes the file itself. The stream editor sed You operate a text editor such as nano from Chapter 3 /wissen/en/informatik/linux und kommandozeile/dateien verzeichnisse und pfade/dateien verzeichnisse und pfade.html by hand place the cursor, type, save. For a hundred identical changes in a thousand lines, that is too tedious. An editor without a screen that applies the same commands to every line of a stream does this in one go. Figure 26 abb 26 shows how it proceeds. The cycle of sed a line comes from the input into a buffer. The commands run over the buffer one after another, here s/,/;/ the first comma becomes a semicolon. Then the buffer is output and the next line is fetched. The file being read stays gray and unchanged. The command sed , short for “stream editor”, reads its input line by line. It puts each line into a buffer, applies to it, one after another, the commands that are in its first argument after the options, and then writes out the buffer. It does not change the files it reads. The first argument is put in single quotes because it usually contains regular expressions. Without file names, sed reads its standard input; it is therefore a filter. In every line, the command s/,/;/ has replaced the first comma with a semicolon. laeufe.csv itself is unchanged. ⁠ In short sed applies its commands to every line of a stream and writes out the result without changing the file. Substituting the s command The most important command of sed searches the line with a regular expression and replaces the match. s/expression/replacement/ replaces the first match of the regular expression in every line with the replacement text. With the flag g after it, s/expression/replacement/g , it replaces all matches in the line. An & in the replacement text stands for the match found. Instead of the slash, any other character except the backslash and the newline may separate the three parts. Without an option, sed uses the basic form from subsection 7.5 regulare ausdrucke wiederholungen gruppen und alternativen.html stufe 7 5 , with E the extended form. The rule of the longest match from subsection 7.6 regulare ausdrucke wiederholungen gruppen und alternativen.html stufe 7 6 applies to the match. With g , all commas become semicolons, just as a spreadsheet program set to German expects. 0 9 0 9 is “one digit and any number of further ones” in the basic form; & puts the number found in square brackets. In the last command, vertical bars separate the parts because the slashes themselves are to be replaced. ⁠ In short s/expression/replacement/ replaces the first match per line, with g all of them; & is the match itself. Selecting lines line addresses, n and p Not every change should affect every line only the header line, only Ben's runs, only lines 2 to 4. Besides, sed can not only change lines but also select them, like grep , head or tail . Figure 27 abb 27 shows four ways of selecting lines. The ten lines of the running log, four times side by side. With 2,4 , lines 2 to 4 light up, with for the last line, /expression/ for all lines with a match or two line addresses with a comma in between for all lines from the one to the other. Without a line address, a command acts on every line. The option n turns off the output after each line; then only the command p writes out lines. So sed n '2,4p' writes only lines 2 to 4. Without n , they would appear twice, once through p and once through the ordinary output. The first three commands do what head with tail , grep and tail n 1 do. In the last one, the substitution acts only on lines with Ben ; the others pass through unchanged. ⁠ In short A line address such as 3 , $ , /expression/ or 2,4 limits a command to certain lines; n with p outputs only these. Deleting lines the d command The counterpart of selecting is leaving out the header line, all runs of one person. The command d deletes the buffer, outputs nothing and starts immediately with the next line. With a line address in front of it, exactly the selected lines drop out of the stream. The deletion happens only in the stream, not in the file. sed '1d' does the same as tail n +2 , sed '/Anna/d' the same as grep v Anna . ⁠ In short d drops the selected lines from the stream; 1d removes the header line. The command q ends sed after the current line has been output. sed 3q therefore writes the first three lines and stops reading, like head n 3 Because sed does not read any further after that, this is fast even with huge files. Groups and backreferences The date in the running log is written as 2026 11 02 ; if you want it in German date notation, 02.11.2026 , you have to insert parts of the match again in a different order. Figure 28 abb 28 shows how that works. At the top, the date 2026 11 02 and the expression ^ 0 9 {4} 0 9 {2} 0 9 {2} . The three groups each color one piece of the date 2026 as 1, 11 as 2, 02 as 3. At the bottom, the replacement \3.\2.\1 the colored pieces move to their places in the new order, with dots in between. The result is 02.11.2026 . Each group of an expression remembers the piece it matched. In the replacement text of s , a backreference \1 to \9 inserts the piece of the first to the ninth group; the opening parentheses are counted from the left. In the extended form, with sed E , you write the groups with plain parentheses. The header line contains no date, so there is no match, and it stays as it was. In the second command, ^, is a field, a sequence of characters without a comma; the first two fields swap places, in every line, including the header line. ⁠ In short Groups remember their matches, and \1 to \9 insert them again in the replacement text in any order. In the basic form, every parenthesis and curly brace needs a backslash, and the command becomes hard to read Backreferences work not only in the replacement text but also in the expression itself. \ .\ \1 means any single character and then the same character once more. Which name contains a double letter? Such an expression has to remember what it has read, and that is exactly what a finite automaton from subsection 7.7 regulare ausdrucke wiederholungen gruppen und alternativen.html stufe 7 7 cannot do. Backreferences in the expression therefore go beyond regular expressions in the mathematical sense. The standard for Unix tools knows them only in the basic form; GNU grep and sed also allow them in the extended form. The GNU grep manual warns that they can slow down a search considerably. Editing the file itself sed i So far, sed has written only to standard output. If you want the result in the file, redirecting into the same file seems the obvious choice. sed 's/Ben/Benjamin/' kopie.csv kopie.csv leaves an empty file the shell empties kopie.csv for the redirection before sed starts, and sed then has nothing left to read. This is the truncation trap from Chapter 4, Section 2.7 /wissen/en/informatik/linux und kommandozeile/strome umleitung pipes und exit status/ausgaben umleiten.html stufe 2 7 ; it applies to every tool, not just to sed . With the option i , sed writes the result not to standard output but into a new file and then replaces the file it has read with this new file. If an extension follows directly after i , such as i.bak , sed keeps the old version under the name with this extension. The “i” stands for “in place”. Figure 29 abb 29 shows why nothing is lost in the process. sed i on the file kopie.csv sed reads the old file line by line and writes each edited line into a new file next to it; the old file stays unchanged in the meantime. Only at the end does the new file take over the name kopie.csv , and the old one disappears. sed writes nothing to the terminal; the three changes are in the file. With an extension, the old version is kept With two files, head writes the name above each one. The header line is now missing from kopie.csv ; the backup still has it. sed i changes the file without asking and without a trash to restore it from. A typo in the expression can delete or destroy lines. So try a command without i first, look at the output, and only then add i or i.bak . ⁠ In short sed i writes the result into a new file that replaces the old one; i.bak keeps the old version. A redirection into the same file, by contrast, empties it. The fact that sed i creates a new file has a consequence for hard links from Chapter 3, Section 8.3 /wissen/en/informatik/linux und kommandozeile/dateien verzeichnisse und pfade/inode und links.html stufe 8 3 . If you give a fresh copy a second name and then change the file with sed i , the change applies only under the one name Before, both names pointed to the same inode; the link count was 2. sed i created a new file and gave it the name kopie.csv ; zweitname.csv German for “second name” still points to the old, unchanged inode, and both counts are now 1. For symbolic links from Chapter 3, Section 8.5 /wissen/en/informatik/linux und kommandozeile/dateien verzeichnisse und pfade/inode und links.html stufe 8 5 , the GNU sed manual explicitly names the same consequence without a further option, sed i replaces the link with a regular file, and the target of the link stays unchanged. Exercises for Section 8 stufe 8 A spreadsheet program set to German expects semicolons and no header line. a Produce this version with two calls of sed in a pipeline. b Produce it with a single call; you separate several commands in the first argument with a semicolon. c In addition, swap date and name, as in the example on backreferences. a The first sed deletes the header line, the second replaces all commas. b Both commands in one call for each line, sed carries them out in turn; for line 1, d ends the work on this line before s gets its turn. head n 3 only shortens the display. c The order of the commands matters first swap while commas still separate the fields, then replace the commas. The other way around, the expression with ^, would no longer find any commas and would take the whole line as one field. Use sed E to convert the date into the notation 02.11.26 with a two digit year. Which groups do you need, and which part of the year belongs in no group? Three groups the last two digits of the year, the month and the day. The first two digits of the year, 20 , must belong to the match so that they are replaced as well and disappear, but they are in no group, because they do not occur in the result. The header line stays, because it does not begin with digits. Copy laeufe.csv to probe2.csv . Predict what the file contains after sed n i 's/Ben/B./p' probe2.csv , and check it. Why is this combination dangerous? Only the three changed lines remain in the file; the other seven are lost. n switches off the ordinary output; only p writes, and only for lines in which s has replaced something. Without i , this would be a convenient way to look at only the changed lines. With i , exactly this output ends up in the file, and all other lines are gone. The manual of GNU sed explicitly warns against this combination; it is one reason to add i only once the command without i outputs what you want.

How many kilometers were run in total, how far did each person run on average, how fast was each run? For this, you have to calculate with fields, including decimal numbers, and collect values separately for each person. This section shows a tool that is built for exactly this a small language for columns and sums. The program awk condition and action grep selects lines, cut fields, sed transforms. So far, only the shell has calculated, and only with integers. A tool that selects lines, knows fields and calculates combines all three tasks. Figure 30 abb 30 shows how it applies a program made of rules to a file. On the left, an awk program with two rules, /Clara/ {print "Clara ist gelaufen"} and {print "Zeile gelesen"} German for “Clara went running” and “line read” . On the right, the lines arrive one after another. For each line, both rules are checked from the top if the condition matches, the rule lights up and its action writes a line to the output; the second rule, with no condition, lights up for every line. The command awk runs a small program that is in its first argument after the options. The program consists of rules of the form condition {action} . awk reads its input line by line and checks every rule for each line in turn if the condition is met, it carries out the action. If the condition is missing, the rule applies to every line; if the action is missing, awk writes out the line. A simple condition is a regular expression between slashes; it is met if the line contains a match. awk uses the extended form for this. The action print writes something out, text in double quotes. The whole program is put in single quotes so that the shell changes nothing in it. Without an action, awk works like grep . With an action, it writes the fixed text for each matching line. ⁠ In short An awk program consists of rules condition {action} , which awk applies to every line. awk was created in 1977 at Bell Labs, where Unix was also developed. The name consists of the initials of the last names of its three developers, Alfred Aho, Peter Weinberger and Brian Kernighan. It shares the idea “first select lines, then do something with them” with the line addresses of sed ; unlike sed , it has had variables, calculations and fields built in from the start. There are several implementations of the same language. On the test system, awk is the GNU implementation gawk; some systems come with the leaner implementation mawk instead. All examples in this chapter give the same results with both. Fields 0 , NF and F What distinguishes awk from grep and sed it splits every line into fields on its own, without your having to ask. Figure 31 abb 31 shows how you address these fields. The line 2026 11 08,Ben,21.1,128 with F, . Above the four fields appear their names 2 , 4 ; an arc over the whole line carries NF points to the same field as 1 , 0 is the whole line, and NF contains the number of fields, so 1 Chapter 5, Section 3.5 /wissen/en/informatik/linux und kommandozeile/wie die shell eine befehlszeile liest expansion quoting variablen umgebung/worttrennung und quoting.html stufe 3 5 . print with several values separated by commas writes them with a space in between. Without F , awk splits the sentence at the spaces, no matter how many there are, into four fields. You check that every line of the running log has exactly four fields like this ⁠ In short NF are the fields of a line, 2 == "Anna" . Three runs over 10 km. In the second program, field 2 matches “begins with A or B”, and awk writes the line number and the name. Without NR 1 , the header line appears. Its field 3 is km , not a number; awk therefore compares as text, km with 10 , and because k comes after 1 in the character order, km is “greater”. ⁠ In short NR is the line number; conditions compare fields with numbers or text and are combined with && , || and . Variables, sums and END For a sum, awk has to remember something from line to line and output the result at the end, when all lines have been read. It can also calculate with decimal numbers Minutes divided by kilometers gives the pace, minutes per kilometer on 2 November, Anna needed 5.6 minutes for each kilometer. A variable in awk is a name made of letters, digits and underscores, without a 3 adds field 3 to s , n++ increases n by 1. A rule with the condition END is carried out once after the last line has been read, one with BEGIN once before the first one is read. A semicolon separates several statements in an action. For neat output, there is printf with a format, like the shell's printf from Chapter 5, Section 3.1 /wissen/en/informatik/linux und kommandozeile/wie die shell eine befehlszeile liest expansion quoting variablen umgebung/worttrennung und quoting.html stufe 3 1 %d stands for an integer, %.2f for a decimal number with two digits after the point, and you write the newline yourself as \n . Together, the three ran 80.2 km in nine runs, on average 8.91 km. For Anna km im Mittel aus 4 Läufen is German for “km on average over 4 runs” , awk counts only the lines whose field 2 is exactly Anna ; this excludes the header line automatically. Figure 32 abb 32 recalculates her mean. Anna's mean distance . First the sum grows step by step, 5.0, 11.4, 23.4, 28.4; then it is divided by the number of runs . ⁠ In short awk variables collect values over all lines and start at 0; END outputs the result after the last line, printf formats it. Collecting values by name associative arrays Calculating the means for each person separately would mean running the program once each for Anna, Ben and Clara. With a hundred people, that no longer works. You need a variable that holds many values under different names. Figure 33 abb 33 shows how it fills up during reading. On the left, the records come in one after another. On the right, a table with the columns key, s and n . Anna's first run creates the row Anna with 5.0 and 1, Ben's the row Ben, Clara's the row Clara; every further run increases the values in the row of its name. At the end, the table shows Anna 28.4 and 4, Ben 36.6 and 3, Clara 15.2 and 2. An associative array is a variable in awk that stores any number of values, each under a key of its own s "Anna" is the value under the key Anna . The key may be any text, including a field such as 2 ; this is how awk collects sums and counters per group in a single pass. Both ways count the runs per person. sort | uniq c first has to order all lines so that identical names stand next to each other; for this, sort holds on to all lines or moves them out to temporary files. awk reads each line exactly once and remembers only one counter per key; its memory grows with the number of different names, not with the number of lines. On the other hand, an associative array has no order internally, awk distributes the keys so that it can find each one again quickly, and for k in s goes through them in this internal arrangement. The gawk manual states explicitly that you cannot rely on this order. A sort afterward therefore provides ordered output, and it only has to deal with one line per person. Create a frequency table of these shells. a Unlike cut , awk writes the fields in any order you like. b Every line has seven fields; sort u leaves only one value. c 160 / 4 = 40.0 221 / 3 \approx 73.7 85 / 2 = 42.5 4 100' laeufe.csv , b awk F, 'NR 1 && 2 "B"' laeufe.csv . Now the whole toolbox is ready. This section shows which tool fits which part of a question, how to build an analysis step by step without getting lost and, with a famous pipeline, how little you need for a surprisingly difficult question. Which tool for what A text file with records is a table. The tools in this chapter differ in what they do with this table. Figure 34 abb 34 arranges them accordingly. The running log as a table. grep and sed n pick out whole lines; cut one column; sort puts the lines in a new order; tr and sed change characters in the cells; uniq c and awk turn many lines into a few result lines. Each tool appears with its effect on the same table. You select lines by content with grep , by number with head , tail or sed n . You select columns with cut or awk . tr replaces characters, sed parts of lines. sort takes care of ordering, sort | uniq c of counting identical lines. awk takes care of calculating with fields and collecting per group. awk can do almost all of this on its own; still, for simple subtasks, you reach for the simple tool because the command is shorter and readable at a glance. ⁠ In short For every part of a question, there is a suitable small tool; awk is the most versatile, but not always the simplest. Building a pipeline step by step Who ran the farthest in total, and who was the fastest? For questions like these, you do not write the pipeline down in one go; you build it stage by stage and check after each stage whether the intermediate result is correct. Build an analysis stage by stage. After each new stage, look at the intermediate result, with head for long outputs. Save an intermediate result that several questions need in a file. Step 1 without the header line, take a quick look. Step 2 add up kilometers and minutes per person, save them sorted in a file. Step 3 the pace, minutes per kilometer. summen.txt German for “sums” separates with spaces, so no F . Step 4 sort twice, depending on the question. Ben ran the farthest with 36.6 km; Clara was the fastest on average with 5.59 minutes per kilometer. Without t , sort splits at spaces, which suits tempo.txt German for “pace” . ⁠ In short A pipeline grows stage by stage, every intermediate result is checked, and whatever is needed more than once goes into a file. Counting words a famous pipeline Which words occur most often in a text? The question sounds like a program of its own with a dictionary and counters. With the tools in this chapter, one line is enough. As the text, we use the license GPL 3 from Chapter 3, Section 4.3 /wissen/en/informatik/linux und kommandozeile/dateien verzeichnisse und pfade/dateien ansehen.html stufe 4 3 , which is present on every Ubuntu system. First, the text has to become a list with one word per line. For this, tr with c takes the complement of the first set, that is, everything except letters, and s squeezes repetitions. Every sequence of characters that are not letters thus becomes a single newline The first line is empty because the license begins with spaces. Then come the words, one per line. The rest is the frequency table from subsection 3.6 sortieren und zahlen sort und uniq.html stufe 3 6 , with a tr beforehand that turns all uppercase letters into lowercase the occurs 345 times in the license. Each stage of this pipeline does one small job separating the words, converting to lowercase, sorting, counting, sorting by count, keeping the first five. None of them knows anything about words or licenses. ⁠ In short Six small tools in a pipeline answer a question for which you would otherwise write a whole program. This pipeline is famous. In the journal Communications of the ACM, Jon Bentley wrote the column “Programming Pearls”. For an installment in 1986, he asked the computer scientist Donald Knuth for a program that outputs the most frequent words of a text. Knuth wrote a carefully explained program several pages long with an ingenious data structure, entirely from scratch. Doug McIlroy, from whom the idea of the pipe from Chapter 4 /wissen/en/informatik/linux und kommandozeile/strome umleitung pipes und exit status/stroeme umleitung pipes und exit status.html comes, was to review it. He acknowledged the careful presentation and set six lines of shell beside it, essentially the pipeline above, only with sed and its command q instead of head at the end. His point was the Unix philosophy from Chapter 4, Section 4.5 /wissen/en/informatik/linux und kommandozeile/strome umleitung pipes und exit status/pipes und filter.html stufe 4 5 instead of programming everything anew, you connect existing small tools that read and write text, and you are often done within a few minutes. For further practice. The freely accessible learning platform pwn.college offers short exercises in the browser under the name “Linux Luminarium”; the module “Data Manipulation” matches this chapter. A table as text consists of records, one per line, and fields, separated by a separator; a CSV file separates with commas and often has a header line. Windows puts a carriage return before every newline, which cat A shows as ^M and tr d '\r' removes. tail n +2 removes the header line, tail f follows a growing file. cut d, f2 cuts out fields, tr replaces or deletes characters, paste puts columns side by side. sort compares character by character, n by numeric value, t, k3,3 by one field; the locale determines the order, LC ALL=C makes it the same everywhere. uniq compares only neighbors; sort | uniq c | sort rn counts frequencies. nl numbers lines, seq generates sequences of numbers, diff uses a , c and d to show what differs between two files. grep writes the lines with a match; i v c n o r l change what it searches for and what it outputs.
